title: Preface
content:
Preface This volume is analysis on the real line: sequences and series, limits and continuity, the derivative, the integral, and power series. It starts from a short list of axioms for the real numbers, the axioms of a complete ordered field, and proves everything else from them. Who it is for. The reader we have in mind can already read and write proofs: negate a quantified statement, name a witness, run an induction, chase an element through a preimage. Logic and Proof and the first three chapters of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality teach exactly these skills, and this volume cites them where it uses them. A reader who comes from elsewhere can test their readiness with Gate 0, the examination at the end of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 3. Number Systems: From 
N to 
R builds 
R from the rationals and proves that the axioms hold for it; this volume does not need that construction, since it takes the axioms as its starting point. What it covers. Chapter Title --------- ----------------------------------------------------------- 1 Ordered Fields and the Least Upper Bound Axiom 2 Sequences, Subsequences, and Cauchy Sequences 3 Infinite Series 4 Open, Closed, and Compact Subsets of 
R 5 Limits of Functions and Continuity 6 Continuous Functions on Compact Sets and Intervals 7 The Derivative and the Mean Value Theorem 8 The Riemann–Darboux Integral 9 Sequences and Series of Functions 10 Power Series, Taylor Series, and the Elementary Functions 11 The Forms of Completeness Chapter 1 states the axioms and draws the first consequences of the one that separates 
R from 
Q, the least upper bound axiom. Chapters 2–10 build the analysis of one real variable on it. Chapter 11 returns to the axiom and shows which other “no gaps” properties could replace it. Only Chapter 1 is written so far; the others will follow in the order of the table. How to read it. Read the chapters in order: each uses the ones before it. Every section has Quick checks with folded answers; answer each one before you unfold it. The exercises of a section come in three groups, A to check understanding, B for practice and C to go deeper, and the last section of each chapter adds R items that reach back to earlier chapters. A chapter’s opening page lists what it needs, with links, and the time it takes. Results marked optional can be skipped, and nothing outside them depends on them. What else you need. Besides the two volumes named above, only school algebra is assumed. A few facts about fields are quoted from the companion Linear Algebra book, each with a link.

title: Ordered Fields and the Least Upper Bound Axiom
content:
Ordered Fields and the Least Upper Bound Axiom Calculus is full of theorems that feel too obvious to need proof. A continuous function that is negative at one end of an interval and positive at the other must vanish somewhere in between. An increasing sequence that stays below some fixed number must settle down to a limit. Both statements are false if “number” means “rational number”. The polynomial x^2 - 2 is negative at 1 and positive at 2, yet no rational x makes it zero, because \sqrt 2 is irrational (@fd1:thm-sqrt2-irrational). The rational numbers 1, 1.4, 1.41, 1.414, 1.4142, \dots, each the largest decimal of its length whose square is below 2, increase and never pass 1.5; yet there is no rational number for them to approach, since its square would have to be 2. The rational line has a gap where \sqrt 2 should be, and calculus falls into it. This chapter finds the one property that separates the real numbers from the rationals: in 
R, every nonempty set that is bounded above has a least upper bound. We take this property as an axiom and learn to use it. The main tool is a test for recognizing a least upper bound using small positive numbers \varepsilon, which will be used throughout the book. From the axiom we derive the first facts that the rationals lack or that need the axiom: the natural numbers are unbounded, the rationals are dense, positive numbers have square roots and n-th roots, nested closed intervals always share a point, and the real numbers cannot be listed. We do not construct 
R here. Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 5 builds it from 
Q by Cauchy sequences and proves the axiom as a theorem, as the optional Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 7 does by Dedekind cuts; Chapter 11 of this volume shows that several other “no gaps” properties are equivalent to it. What you need. From Logic and Proof, Chapter 1: proof by cases (@fd1:def-rules-disjunction). From Logic and Proof, Chapter 2: the irrationality of \sqrt 2 (@fd1:thm-sqrt2-irrational), the rules for negation (@fd1:def-rules-negation), and the contrapositive (@fd1:prp-contrapositive). From Logic and Proof, Chapters 3–5, and Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapters 1–3: induction (@fd1:ax-induction), quantifiers and how to negate them (Logic and Proof, Chapter 4), sets and images of sets (Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 1), the well-ordering of 
N, definition by recursion, and the arithmetic of 
N and 
Z (Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 2), and countable sets (Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 3). No linear algebra is needed. The elementary rules of field arithmetic are either cited from the linear-algebra companion, Chapter 0, whose field axioms are ours, or proved in the first section. Time. About 30 hours on the core track (all of A, one B, and one C per section, the exit checks); about 45 hours for everything. Roadmap - Ordered fields and the gap in the rationals. The axioms that 
Q and 
R share, the rules for inequalities they imply, and absolute value with the triangle inequality. - Upper bounds, maxima and suprema. The vocabulary for sets of numbers, and a proof that a bounded set of rationals can have no rational supremum. - The least upper bound axiom. The single assumption that distinguishes 
R from 
Q, and why infima then come free. - Working with the supremum. The \varepsilon characterization of the supremum, sup approximation, and the rules for suprema of scaled sets and sums. - The Archimedean property. Where 
N sits in 
R, and the Archimedean property: 
N is not bounded above, which fails in some ordered fields. - Density of 
Q and the existence of roots. A rational between any two reals, and \sqrt 2 (and every n-th root) constructed as a supremum. - Nested intervals, and why 
R is uncountable. Shrinking closed intervals share a point, and no list contains every real number. Named moves - Split the supremum into its two properties. To prove s = \sup A, prove that s is an upper bound, and then that it is the least one. - Sup approximation. “\sup A - \varepsilon is not an upper bound, so some a \in A exceeds it.” With \varepsilon =  rac1n this gives a_n \in A with a_n > \sup A -  rac1n. - Equality of suprema by two inequalities. Prove \le by exhibiting an upper bound, then prove \ge with an \varepsilon, splitting the budget as \varepsilon/2 + \varepsilon/2 when two sets are involved. - Construct a point as a supremum. Define the set of points where “things are still fine”, take its supremum, and rule out each way it could fail. The existence of \sqrt 2 is the first instance; the intermediate value theorem and the Heine–Borel theorem are proved the same way.

title: 1.1 Ordered Fields and the Gap in the Rationals
content:
Ordered Fields and the Gap in the Rationals Calculus takes for granted that a continuous curve which starts below the axis and ends above it must cross the axis somewhere. Over the rational numbers that is false, and the failure is already visible in the simplest polynomial one can think of. This section shows the failure, then records exactly what the rationals and the reals have in common: the arithmetic of a field and an order compatible with it. Everything in this section holds in both. The one property that separates them is the subject of the rest of the chapter. A sign change with no zero Consider f(x) = x^2 - 2 on the rational numbers between 1 and 2. At the left end f(1) = -1 < 0, and at the right end f(2) = 2 > 0. If the rational line had no holes, the graph would have to cross zero somewhere in between. It never does: a rational x with f(x) = 0 would be a rational number whose square is 2, and @fd1:thm-sqrt2-irrational says there is none. So the rational numbers have a gap, exactly where \sqrt{2} ought to be. The real numbers are meant to be “the rationals with the gaps filled”, and the first task is to say what that means precisely. Before we can name what 
R has and 
Q lacks, we must list what the two share. That list is short: four operations with the usual rules, and a way of comparing two numbers that respects those operations. Ordered fields A field is a number system in which one can add, subtract, multiply, and divide by anything nonzero, with the usual rules. The rational, real, and complex numbers are fields; so is the arithmetic of remainders modulo a prime. What 
Q and 
R have beyond this, and 
C does not, is an order: any two numbers can be compared, and the comparison behaves well under addition and multiplication. Every inequality we manipulate in analysis rests on four rules about that comparison, and the definition below states them. An ordered field is a number system where we can do arithmetic and compare, and where comparison respects arithmetic. [Ordered Field] An ordered field consists of a set F, two operations, addition (a, b) \mapsto a + b and multiplication (a, b) \mapsto ab, and a relation < on F, such that the following hold. The field axioms: for all a, b, c \in F, 1. a + b = b + a; 2. (a + b) + c = a + (b + c); 3. there is an element 0 \in F with a + 0 = a for every a \in F; 4. for every a \in F there is an element -a \in F with a + (-a) = 0; 5. (ab)c = a(bc); 6. ab = ba; 7. there is an element 1 \in F with 1 
e 0 and a \cdot 1 = a for every a \in F; 8. for every nonzero a \in F there is an element a^{-1} \in F with a a^{-1} = 1; 9. a(b + c) = ab + ac. The order axioms: for all a, b, c \in F, 1. (trichotomy) exactly one of a < b, a = b, b < a holds; 2. (transitivity) if a < b and b < c, then a < c; 3. (addition) if a < b, then a + c < b + c; 4. (multiplication) if 0 < a and 0 < b, then 0 < ab. The field axioms are the ones of the linear-algebra companion, Chapter 0, in the same numbering. We write a - b \coloneqq a + (-b) and a / b \coloneqq a b^{-1} for b 
e 0. We write b > a to mean a < b, and a \le b to mean “a < b or a = b”. An element a is positive if a > 0 and negative if a < 0. It is nonnegative if a \ge 0. In words, the four order axioms say: - (O1) any two elements can be compared, and the three outcomes exclude one another. In particular a < a never holds. - (O2) comparisons chain. - (O3) adding the same thing to both sides of a strict inequality keeps it strict and keeps its direction. - (O4) the product of two positive elements is positive. This is the only axiom that links the order to multiplication, and every rule about multiplying inequalities will come from it. From (O1) and (O2), the relation \le is transitive as well, and a mixed chain a \le b < c gives a < c: if a = b this is the hypothesis b < c, and otherwise it is (O2). Field algebra. The field axioms alone imply the familiar algebraic identities. Their proofs use no order at all. Most of them are already proved in the linear-algebra companion, from the same axioms, and we cite those; the few that are not there are short, and we prove them here. [Field Algebra] Let F be an ordered field (only (F1)–(F9) are used) and let a, b \in F. 1. The elements 0 and 1 are unique, and so are -a and, for a 
e 0, a^{-1}. In particular -(-a) = a. 2. a \cdot 0 = 0. 3. (-a)b = -(ab) and (-a)(-b) = ab. 4. If ab = 0, then a = 0 or b = 0. 5. (a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2, where x^2 \coloneqq xx and 2 \coloneqq 1 + 1. Each identity is forced by uniqueness. An element is pinned down by the equation it satisfies, so to show that (-a)b is -(ab), we show that it satisfies the equation defining -(ab), namely that it adds to ab to give 0. Part (a) is the uniqueness, and the other parts use it. (a), (b) and (d). Apart from -(-a) = a, these are parts of @la:thm-field-basic-properties: the uniqueness of 0 and of -a; the rule 0 \cdot a = 0, which gives a \cdot 0 = 0 by (F6); and “if ab = 0, then a = 0 or b = 0”. The field axioms there are (F1)–(F9) of @def-ordered-field, in the same numbering, so the proofs there apply verbatim, and we do not repeat them. For -(-a) = a: (-a) + a = 0 by (F1) and (F4), so a is an additive inverse of -a, and -(-a) = a by the uniqueness of additive inverses. The multiplicative halves of (a) are proved the same way. If 1' also satisfies x \cdot 1' = x for every x, then 1 = 1 \cdot 1' = 1' \cdot 1 = 1', by that property of 1', commutativity (F6), and the property of 1. If ab = 1 for some b, then b = b(aa^{-1}) = (ba)a^{-1} = 1 \cdot a^{-1} = a^{-1}, by associativity and commutativity of multiplication; so a^{-1} is unique. (c) By (F6), (F9), (F4) and (b), ab + (-a)b = (a + (-a))b = 0 \cdot b = 0, so (-a)b is an additive inverse of ab, and (-a)b = -(ab) by (a). Using this twice, with (F6), and then (a), (-a)(-b) = -(a(-b)) = -(-(ab)) = ab. (d) By (F9) and (F6), (a + b)(a + b) = a^2 + ba + ab + b^2, and ba + ab = ab \cdot 1 + ab \cdot 1 = ab(1 + 1) = 2ab by (F6), (F7) and (F9). From now on these identities, and the rules of fraction arithmetic that follow from them in the same way, are used without comment. [The rationals and the reals] Explain why 
Q is an ordered field, and what we are assuming when we say 
R is one. For 
Q, the field axioms are the rules of fraction arithmetic. The order is p/q < p'/q' (with q, q' > 0) exactly when pq' < p'q as integers. Trichotomy, transitivity, (O3), and (O4) then come from the corresponding facts about integers. Checking them is routine and belongs to the construction of 
Q from 
Z; here we accept them. For 
R we have not yet said what a real number is, and this chapter deliberately does not. Instead we assume that 
R is an ordered field containing 
Q, with its usual operations and order; in particular 
R contains 
N and 
Z, with their usual arithmetic. (Later in this chapter we locate 
N inside 
R using the axioms alone.) A later section of this chapter completes the list of assumptions by adding exactly one more. Everything proved in this section from (F1)–(F9) and (O1)–(O4) therefore holds in 
Q and in 
R alike. [A minimal change: the integers] The integers 
Z, with the usual operations and order, satisfy (O1)–(O4) and every field axiom except one. Which one fails, and does the failure matter for inequalities? Axiom (F8) fails: 2 
e 0, but no integer m has 2m = 1. Everything else holds, including all four order axioms. So 
Z is not an ordered field, although it is an “ordered ring”. The failure matters as soon as we divide: the rule “if 0 < a < b then 1/b < 1/a” proved below has no meaning in 
Z, because 1/a is not an integer unless a = 1. The two examples mark the scope of the definition. 
Q and 
R are the main examples, and the rest of the section is about what the axioms force in both. The complex numbers are the instructive nonexample, and they appear as the first payoff of the next theorem. Why state the order axioms with the strict relation < rather than with \le? Either could come first, since each can be defined from the other. We take < because analysis constantly asks whether a strict inequality survives an operation. Adding survives (O3); passing to a limit does not: a number that exceeds 1 - \varepsilon for every \varepsilon > 0 is only guaranteed to be \ge 1, not > 1. Keeping < primary keeps that question in view. The rules for inequalities Logic and Proof, Chapters 1 and 2 used facts such as x^2 \ge 0 (in @fd1:exm-square-plus-one) and the sign rules for products (in @fd1:exm-abs-product-cases) as school algebra. We now prove them from (O1)–(O4) and the field axioms. So nothing earlier was circular: those facts were true, and here is why. [Rules for Inequalities] Let F be an ordered field and let a, b, c, d \in F. 1. a < b exactly when b - a > 0, and exactly when -b < -a; in particular a > 0 if and only if -a < 0. 2. If a \le b and c \le d, then a + c \le b + d, and the conclusion is strict if at least one hypothesis is strict. 3. If a < b and c > 0, then ac < bc. 4. If a < b and c < 0, then ac > bc. 5. If a 
e 0, then a^2 > 0. Hence a^2 \ge 0 for every a, and 1 > 0. 6. If a > 0, then 1/a > 0. If 0 < a < b, then 0 < 1/b < 1/a. 7. If a \ge 0 and b \ge 0, then a < b if and only if a^2 < b^2. 8. 2 \coloneqq 1 + 1 is positive, and if a < b, then a <  rac{a + b}{2} < b. Every rule is proved by the same move: turn a comparison into a statement about a single positive element, using (a), and then apply (O3) or (O4) to that element. For instance “a < b and c > 0” becomes “b - a and c are positive”, and (O4) says their product bc - ac is positive. The later parts then lean on the earlier ones, so the proof reads top to bottom. (a) If a < b, then (O3) with c = -a gives a + (-a) < b + (-a), that is, 0 < b - a. Conversely, if 0 < b - a, then (O3) with c = a gives a < b. For the second statement, (-a) - (-b) = b - a, so by what was just shown both a < b and -b < -a are equivalent to b - a > 0. Taking a = 0 and replacing b by a gives: 0 < a if and only if -a < 0. (b) From a \le b we get a + c \le b + c: by (O3) if a < b, and trivially if a = b. In the same way c \le d gives b + c \le b + d, using (F1) to add b on the left. Chaining the two by transitivity gives a + c \le b + d, and if either link is strict the chain is strict. (c) By (a), b - a > 0. Since also c > 0, (O4) gives (b - a)c > 0, that is, bc - ac > 0 by (F9). By (a) again, ac < bc. (d) By (a), -c > 0. Applying (c) with the positive element -c gives a(-c) < b(-c), that is, -(ac) < -(bc). By the second statement of (a), this says bc < ac. (e) Since a 
e 0, trichotomy (O1) leaves two cases. Case 1: a > 0. Then a^2 = a \cdot a > 0 by (O4). Case 2: a < 0. Then -a > 0 by (a), and a^2 = (-a)(-a) > 0 by (O4). So a^2 > 0 whenever a 
e 0, and a^2 = 0 when a = 0; either way a^2 \ge 0. Finally 1 = 1^2 and 1 
e 0 by (F7), so 1 > 0. (f) Let a > 0. Then a^{-1} 
e 0, since otherwise 1 = a a^{-1} = a \cdot 0 = 0, contradicting (F7). Hence (a^{-1})^2 > 0 by (e), and a^{-1} = a \cdot (a^{-1})^2 is a product of two positive elements, so a^{-1} > 0 by (O4). Now let 0 < a < b. Then b > 0 by (O2), so a^{-1} > 0 and b^{-1} > 0, and a^{-1} b^{-1} > 0 by (O4). Multiplying a < b by this positive element, (c) gives a \cdot a^{-1} b^{-1} < b \cdot a^{-1} b^{-1}, which simplifies to b^{-1} < a^{-1}. (g) (\Rightarrow) Suppose 0 \le a < b. Then b > 0 by the mixed chain 0 \le a < b. If a = 0, then a^2 = 0 < b^2 by (e). If a > 0, then (c) applied to a < b, once with the positive factor a and once with the positive factor b, gives a^2 < ab and ab < b^2, so a^2 < b^2 by (O2). (\Leftarrow) Suppose a^2 < b^2. By (O1), either a < b, or a = b, or b < a. If a = b then a^2 = b^2, and if 0 \le b < a then b^2 < a^2 by the forward direction with the roles of a and b swapped. Either conclusion contradicts a^2 < b^2 by (O1). Hence a < b. (h) By (e) and (O3), 1 + 1 > 0 + 1 = 1 > 0, so 2 > 0 by (O2); in particular 2 
e 0 and  rac12 > 0 by (f). If a < b, then (O3) gives a + a < a + b and a + b < b + b, that is, 2a < a + b < 2b, where a + a = (1 + 1)a = 2a by (F9). Multiplying by  rac12 > 0 using (c) gives a <  rac{a + b}{2} < b. This proves the theorem. Three more rules of the same kind are @exr-ordered-fields-b1. With (a)–(h) in hand, every inequality manipulation in this chapter is justified by name. Part (h) looks modest, but it already tells us something structural: between any two elements of an ordered field there is a third, so an ordered field has no “next” element after any given one. The first payoff is a nonexample. The complex numbers form a field, but no relation < on 
C satisfies (O1)–(O4). Indeed, if one did, then i 
e 0 would give i^2 > 0 by (e), that is, -1 > 0. But (e) also gives 1 > 0, and then (a) gives -1 < 0. Having both -1 > 0 and -1 < 0 contradicts trichotomy. So 
C is a field that cannot be ordered, and this is why the book compares real numbers and never complex ones. Inequalities may be added (part (b)) but not freely multiplied. From a \le b and c \le d it does not follow that ac \le bd: take a = c = -3 and b = d = -1. Then a \le b and c \le d, but ac = 9 and bd = 1. Multiplying an inequality needs the sign of the factor, as in (c) and (d), and multiplying two inequalities needs nonnegativity, as in @exr-ordered-fields-b1. The set \{ 0, 1 \}, with addition and multiplication modulo 2, is a field (so 1 + 1 = 0). Can it be made into an ordered field by some choice of <? No. In any ordered field 1 > 0 by @thm-ordered-field-rules (e), and then (O3) gives 1 + 1 > 0 + 1 = 1, so 1 + 1 > 0 by (O2). Here 1 + 1 = 0, so this says 0 > 0, which trichotomy forbids. The argument never used which relation was chosen, so no choice works. Absolute value and distance In analysis, the question is almost never “is x equal to a?” but “how far is x from a?”. An answer should be a nonnegative number that ignores on which side of a the point x lies. The absolute value supplies it. \abs{x} is the size of x with its sign removed, and \abs{x - a} is the distance from x to a. [Absolute Value] Let F be an ordered field. The absolute value of x \in F is \abs{x} \coloneqq  egin{cases} x & 	ext{if } x \ge 0, \ -x & 	ext{if } x < 0. \end{cases} The definition is by cases, and trichotomy guarantees that exactly one case applies, so \abs{x} is well defined. For example \abs{3} = 3, \abs{-3} = -(-3) = 3, and \abs{0} = 0; the degenerate point 0 falls in the first case, and it is the only element of absolute value 0. A minimal change shows that the case split is doing real work: the rule “\abs{x} = x for all x” agrees with the definition on every nonnegative x and fails at every negative one, where it would make \abs{-3} = -3 < 0. The next proposition collects the facts about absolute value that we use constantly. Logic and Proof, Chapter 1 proved some of them by cases (@fd1:exm-triangle-inequality-cases begins with a \le \abs{a} and -a \le \abs{a}), taking the sign rules on trust; the sign rules are now @thm-ordered-field-rules. [Rules for Absolute Value] Let F be an ordered field and let x, y, r \in F. 1. \abs{x} \ge 0, and \abs{x} = 0 if and only if x = 0. 2. \abs{-x} = \abs{x}, \abs{xy} = \abs{x} \abs{y}, and \abs{x}^2 = x^2. 3. -\abs{x} \le x \le \abs{x}. 4. \abs{x} \le r if and only if -r \le x \le r; and \abs{x} < r if and only if -r < x < r. The definition of \abs{x} has two cases, so each part is proved by checking x \ge 0 and x < 0 separately and quoting the sign rules of @thm-ordered-field-rules in each case. Part (d) is the exception. Once (c) is available, (d) needs no new case split for its forward direction. (a) If x \ge 0 then \abs{x} = x \ge 0, with equality exactly when x = 0. If x < 0 then \abs{x} = -x > 0 by @thm-ordered-field-rules (a). (b) If x > 0 then -x < 0, so \abs{-x} = -(-x) = x = \abs{x}; if x < 0 then -x > 0, so \abs{-x} = -x = \abs{x}; and \abs{-0} = \abs{0}. For the product, both \abs{xy} and \abs{x}\abs{y} are one of the two elements xy and -xy, since each absolute value is its argument up to sign. Both are nonnegative: \abs{xy} \ge 0 by (a), and \abs{x}\abs{y} \ge 0 by (O4) when both factors are positive and trivially when one is 0. If xy = 0, both are 0. If xy 
e 0, then exactly one of xy and -xy is positive, by trichotomy and @thm-ordered-field-rules (a), so both must be that one. Either way \abs{xy} = \abs{x}\abs{y}. Finally \abs{x}^2 = (\pm x)^2 = x^2. (c) If x \ge 0, then x = \abs{x}, and -\abs{x} = -x \le 0 \le x. If x < 0, then -\abs{x} = x, and x < 0 < -x = \abs{x}. (d) (\Rightarrow) Suppose \abs{x} \le r. By (c), x \le \abs{x} \le r. Also -r \le -\abs{x} by @thm-ordered-field-rules (a), and -\abs{x} \le x by (c), so -r \le x. (\Leftarrow) Suppose -r \le x \le r. If x \ge 0, then \abs{x} = x \le r. If x < 0, then \abs{x} = -x \le r, because -r \le x gives -x \le r by @thm-ordered-field-rules (a). The strict version is the same argument with < in place of \le wherever r appears. Part (d), applied to x - a in place of x, is the single most used equivalence in this book. Adding a throughout by (O3), it reads \abs{x - a} < r \quad\iff\quad a - r < x < a + r . {#eq-abs-interval} In words: x is within distance r of a exactly when x lies in the open interval of radius r centered at a. Here, for a \le b in F, the intervals are (a, b) \coloneqq \{ x \in F : a < x < b \}, [a, b] \coloneqq \{ x \in F : a \le x \le b \}, and (a, b], [a, b) similarly; in the degenerate case a = b, the closed interval [a, a] = \{ a \} is a single point and the other three are empty; (a, \infty) \coloneqq \{ x \in F : x > a \}, and the other unbounded intervals are defined in the same way. The symbol \infty here is part of the name of a set, not an element of F. From Chapter 2 on, every statement “a_n is close to L” is turned into two inequalities by @eq-abs-interval, and back. [Reading an absolute-value inequality as an interval] Find all real x with \abs{4 - 3x} < 2. By @prp-absolute-value-rules (d), \abs{4 - 3x} < 2 holds if and only if -2 < 4 - 3x < 2. Subtracting 4 throughout (O3) gives -6 < -3x < -2. Multiplying by the negative number - rac13 reverses both inequalities, by @thm-ordered-field-rules (d): 2 > x >  rac23. Every step was an equivalence, so the solution set is the interval \left(  rac23, 2 ight). As a check against @eq-abs-interval: \abs{4 - 3x} = \abs{-3} \abs{x -  rac43} = 3 \abs{x -  rac43} by @prp-absolute-value-rules (b), so the condition says \abs{x -  rac43} <  rac23, the interval of radius  rac23 about  rac43, which is \left(  rac23, 2 ight) again. Distance should satisfy one more law: going from x to z directly is never longer than going via a third point y. For numbers, that law is the triangle inequality. [Triangle Inequality] Let F be an ordered field. For all x, y \in F, 1. \abs{x + y} \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}; 2.  igl| \abs{x} - \abs{y}  igr| \le \abs{x - y} (the reverse triangle inequality). Logic and Proof, Chapter 1 proved (a) in @fd1:exm-triangle-inequality-cases with two case splits: one to show a \le \abs{a} and -a \le \abs{a}, and then one on the sign of x + y. Here the first split is already done, as @prp-absolute-value-rules (c), and the second is not needed. By @prp-absolute-value-rules (d), the goal \abs{x + y} \le \abs{x} + \abs{y} is the pair of inequalities -(\abs{x} + \abs{y}) \le x + y \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}, and these come from adding the two sandwiches -\abs{x} \le x \le \abs{x} and -\abs{y} \le y \le \abs{y}. For (b), write x as (x - y) + y and apply (a). (a) By @prp-absolute-value-rules (c), -\abs{x} \le x \le \abs{x} and -\abs{y} \le y \le \abs{y}. Adding these by @thm-ordered-field-rules (b) gives -(\abs{x} + \abs{y}) \le x + y \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}. By @prp-absolute-value-rules (d) with r = \abs{x} + \abs{y}, this says \abs{x + y} \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}. (b) By (a) applied to x - y and y, \abs{x} = \abs{(x - y) + y} \le \abs{x - y} + \abs{y}, so \abs{x} - \abs{y} \le \abs{x - y}. Swapping the roles of x and y gives \abs{y} - \abs{x} \le \abs{y - x} = \abs{x - y}, using @prp-absolute-value-rules (b). The two inequalities together say -\abs{x - y} \le \abs{x} - \abs{y} \le \abs{x - y}, which is (b) by @prp-absolute-value-rules (d). This proves the theorem. The case-free proof is typical of what the axioms buy: once a fact such as -\abs{x} \le x \le \abs{x} is proved, it can be added, multiplied, and chained without redoing sign cases. The triangle inequality is the engine of every estimate in this volume. Its standard use is “insert a third point”: to bound \abs{x - z}, write x - z = (x - y) + (y - z) for a well-chosen y, and bound the two pieces separately (@exr-ordered-fields-b2). The inequality in (a) can be strict: \abs{1 + (-1)} = 0 < 2 = \abs{1} + \abs{-1}. Equality holds exactly when x and y do not have strictly opposite signs, that is, when xy \ge 0 (@exr-ordered-fields-b2). Comparing by squaring. Two absolute values can often be compared without any case split, by squaring. For nonnegative a and b, @thm-ordered-field-rules (g) says that a < b holds exactly when a^2 < b^2, and @prp-absolute-value-rules (b) gives \abs{u}^2 = u^2. For example, which x satisfy \abs{x - 2} < \abs{x}? Both sides are nonnegative, so the inequality holds if and only if (x - 2)^2 < x^2, that is, x^2 - 4x + 4 < x^2. By (O3) this is 4 < 4x, and multiplying by  rac14 > 0 gives x > 1. Every step was an equivalence, so the solution set is (1, \infty): the points closer to 2 than to 0. Where this leaves us Everything proved so far holds in 
Q and in 
R equally. So none of it can explain why x^2 - 2 has a zero in [1, 2] over 
R and not over 
Q. The difference between the two fields is not arithmetic and not the order rules; it is a property of sets of numbers. The next section introduces the language for that property: upper bounds, maxima, and the least upper bound. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Here is a derivation, in an ordered field, of “if a > 0 and b > 0 then a + b > 0”: from b > 0 we get a + b > a + 0; and a + 0 = a; and a > 0; hence a + b > 0. Name the axiom that justifies each of the four steps. 2. True or false, with a reason: in an ordered field, if a < b then a^2 < b^2. 3. True or false, with a reason: \abs{x} = \max \{ x, -x \} for every x in an ordered field. (Here \max\{ a, b \} is the larger of a and b: it is a if a \ge b, and b otherwise.) 4. The integers satisfy all four order axioms. Why is 
Z not an ordered field? (a) The first step is (O3), adding a to both sides of 0 < b (with (F1) to put a on the left). The second is (F3), the defining property of 0. The third is the hypothesis. The last is transitivity (O2): 0 < a and a < a + b give 0 < a + b. (b) False. Take a = -2 and b = 1: then a < b, but a^2 = 4 > 1 = b^2. @thm-ordered-field-rules (g) needs both numbers nonnegative. (c) True. If x \ge 0, then -x \le 0 \le x, so the larger of x and -x is x = \abs{x}. If x < 0, then x < 0 < -x, so the larger is -x = \abs{x}. (d) Axiom (F8) fails: 2 has no multiplicative inverse in 
Z, since 2m = 1 has no integer solution. B. Practice [B1: Three more rules] Let F be an ordered field and a, b, c, d \in F. Prove the following from the axioms and @thm-ordered-field-rules. 1. If a > 0 and b < 0, then ab < 0. 2. If 0 \le a < b and 0 \le c < d, then ac < bd. 3. If a > 0 and ab > 0, then b > 0. (a) Since b < 0, @thm-ordered-field-rules (a) gives -b > 0. By (O4), a(-b) > 0, that is, -(ab) > 0. By @thm-ordered-field-rules (a) again, ab < 0. (b) Since 0 \le c < d, we have d > 0. From a < b and d > 0, @thm-ordered-field-rules (c) gives ad < bd. From c < d and a \ge 0 we get ac \le ad: by @thm-ordered-field-rules (c) if a > 0, and because both sides are 0 if a = 0. Chaining, ac \le ad < bd, so ac < bd. (c) By trichotomy, b > 0, b = 0, or b < 0. If b = 0 then ab = 0, and if b < 0 then ab < 0 by (a). Both contradict ab > 0 by (O1). Hence b > 0. [B2: Inserting a third point] Let F be an ordered field and x, y, z \in F. 1. Prove that \abs{x - z} \le \abs{x - y} + \abs{y - z}. 2. Prove that \abs{x + y} = \abs{x} + \abs{y} if and only if xy \ge 0. (a) Since x - z = (x - y) + (y - z), @thm-triangle-inequality (a) gives \abs{x - z} \le \abs{x - y} + \abs{y - z}. (b) Both sides are nonnegative, so by @thm-ordered-field-rules (g) they are equal if and only if their squares are equal (apply (g) in both directions and use trichotomy). Using @prp-absolute-value-rules (b), \abs{x + y}^2 = x^2 + 2xy + y^2, \qquad (\abs{x} + \abs{y})^2 = x^2 + 2\abs{xy} + y^2 . These are equal if and only if xy = \abs{xy}, which by the definition of absolute value happens if and only if xy \ge 0. [B3: Solving inequalities] Find all real x satisfying each inequality. Hence write each solution set as an interval. 1. \abs{2x - 3} < 5. 2. \abs{x - 1} < \abs{x + 1}. (a) By @prp-absolute-value-rules (d), the inequality holds if and only if -5 < 2x - 3 < 5. Adding 3 gives -2 < 2x < 8, and multiplying by  rac12 > 0 gives -1 < x < 4. Each step is reversible, so the solution set is (-1, 4). (b) Both sides are nonnegative, so by @thm-ordered-field-rules (g) and @prp-absolute-value-rules (b) the inequality holds if and only if (x - 1)^2 < (x + 1)^2. Expanding, this is x^2 - 2x + 1 < x^2 + 2x + 1, which by (O3) is equivalent to 0 < 4x, and by multiplying with  rac14 > 0 to x > 0. The solution set is (0, \infty): the points closer to 1 than to -1. C. Going deeper [C1: Ordered fields contain the counting numbers] 1. The field \{ 0, 1, 2 \} with arithmetic modulo 3 has 1 + 1 + 1 = 0. Show that it admits no order satisfying (O1)–(O4). 2. In an ordered field F, define n \cdot 1 for n \in 
N by 0 \cdot 1 \coloneqq 0 and (n + 1) \cdot 1 \coloneqq n \cdot 1 + 1. Prove that n \cdot 1 > 0 for every n \in 
N with n \ge 1, and that m \cdot 1 < n \cdot 1 whenever m < n. 3. Deduce that the elements 0, 1, 1 + 1, 1 + 1 + 1, \dots of an ordered field are all different, so every ordered field contains a copy of 
N (and in particular is infinite). Hint: for (b), use induction on n (@fd1:ax-induction). (a) Suppose an order existed. By @thm-ordered-field-rules (e), 1 > 0. By (O3), 1 + 1 > 0 + 1 = 1, so 1 + 1 > 0 by (O2), and again 1 + 1 + 1 > 1 > 0. But 1 + 1 + 1 = 0, so this says 0 > 0, contradicting trichotomy (O1). (b) We prove n \cdot 1 > 0 by induction on n, starting at n = 1. For n = 1, 1 \cdot 1 = 0 \cdot 1 + 1 = 0 + 1 = 1 > 0 by @thm-ordered-field-rules (e). If n \cdot 1 > 0, then by (O3), (n + 1) \cdot 1 = n \cdot 1 + 1 > n \cdot 1, and (O2) gives (n + 1) \cdot 1 > 0. The same step shows (k + 1) \cdot 1 > k \cdot 1 for every k. Now fix m and prove m \cdot 1 < n \cdot 1 for every n > m by induction on n, starting at n = m + 1: the base case is the step just shown with k = m, and if m \cdot 1 < n \cdot 1, then m \cdot 1 < n \cdot 1 < (n + 1) \cdot 1, so (O2) gives m \cdot 1 < (n + 1) \cdot 1. (c) If m 
e n, say m < n, then m \cdot 1 < n \cdot 1 by (b), so m \cdot 1 
e n \cdot 1 by trichotomy. Hence n \mapsto n \cdot 1 is injective from 
N into F, and by (b) it respects order. It also respects addition: (m + n) \cdot 1 = m \cdot 1 + n \cdot 1, by induction on n with m fixed. For n = 0 both sides are m \cdot 1, since 0 \cdot 1 = 0. If it holds for n, then (m + (n + 1)) \cdot 1 = ((m + n) + 1) \cdot 1 = (m + n) \cdot 1 + 1 = m \cdot 1 + n \cdot 1 + 1 = m \cdot 1 + (n + 1) \cdot 1, using the definition twice and (F2). This is the sense in which F contains a copy of 
N. The section on the natural numbers inside 
R, later in this chapter, starts from exactly this copy. [C2: Max and min without cases] Let F be an ordered field and a, b \in F. Write \max\{ a, b \} for the larger of a and b and \min\{ a, b \} for the smaller (as in @exr-ordered-fields-a1). Prove that \max \{ a, b \} =  rac{a + b + \abs{a - b}}{2}, \qquad \min \{ a, b \} =  rac{a + b - \abs{a - b}}{2}. Hence show that \abs{\max\{a, b\} - \max\{c, d\}} \le \max\{ \abs{a - c}, \abs{b - d} \} for all a, b, c, d \in F. Hint: for the last part, bound \max\{a, b\} above by \max\{c, d\} + \max\{ \abs{a - c}, \abs{b - d} \}. If a \ge b, then \abs{a - b} = a - b, so  rac{a + b + \abs{a - b}}{2} =  rac{2a}{2} = a = \max\{a, b\} and  rac{a + b - \abs{a - b}}{2} = b = \min\{a, b\}. If a < b, then \abs{a - b} = b - a, and the same computation gives b and a. By trichotomy these cases cover everything. For the inequality, put m \coloneqq \max\{ \abs{a - c}, \abs{b - d} \}. By @prp-absolute-value-rules (c), a \le c + \abs{a - c} \le \max\{c, d\} + m, and likewise b \le d + \abs{b - d} \le \max\{c, d\} + m. Hence \max\{a, b\} \le \max\{c, d\} + m, that is, \max\{a, b\} - \max\{c, d\} \le m. Swapping the roles of (a, b) and (c, d), which leaves m unchanged, gives \max\{c, d\} - \max\{a, b\} \le m. By @prp-absolute-value-rules (d), the two together say \abs{\max\{a, b\} - \max\{c, d\}} \le m.

title: 1.2 Upper Bounds, Maxima and Suprema
content:
Upper Bounds, Maxima and Suprema The previous section ended with a puzzle. The rationals and the reals obey the same rules of arithmetic and the same rules of order (@def-ordered-field), yet x^2 - 2 has a zero in one (as @thm-sqrt2-exists will prove) and not in the other. The difference lies in how sets of numbers behave: in 
Q, a set can press against a point that is not there. This section builds the vocabulary to say that precisely. Everything happens in an arbitrary ordered field F, because we need to compare F = 
Q with F = 
R, and the definitions must not already take a side. A largest element that is not there Ask for the largest element of the open interval (0, 1) in 
R. There is none. Whatever a \in (0, 1) you propose, the midpoint  rac{a + 1}{2} lies strictly between a and 1 by @thm-ordered-field-rules (h), so it belongs to (0, 1) and beats a. The same happens, less visibly, for the set of positive rationals whose square is less than 2; Case 1 of the proof at the end of this section is the reason, and @exr-suprema-c1 writes it out. And yet both sets are heading somewhere. The interval (0, 1) is pressed against 1: nothing in it reaches 1, and nothing smaller than 1 stays above it. “Largest element” is the wrong notion, because it demands that the target belong to the set. What survives is the smallest number that sits above the whole set. To define it we first need words for “sits above”. Upper and lower bounds Upper and Lower Bounds Let F be an ordered field and A \subseteq F. An element M \in F is an upper bound of A if a \le M for every a \in A. An element m \in F is a lower bound of A if m \le a for every a \in A. In symbols, M is an upper bound of A when  orall a \in A : \ a \le M . The bound is an element of F, and nothing requires it to belong to A. For the interval (0, 1) in 
R, the numbers 1,  rac32, and 2026 are all upper bounds, and 0 and -17 are lower bounds. Upper bounds are never unique: if M is one, so is every M' \ge M, by transitivity. A minimal change gives a nonexample:  rac12 is not an upper bound of (0, 1), because  rac34 \in (0, 1) and  rac34 >  rac12. One element above M is enough to spoil it. Negating the definition quantifier by quantifier (the negation rules are the subject of Logic and Proof, Chapter 4), M 	ext{ is not an upper bound of } A \quad\iff\quad \exists a \in A : \ a > M , where we have used trichotomy to rewrite “not a \le M” as “a > M”. The empty set is the degenerate case, and it will matter. Every M \in F is an upper bound of \emptyset: the condition “a \le M for every a \in \emptyset” has no instances to check, so it holds vacuously. Instance by instance it is the implication “if a \in \emptyset, then a \le M”, whose hypothesis is false, and @fd1:prp-vacuous-implication derives an implication from the negation of its hypothesis. Likewise every element of F is a lower bound of \emptyset. [Bounded Sets] Let F be an ordered field and A \subseteq F. The set A is bounded above if it has at least one upper bound, bounded below if it has at least one lower bound, and bounded if it is both bounded above and bounded below. In symbols, A is bounded above when \exists M \in F \ \  orall a \in A : \ a \le M . The order of the quantifiers carries the meaning. One M is chosen first and must then work for every a. Swap them, to “ orall a \in A \ \exists M \in F : a \le M”, and the statement becomes empty of content: every set satisfies it, since each a can take M = a. Examples in 
R: the interval (0, 1) is bounded; the empty set is bounded (by anything); the interval [0, \infty) is bounded below by 0 but not bounded above. To see the last claim, negate the definition: we must show that for every M \in 
R there is a \in [0, \infty) with a > M. Given M, the element a \coloneqq \max\{ M, 0 \} + 1 works, where \max\{ M, 0 \} is the larger of M and 0 (maxima are defined in general just below): it is at least 1 > 0, so it lies in [0, \infty), and it exceeds M by (O3). The witness a depends on M, as the order  orall M \ \exists a allows. Whether 
N is bounded above in 
R looks like the same kind of question, but it is not. The answer, “no”, is the Archimedean property, and it is proved later in this chapter from the axiom of the next section. It cannot be proved from the ordered-field axioms alone. Maximum and minimum Maximum and Minimum Let F be an ordered field and A \subseteq F. An element m is a maximum (or greatest element) of A if m \in A and m is an upper bound of A. It is a minimum (or least element) of A if m \in A and m is a lower bound of A. A set has at most one maximum. If m and m' are both maxima, then m \in A and m' is an upper bound, so m \le m'; by the same argument with the roles swapped, m' \le m; and trichotomy forces m = m'. So when it exists we may write \max A, and likewise \min A. Examples: the set \{ -1, 3,  rac72 \} has maximum  rac72, since  rac72 is in the set and -1 \le  rac72, 3 \le  rac72,  rac72 \le  rac72. The interval (0, 1] has maximum 1. The minimal change from (0, 1] to (0, 1) keeps every upper bound but removes the only candidate: (0, 1) has no maximum, as the opening subsection showed. The empty set has no maximum, since it has no elements at all. The supremum Here is the notion that survives where “maximum” fails. Look again at (0, 1). Its upper bounds form the set [1, \infty), and that set has a least element, namely 1. The number we want is the least element of the set of upper bounds. The supremum is the upper bound that cannot be lowered. [Supremum] Let F be an ordered field and A \subseteq F. An element s \in F is a supremum (or least upper bound) of A in F if 1. s is an upper bound of A, and 2. s \le M for every upper bound M of A. In symbols, s is a supremum of A in F when  igl(  orall a \in A : \ a \le s  igr) \ 	ext{ and } \  igl(  orall M \in F : \ ( orall a \in A : a \le M) \Rightarrow s \le M  igr). In words: (S1) says that s sits above the whole set. (S2) says that no upper bound sits below s; every upper bound is at least s. So s is an upper bound (S1), and it is the least one (S2). The words “in F” matter: s must be an element of F, and the upper bounds M in (S2) range over F. The same set of rationals can have a supremum when viewed in one field and none when viewed in another, and that is precisely the phenomenon this chapter is about. Before we write “the supremum”, we must know there cannot be two. [Uniqueness of the Supremum] Let F be an ordered field and A \subseteq F. If s and s' are both suprema of A in F, then s = s'. By (S1) for s', the element s' is an upper bound of A. So (S2) for s gives s \le s'. Swapping the roles of s and s' gives s' \le s. By trichotomy, s = s'. The proof is the standard uniqueness move: suppose there are two, use the first property of one against the second property of the other, and then swap. From now on, when A has a supremum in F, we call it the supremum and write \sup A. Existence is a different matter, and nothing so far guarantees it. It can fail in three ways: the set may have no upper bound at all, like [0, \infty) above; it may have no elements; or it may press against a gap in the field. The rest of this section shows the last two. The mirror-image notion comes with its own definition, since we use it as often. [Infimum] Let F be an ordered field and A \subseteq F. An element t \in F is an infimum (or greatest lower bound) of A in F if 1. t is a lower bound of A, and 2. M \le t for every lower bound M of A. The proof of @thm-sup-unique, with every inequality reversed, shows that a set has at most one infimum, written \inf A. The names are Latin: supremum is “the highest”, infimum “the lowest”. [A finite set, and a half-open interval] Find the supremum of A = \{ -1, 3,  rac72 \} and of B = (0, 1] in 
R. For A: the element  rac72 is an upper bound, as checked above, so (S1) holds. For (S2), let M be any upper bound of A. Since  rac72 \in A, the definition of upper bound gives  rac72 \le M. So \sup A =  rac72 = \max A. For B: the same two lines work with 1 in place of  rac72. It bounds (0, 1] from above by the definition of that interval, and it is least because 1 \in B, so every upper bound M satisfies 1 \le M. So \sup B = 1 = \max B. The argument used only that the candidate is a maximum. It shows that a maximum, when it exists, is the supremum (@exr-suprema-b1). Every nonempty finite set has a maximum, by an induction on the number of elements of the kind practiced in Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 2, so for finite sets the supremum is nothing new. [The supremum need not belong to the set] Show that \sup (0, 1) = 1 in 
R, although 1 
otin (0, 1). (S1): every a \in (0, 1) satisfies a < 1, so 1 is an upper bound. (S2): let M be an upper bound of (0, 1); we show 1 \le M. Suppose instead that M < 1. Since  rac12 \in (0, 1), we have  rac12 \le M, so M > 0. By @thm-ordered-field-rules (h), the midpoint a \coloneqq  rac{M + 1}{2} satisfies M < a < 1. Then 0 < M < a < 1, so a \in (0, 1), and a > M. This contradicts M being an upper bound. Hence 1 \le M, by trichotomy. So 1 is the supremum. It is not a maximum, since 1 
otin (0, 1). Nothing in the argument used anything beyond the ordered-field axioms; the same proof shows that \{ x \in 
Q : 0 < x < 1 \} has supremum 1 in 
Q. [A supremum we cannot yet prove] Let A = \{ 1 -  rac1n : n \in 
Z_{>0} \} = \{ 0,  rac12,  rac23,  rac34, \dots \} in 
R, where 
Z_{>0} = \{ 1, 2, 3, \dots \} is the set of positive integers (taken informally for now; later in this chapter, once the natural numbers are defined inside 
R, it becomes a defined subset of 
R). Show that 1 is an upper bound of A and that A has no maximum. Each n \in 
Z_{>0} is positive, so  rac1n > 0 by @thm-ordered-field-rules (f), and hence 1 -  rac1n < 1 by @thm-ordered-field-rules (a). So 1 is an upper bound, and 1 
otin A. No element is a maximum either: 1 -  rac1n < 1 -  rac1{n + 1}, because  rac1{n + 1} <  rac1n by @thm-ordered-field-rules (f), so every element is beaten by the next one. It is true that \sup A = 1, but (S2) is harder than it looks. It says that no M < 1 is an upper bound, that is, for every M < 1 some 1 -  rac1n exceeds M. That requires  rac1n < 1 - M for some n. The existence of such an n says, in effect, that the natural numbers are not bounded above, and that does not follow from the ordered-field axioms. We prove it later in this chapter, from the axiom of the next section, and prove \sup A = 1 right after it. The degenerate case is the empty set. By the vacuous-truth remark above, every element of F is an upper bound of \emptyset. If s were a supremum, then s - 1 would be an upper bound too, and (S2) would give s \le s - 1, that is, 1 \le 0, contradicting 1 > 0. So the empty set has no supremum, although it is bounded above. This is why the axiom of the next section has to say “nonempty”. A nonexample by minimal change shows why both clauses are needed. Keep A = (0, 1). The number 2 satisfies (S1) but fails (S2): the upper bound 1 lies below it. The number  rac12 satisfies (S2), since every upper bound is at least 1 \ge  rac12, but it fails (S1). Drop (S1) from the definition and every number below 1, such as  rac12 or -5, would qualify. Drop (S2) and every upper bound would. Only the two clauses together pin down a single number. The supremum is not the maximum. The supremum of a set need not belong to the set: \sup (0, 1) = 1 
otin (0, 1). The two notions agree exactly when the supremum lies in the set (@exr-suprema-b1). A proof that writes “let a = \sup A \in A” has assumed something false in general; the section on working with the supremum contains a proof that fails for exactly this reason. A bounded set need not have a maximum. The interval (0, 1) is bounded, and it has no greatest element. “Bounded” promises upper bounds, which live outside the set; it promises nothing about the elements themselves. Let A = \{  rac{(-1)^n}{n} : n \in 
Z_{>0} \} = \{ -1,  rac12, - rac13,  rac14, \dots \}. Find \max A and \sup A in 
R, if they exist. Do the same for \min A and \inf A. For odd n the element is - rac1n < 0. For even n \ge 2 it is  rac1n \le  rac12, by @thm-ordered-field-rules (f). So  rac12 is an upper bound, and it is attained at n = 2. Hence \max A =  rac12, and by the argument of @exm-sup-finite-and-closed (a maximum is the supremum), \sup A =  rac12. Similarly, every element is at least -1: even-indexed ones are positive, and odd-indexed ones are - rac1n \ge -1 because  rac1n \le 1. The value -1 is attained at n = 1. So \min A = \inf A = -1. Although A is infinite, both extremes are attained, at its first two elements. A bounded set of rationals with no rational supremum We now prove what the opening section promised: in 
Q, a nonempty set that is bounded above can fail to have a supremum. This is the gap in 
Q, expressed in the language of this section. [No Rational Supremum for the Rationals Below the Square Root of Two] Let A = \{ x \in 
Q : x > 0 	ext{ and } x^2 < 2 \}. Then A is nonempty and bounded above in 
Q, but A has no supremum in 
Q. Suppose a rational s were the supremum. By @fd1:thm-sqrt2-irrational, s^2 
e 2, so s^2 < 2 or s^2 > 2, and each case is a disaster. If s^2 < 2, then s is too small: there is room to step right to a rational s + h whose square is still below 2, and then s + h \in A beats s. To find h, work backwards from the goal (s + h)^2 < 2. Expanding, (s + h)^2 = s^2 + 2sh + h^2. The h^2 is awkward, so bound it by something simpler: if 0 < h \le 1, then h^2 \le h, and (s + h)^2 \le s^2 + h(2s + 1). The room available is 2 - s^2. Asking h(2s + 1) to use only half of it, h(2s + 1) =  rac{2 - s^2}{2}, gives h =  rac{2 - s^2}{4s + 2}. We then owe a check of the condition h \le 1 that we assumed along the way. If s^2 > 2, then s is too big: step left to s - h, still an upper bound, and then s was not the least one. Now (s - h)^2 = s^2 - 2sh + h^2 > s^2 - 2sh, and the right side equals 2 exactly when h =  rac{s^2 - 2}{2s}. In both cases h depends only on s, and it is rational because s is. Before reading on: where does the proof use that s is rational, and where does it use @fd1:thm-sqrt2-irrational? Since 1 > 0 and 1^2 = 1 < 2, we have 1 \in A, so A is nonempty. The rational number 2 is an upper bound: if some x \in A had x > 2, then x^2 > 4 by @thm-ordered-field-rules (g), contradicting x^2 < 2, so x \le 2 by trichotomy. Suppose, for a contradiction, that s \in 
Q is a supremum of A in 
Q. Since 1 \in A, (S1) gives s \ge 1; in particular s > 0, and s^2 \ge 1 by @thm-ordered-field-rules (g). By @fd1:thm-sqrt2-irrational, s^2 
e 2, so by trichotomy either s^2 < 2 or s^2 > 2. Case 1: s^2 < 2. Let h \coloneqq  rac{2 - s^2}{4s + 2} . Then h \in 
Q, and h > 0 because 2 - s^2 > 0 and 4s + 2 > 0. Moreover h \le  rac16, since 2 - s^2 \le 1 (as s^2 \ge 1) and 4s + 2 \ge 6 (as s \ge 1). Hence h \le 1, and multiplying by h > 0 gives h^2 \le h. Therefore  egin{aligned} (s + h)^2 &= s^2 + 2sh + h^2 \ &\le s^2 + h(2s + 1) \ &= s^2 + 	frac{2 - s^2}{2} = 1 + 	frac{s^2}{2} < 2, \end{aligned} where the last inequality holds because s^2 < 2. So s + h is a positive rational with square less than 2, that is, s + h \in A. But s + h > s, so s is not an upper bound of A, contradicting (S1). Case 2: s^2 > 2. Let h \coloneqq  rac{s^2 - 2}{2s} . Then h \in 
Q and h > 0. Also s - h =  rac{s^2 + 2}{2s} > 0, and (s - h)^2 = s^2 - 2sh + h^2 = s^2 - (s^2 - 2) + h^2 = 2 + h^2 > 2 . We claim that s - h is an upper bound of A. Indeed, if some x \in A had x > s - h, then, as s - h > 0, @thm-ordered-field-rules (g) would give x^2 > (s - h)^2 > 2, contradicting x^2 < 2. So s - h is a rational upper bound of A with s - h < s, contradicting (S2). Both cases are impossible. Hence A has no supremum in 
Q. This proves the theorem. Rationality of s was used in exactly two places: to make h, and so s \pm h, rational, which is what membership in A and “upper bound in 
Q” require; and to rule out s^2 = 2 by @fd1:thm-sqrt2-irrational. The logical shape is the same as in the irrationality of \sqrt2: assume the object exists, reach a contradiction, conclude that it does not. To see the constants at work, start from the rational upper bound s =  rac32, whose square  rac94 exceeds 2. Case 2 gives h =  rac{1}{12} and the smaller upper bound s - h =  rac{17}{12}, with ( rac{17}{12})^2 =  rac{289}{144} = 2 +  rac{1}{144}. Starting instead from s = 1 \in A, Case 1 gives h =  rac16, and  rac76 \in A because  rac{49}{36} < 2. Each step can be repeated forever from either side, and no rational number is ever reached at which both processes stop. This is the gap in 
Q in its final form. The next section adds to the ordered-field axioms the single statement that such gaps do not occur in 
R. Later in the chapter, the same two-case argument, with s now a real number supplied by that axiom, proves that \sqrt 2 exists. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] In (a)–(d), give the supremum, infimum, maximum, and minimum of the set in 
R, or say that it does not exist. Justify each answer in a line or two. Parts (e) and (f) are about the proof of @thm-no-rational-sup-sqrt2. 1. \{ -2, 0,  rac73 \}. 2. [-1, 4). 3. \{ x \in 
R : x^2 \le 4 \}. 4. \emptyset. 5. Run Case 2 of the proof on the rational upper bound s =  rac{17}{12}: compute h and s - h, and check that (s - h)^2 > 2. 6. Replace 
Q by 
R throughout the statement and the proof. Which single step of the proof can no longer be justified, and what possibility does it leave open? (a) \max = \sup =  rac73 and \min = \inf = -2: both are elements of the set, and comparing with the three elements shows they are an upper and a lower bound. A maximum is the supremum and a minimum is the infimum (@exr-suprema-b1). (b) \min = \inf = -1, since -1 belongs to the set and is a lower bound. \sup = 4 and there is no maximum: 4 is an upper bound not in the set, and the midpoint argument of @exm-sup-open-interval shows that no M < 4 is an upper bound (if M < 4 is an upper bound, then M \ge -1 and  rac{M + 4}{2} is in the set and exceeds M). (c) The set is [-2, 2]: by @thm-ordered-field-rules (g) applied to \abs{x} and 2, and @prp-absolute-value-rules (b), x^2 \le 4 holds if and only if \abs{x} \le 2, which by @prp-absolute-value-rules (d) means -2 \le x \le 2. So \max = \sup = 2 and \min = \inf = -2. (d) None of the four exists. Every real number is an upper and a lower bound of \emptyset, so there is no least upper bound and no greatest lower bound (as shown in the text), and \emptyset has no elements to be a maximum or minimum. (e) Here s^2 =  rac{289}{144} = 2 +  rac1{144}, so h =  rac{s^2 - 2}{2s} =  rac{1/144}{17/6} =  rac{1}{408}, \qquad s - h =  rac{17}{12} -  rac{1}{408} =  rac{577}{408} . Then (s - h)^2 = 2 + h^2 = 2 +  rac{1}{166464} > 2, as the proof’s display predicts; directly, 577^2 = 332929 = 2 \cdot 408^2 + 1. So  rac{577}{408} is a smaller rational upper bound, and the step can be repeated from it. (f) The step “by @fd1:thm-sqrt2-irrational, s^2 
e 2”. Over 
R nothing rules out s^2 = 2, so after Cases 1 and 2 the possibility s^2 = 2 remains, and no contradiction is reached. Every other step is algebra valid in any ordered field, 
R included. This is exactly the opening that the existence proof for \sqrt2, later in this chapter, walks through. B. Practice [B1: Maxima are suprema] Let F be an ordered field and A \subseteq F. 1. Prove that if A has a maximum m, then m is the supremum of A. 2. Prove that if A has a supremum s and s \in A, then s is the maximum of A. 3. State and prove the corresponding facts for minimum and infimum. (a) By @def-maximum, m is an upper bound of A, which is (S1). For (S2), let M be any upper bound of A. Since m \in A, the definition of upper bound gives m \le M. Hence m is a supremum of A, and by @thm-sup-unique it is the supremum. (b) By (S1), s is an upper bound of A, and s \in A by hypothesis. That is exactly @def-maximum. (c) If A has a minimum m, then m = \inf A; and if \inf A exists and belongs to A, it is the minimum. The proofs are those of (a) and (b) with every inequality reversed: m is a lower bound (I1), and any lower bound M satisfies M \le m because m \in A (I2). [B2: Negating the definitions] Let F be an ordered field and A \subseteq F. 1. Write in symbols the statement “s is not an upper bound of A”. 2. Write in symbols the statement “s is not a supremum of A”, as a disjunction of two statements. 3. Use (b) to show directly that 2 is not the supremum of (0, 1) in 
R, by exhibiting a witness. (a) \exists a \in A : a > s. (b) Negating the conjunction (S1) and (S2) gives: (S1) fails or (S2) fails. So “s is not a supremum of A” is  igl( \exists a \in A : a > s  igr) \ 	ext{ or } \  igl( \exists M \in F : ( orall a \in A : a \le M) 	ext{ and } M < s  igr). The second disjunct says: some upper bound lies strictly below s. (c) The first disjunct fails for s = 2, since every element of (0, 1) is below 2. The second holds with the witness M = 1: it is an upper bound of (0, 1), and 1 < 2. Hence 2 is not the supremum. [B3: A supremum that is approached but not attained] Let A = \{  rac{x}{x + 1} : x \in 
R, \ x > 0 \}. Prove that \sup A = 1 and that A has no maximum. For x > 0, the denominator x + 1 is positive, and x < x + 1; multiplying by  rac{1}{x + 1} > 0 (@thm-ordered-field-rules (c) and (f)) gives  rac{x}{x + 1} < 1. So 1 is an upper bound (S1), and 1 
otin A. For (S2), let M be an upper bound of A, and suppose M < 1. Since  rac12 =  rac{1}{1 + 1} \in A, we have M \ge  rac12 > 0. Let x \coloneqq  rac{M}{1 - M} + 1, which is positive because M > 0 and 1 - M > 0. Then x(1 - M) = M + (1 - M) = 1 > M , so x > Mx + M = M(x + 1), and dividing by x + 1 > 0 gives  rac{x}{x + 1} > M. This element of A exceeds the upper bound M, a contradiction. Hence M \ge 1 for every upper bound M, and \sup A = 1. Finally, A has no maximum: by @exr-suprema-b1 (a), a maximum would be the supremum 1, but 1 
otin A. (The choice of x comes from solving  rac{x}{x + 1} > M backwards: it is equivalent to x(1 - M) > M, that is, x >  rac{M}{1 - M}, and adding 1 gives a strict margin.) C. Going deeper [C1: The two sides of the gap] 1. Give a set A \subseteq 
Q that is bounded above and has a supremum in 
Q that does not belong to A. 2. Let B = \{ x \in 
Q : x > 0, \ x^2 < 2 \}, and let U be the set of rational upper bounds of B. Prove that U = \{ u \in 
Q : u > 0, \ u^2 > 2 \}. 3. Deduce that every positive rational number lies in exactly one of B and U, that B has no largest element, and that U has no smallest element. Hint: the two cases in the proof of @thm-no-rational-sup-sqrt2 each produce a new rational from an old one. (a) A = \{ x \in 
Q : 0 < x < 1 \}. The argument of @exm-sup-open-interval works in the ordered field 
Q, because the midpoint of two rationals is rational; it shows \sup A = 1 in 
Q, and 1 
otin A. (b) (\subseteq) Let u \in U. Since 1 \in B, we get u \ge 1 > 0. By @fd1:thm-sqrt2-irrational, u^2 
e 2. If u^2 < 2, then u \in B, and Case 1 of the proof of @thm-no-rational-sup-sqrt2, applied to s = u (which used only s \in 
Q, s \ge 1, and s^2 < 2), produces u + h \in B with u + h > u, contradicting u \in U. Hence u^2 > 2. (\supseteq) Let u \in 
Q with u > 0 and u^2 > 2. If some x \in B had x > u, then x^2 > u^2 > 2 by @thm-ordered-field-rules (g), contradicting x^2 < 2. So u is an upper bound of B, and u \in U. (c) Let q \in 
Q with q > 0. By @fd1:thm-sqrt2-irrational, q^2 
e 2, so by trichotomy exactly one of q^2 < 2 and q^2 > 2 holds, that is, q lies in exactly one of B and U, by (b). If B had a largest element b, Case 1 of the proof (with s = b, valid since b \ge 1 when b is largest, as 1 \in B) would give a larger element b + h \in B. If U had a smallest element u, Case 2 of the proof (with s = u, which needs only s > 0, s \in 
Q, and s^2 > 2) would give u - h \in U, smaller. So the positive rationals split into a lower piece with no top and an upper piece with no bottom. Nothing rational sits between the two pieces; that missing point is the gap. [C2: The least element of the upper bounds] Let F be an ordered field, A \subseteq F, and let U(A) be the set of all upper bounds of A in F. 1. Prove that s is a supremum of A if and only if s is the minimum of U(A). (This explains the name “least upper bound”.) 2. Prove that if A \subseteq B \subseteq F, then U(B) \subseteq U(A). 3. Describe U(\emptyset) and U(F), and use (a) to decide whether \emptyset and F have suprema. (a) (\Rightarrow) If s is a supremum, then s \in U(A) by (S1), and s \le M for every M \in U(A) by (S2). So s is an element of U(A) and a lower bound of U(A), which is @def-maximum’s definition of minimum. (\Leftarrow) If s = \min U(A), then s \in U(A), which is (S1), and s \le M for every M \in U(A), which is (S2). (b) Let M \in U(B). For every a \in A we have a \in B, so a \le M. Hence M \in U(A). (c) U(\emptyset) = F, since every element is an upper bound of the empty set vacuously; and F has no minimum, because m - 1 < m for every m \in F. So \emptyset has no supremum. U(F) = \emptyset, since for any M the element M + 1 \in F exceeds M; and \emptyset has no minimum. So F has no supremum either. The two degenerate cases fail for opposite reasons: too many upper bounds, and none.

title: 1.3 The Least Upper Bound Axiom
content:
The Least Upper Bound Axiom We now know exactly what goes wrong in the rationals. The set of positive rationals whose square is less than 2 is nonempty and bounded above, and yet it has no supremum in 
Q (@thm-no-rational-sup-sqrt2). Every failure of calculus over 
Q traces back to gaps of this kind. This section adds one axiom to the ordered-field axioms, stating that such gaps do not occur in 
R. Then it draws the first consequence: infima exist too, for free. The axiom Up to now, “
R is an ordered field containing 
Q” has been our only assumption about the real numbers (@exm-ordered-fields-q-r). That assumption holds for 
Q itself, so it cannot be what makes 
R different. We add exactly one more. Every set of reals that is bounded above has a least upper bound, unless it is empty. [Least Upper Bound Axiom] Every nonempty subset of 
R that is bounded above has a supremum in 
R. In symbols: for every A \subseteq 
R, \Bigl( A 
e \emptyset \ 	ext{ and } \ \exists M \in 
R \  orall a \in A : a \le M \Bigr) \ \Rightarrow \ \exists s \in 
R : s = \sup A . Standing assumption. From now on, 
R is an ordered field (@def-ordered-field), containing 
Q, that satisfies @ax-least-upper-bound. Every theorem about real numbers in this book is proved from these assumptions, together with the logic and set theory of Logic and Proof and Sets, Relations, and Cardinality (including, where it is flagged, a choice principle). In words, the axiom has two hypotheses and one conclusion. The hypotheses are about the set A: it has at least one element, and at least one upper bound. The conclusion is about 
R: among the upper bounds of A there is a least one, and it is a real number. By @thm-sup-unique it is unique, so the notation \sup A is justified whenever the two hypotheses hold. The axiom is also called the completeness axiom; “complete” will acquire a second, related meaning in Chapter 2, and the two are reconciled in Chapter 11. Each hypothesis is there because without it the conclusion is false. - Nonempty. The empty set is bounded above, by every real number, and it has no supremum (shown in the section on suprema). Without “nonempty”, the axiom would be false. - Bounded above. The interval [0, \infty) contains 0, but no real number sits above all of it, so there is no least such number either. The set 
N is a subtler example of the same failure; that it is not bounded above in 
R is proved later in this chapter, from this very axiom. The axiom is a statement about 
R and not about ordered fields in general. It fails in 
Q: some nonempty subset of 
Q, bounded above in 
Q, has no supremum in 
Q. Which result of the previous section shows this, and whether it needs adapting, is @exr-the-axiom-c1 (a). So the axiom is exactly the property that separates the two fields we have been comparing. Why is this an axiom and not a theorem? Because we have not said what a real number is. One can construct 
R from 
Q and then prove the least upper bound property as a theorem. Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapters 5 and 6 take this route with Cauchy sequences of rationals, and show that any two ordered fields satisfying the axiom are the same up to relabeling, so the axiom pins 
R down completely; the optional Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 7 builds 
R by Dedekind cuts instead. This volume does not use those chapters: everything we need follows from the axiom. [A set of reals that must have a supremum] Let S = \{ x \in 
R : x > 0 	ext{ and } x^2 < 2 \}. Show that \sup S exists in 
R. What can be said about it so far? We check the two hypotheses of @ax-least-upper-bound. S is nonempty, since 1 > 0 and 1^2 < 2. S is bounded above by 2: if x \in S had x > 2, then x^2 > 4 by @thm-ordered-field-rules (g), contradicting x^2 < 2. So the axiom gives a real number s = \sup S. So far we know only what (S1) and (S2) give: 1 \le s \le 2, since 1 \in S and 2 is an upper bound. Compare this with @thm-no-rational-sup-sqrt2. The rational version of this set has no supremum in 
Q, and the proof of that theorem showed that a rational candidate s with s^2 < 2 or s^2 > 2 cannot be the supremum. Neither case used rationality except to keep s \pm h rational. So we can guess the answer: s^2 = 2. Proving it, and so proving that \sqrt 2 exists, is done later in this chapter. The example shows the pattern of every use of the axiom. First check the two hypotheses, which is usually routine. Then the axiom hands over a number s, and all we know about s is (S1) and (S2). Everything else must be extracted from those two properties. Do not forget “nonempty”. The empty set is bounded above and has no supremum, so an argument that applies the axiom to a set without first producing an element of that set is incomplete. The failure is easy to commit when the set is defined by a condition, such as \{ x \in 
R : x^2 < c \}: for c \le 0 that set is empty. The axiom gives existence, not a formula. It says that \sup A exists; it does not say what it is, and it is usually not the upper bound M used to check the hypothesis. For S above, the hypothesis was checked with M = 2, and \sup S 
e 2: the smaller number  rac32 is also an upper bound, since any x >  rac32 has x^2 >  rac94 > 2 by @thm-ordered-field-rules (g). To identify a supremum we must still verify (S1) and (S2) for a specific candidate. Let A = \{ n \in 
Z : n \le 3.5 \} = \{ \dots, 1, 2, 3 \}. Does A satisfy the hypotheses of @ax-least-upper-bound? What is \sup A, and is it a maximum? Yes: 3 \in A, so A is nonempty, and 3.5 is an upper bound by definition of A. So \sup A exists. It is 3, not 3.5: the element 3 is an upper bound, because an integer greater than 3 is at least 4, which exceeds 3.5 (arithmetic of the integers, Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 2), and it belongs to A, so it is the maximum, and a maximum is the supremum (@exr-suprema-b1). The bound used to check the hypothesis was not the supremum. Infima come free The axiom is stated for suprema only. We do not need a second axiom for infima: reflecting the line through 0 turns lower bounds into upper bounds and “greatest” into “least”. To say this precisely we need the reflected set. For A \subseteq 
R, let -A \coloneqq \{ -a : a \in A \} . So x \in -A if and only if -x \in A, and -(-A) = A. For example, -(0, 1] = [-1, 0), and -\{ -1, 3 \} = \{ 1, -3 \}. The definition makes sense in any ordered field, and the next theorem holds in any ordered field; the axiom enters only afterwards. [Infimum by Reflection] Let F be an ordered field, A \subseteq F, and m, t \in F. 1. m is a lower bound of A if and only if -m is an upper bound of -A. 2. t is an infimum of A if and only if -t is a supremum of -A. In particular, if -A has a supremum, then A has an infimum, and \inf A = -\sup(-A). Reflection x \mapsto -x reverses every inequality (@thm-ordered-field-rules (a)), so it should carry each property of an infimum to the matching property of a supremum. The proof checks this property by property: (I1) against (S1), and (I2) against (S2), which is the “split into two properties” move for suprema. (a) By @thm-ordered-field-rules (a), m \le a if and only if -a \le -m. So m \le a for every a \in A if and only if -a \le -m for every a \in A. The elements -a with a \in A are exactly the elements of -A, so the last statement says that -m is an upper bound of -A. (b) (\Rightarrow) Suppose t is an infimum of A. By (I1), t is a lower bound of A, so by (a), -t is an upper bound of -A: this is (S1) for -t. For (S2), let M be an upper bound of -A. By (a) applied to m = -M, the element -M is a lower bound of A. By (I2), -M \le t, and so -t \le M by @thm-ordered-field-rules (a). Hence -t is a supremum of -A. (\Leftarrow) Suppose -t is a supremum of -A. By (S1) and (a), t is a lower bound of A: this is (I1). For (I2), let m be a lower bound of A. By (a), -m is an upper bound of -A, so (S2) gives -t \le -m, that is, m \le t. Hence t is an infimum of A. The final sentence follows from (b) with t \coloneqq -\sup(-A), since -t = \sup(-A). Now the axiom can be applied to -A. [Greatest Lower Bound Property] Every nonempty subset A of 
R that is bounded below has an infimum in 
R, and \inf A = -\sup(-A) . Since A is nonempty, so is -A. Let m be a lower bound of A. By @thm-inf-neg-sup (a), -m is an upper bound of -A, so -A is bounded above. By @ax-least-upper-bound, -A has a supremum, and by @thm-inf-neg-sup, A has the infimum -\sup(-A). Alternatively, one can take the supremum of the lower bounds. Let L be the set of lower bounds of A. It is nonempty, because A is bounded below, and any element of A, of which there is at least one because A is nonempty, sits above all of L. So \ell \coloneqq \sup L exists by @ax-least-upper-bound. Each a \in A is an upper bound of L, so \ell \le a by (S2); hence \ell is a lower bound of A. And every lower bound of A lies in L, so it is at most \ell by (S1). Thus \ell = \inf A. In this route the two hypotheses on A swap roles: “bounded below” makes L nonempty, and “nonempty” makes L bounded above. The hypotheses of @thm-greatest-lower-bound are needed for the same reasons as those of the axiom. The empty set is bounded below and has no infimum, since every real number is a lower bound of it and t + 1 beats any candidate t. The interval (-\infty, 0] is nonempty but not bounded below, and has no infimum. So in 
R, suprema and infima exist under mirror-image hypotheses, and each can be computed from the other. The mirror identity \sup A = -\inf(-A), for A nonempty and bounded above, is @exr-the-axiom-b1. Unbounded and empty sets It is sometimes convenient to give \sup A a meaning even when the axiom does not apply. For a nonempty set A that is not bounded above one writes \sup A = +\infty, and one sets \sup \emptyset = -\infty; symmetrically, \inf A = -\infty for a nonempty set not bounded below, and \inf \emptyset = +\infty. The strange-looking value \sup \emptyset = -\infty is chosen so that “A \subseteq B implies \sup A \le \sup B” stays true when A = \emptyset. These are conventions of notation, and \pm\infty are not real numbers: they obey none of the field axioms, and no rule of @thm-ordered-field-rules applies to them. The series uses them from Measure and Integration on, where measure theory needs suprema of arbitrary sets, and announces them again there. Until then, whenever we write \sup A, the set A is nonempty and bounded above, and \sup A is a real number. What the axiom will do With the axiom in place, the rest of the chapter extracts its first consequences: a practical test for recognizing a supremum, the Archimedean property, the density of the rationals, the existence of roots, and the nested interval property. The first, the test, holds in every ordered field; it is the tool for the others. Each of the rest fails in 
Q or in some other ordered field. Three of them, the Archimedean property, the roots, and the nested interval property, are proved by the same pattern: define a set, check the two hypotheses, take its supremum, and extract what is needed from (S1) and (S2). The density of the rationals then follows from the Archimedean property, with no new supremum. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] For each set, decide whether it satisfies both hypotheses of @ax-least-upper-bound. If a hypothesis fails, name it; if both hold, find the supremum. 1. \{ x \in 
R : x^2 < 0 \}. 2. \{ x^2 : x \in 
R \}. 3. (-\infty, 0). 4. \{ x \in 
Q : x > 0, \ x^2 < 2 \}, regarded as a subset of the ordered field 
Q. (a) The set is empty, since x^2 \ge 0 for every x (@thm-ordered-field-rules (e)). “Nonempty” fails. (b) “Bounded above” fails. Given M \in 
R, let x \coloneqq \abs{M} + 1. Then x \ge 1, so x^2 \ge x (multiply x \ge 1 by x > 0), and x > \abs{M} \ge M. Hence x^2 > M, and M is not an upper bound. (c) Both hold: -1 is an element and 0 is an upper bound. The supremum is 0: it is an upper bound, and if M < 0 were an upper bound, then M \ge -1 and the midpoint  rac{M}{2} would satisfy M <  rac{M}{2} < 0, so it lies in the set and exceeds M. (d) Both hypotheses hold in 
Q (@thm-no-rational-sup-sqrt2), but the axiom is a statement about 
R, not about 
Q. In 
Q the conclusion fails: the set has no supremum in 
Q, by the same theorem. This is exactly why 
Q does not satisfy the axiom. B. Practice [B1: The mirror identity] Let A \subseteq 
R be nonempty and bounded above. Show that -A has a lower bound, and that \sup A = -\inf(-A). Since A is nonempty, so is -A. Let M be an upper bound of A. For every x \in -A we have -x \in A, so -x \le M, and hence -M \le x by @thm-ordered-field-rules (a). So -M is a lower bound of -A, and -A is bounded below. By @thm-greatest-lower-bound, \inf(-A) exists and equals -\sup(-(-A)) = -\sup A, because -(-A) = A. Negating both sides gives \sup A = -\inf(-A). [B2: The infimum is below the supremum] Let A \subseteq 
R be nonempty and bounded. Prove that \inf A \le \sup A, with equality if and only if A has exactly one element. Both exist, by @ax-least-upper-bound and @thm-greatest-lower-bound. Since A is nonempty, choose a \in A. By (I1), \inf A \le a, and by (S1), a \le \sup A. Hence \inf A \le \sup A. If A = \{ a \}, then a is both the maximum and the minimum of A, so \sup A = a = \inf A by @exr-suprema-b1. Conversely, suppose \inf A = \sup A = c. For every a \in A, c \le a \le c, so a = c by trichotomy. Hence A \subseteq \{ c \}, and since A is nonempty, A = \{ c \}. C. Going deeper [C1: The axiom in other ordered fields] 1. Say what it would mean for the ordered field 
Q to satisfy the least upper bound property, and show that it does not. Is @thm-no-rational-sup-sqrt2 exactly a witness, or does it need to be adapted? 2. Say that an ordered field F has the greatest lower bound property if every nonempty subset of F that is bounded below has an infimum in F. Prove that if F has the greatest lower bound property, then it has the least upper bound property. 3. Conclude that, for an ordered field, the two properties are equivalent. (a) 
Q would satisfy it if every nonempty subset of 
Q that is bounded above in 
Q had a supremum in 
Q. @thm-no-rational-sup-sqrt2 is exactly a witness that it does not: its set is a subset of 
Q, nonempty, bounded above by the rational 2, and has no supremum in 
Q. Nothing needs adapting, because the theorem was stated and proved inside the ordered field 
Q, with the upper bounds in (S2) ranging over 
Q. (b) Let A \subseteq F be nonempty and bounded above, with upper bound M. Then -A is nonempty, and it is bounded below by -M, by @thm-inf-neg-sup (a) applied with m = -M and the set -A in place of A (so that -(-A) = A). By the greatest lower bound property, -A has an infimum t in F. By @thm-inf-neg-sup (b), applied to the set -A, -t is a supremum of -(-A) = A. So A has a supremum in F. (c) The converse direction is the proof of @thm-greatest-lower-bound, which used only @thm-inf-neg-sup (valid in every ordered field) and the least upper bound property. So in any ordered field each property implies the other. [C2: The upper bounds form a ray] 1. Let A \subseteq 
R be nonempty and bounded above, and let U(A) be its set of upper bounds. Prove that U(A) = [\sup A, \infty). 2. Let B = \{ x \in 
Q : x > 0, \ x^2 < 2 \}, and let U be its set of upper bounds in 
Q. Prove that there is no rational q with U = \{ u \in 
Q : u \ge q \}. 3. Explain in one sentence how (a) and (b) restate the difference between 
R and 
Q. (a) (\subseteq) If M \in U(A), then \sup A \le M by (S2), so M \in [\sup A, \infty). (\supseteq) If M \ge \sup A, then for every a \in A, a \le \sup A \le M by (S1), so M \in U(A). (b) Suppose U = \{ u \in 
Q : u \ge q \} for some rational q. Then q \in U, and q \le u for every u \in U. So q is the minimum of U, that is, a rational upper bound of B below every other rational upper bound. That makes q a supremum of B in 
Q, which contradicts @thm-no-rational-sup-sqrt2. (c) In 
R the upper bounds of a nonempty bounded-above set always form a closed ray that starts at a point, while in 
Q they can form a ray whose starting point is missing.

title: 1.4 Working with the Supremum
content:
Working with the Supremum The least upper bound axiom (@ax-least-upper-bound) tells us that suprema exist. To use a supremum, or to recognize one, we need a handle on its second property. As defined (@def-supremum), (S2) quantifies over all upper bounds of the set, and in practice there is no way to list them. This section replaces (S2) by an equivalent statement quantified over small positive numbers \varepsilon, which can be checked by exhibiting elements. With it we prove the rules for computing suprema of scaled sets and of sums of sets, and meet the first \varepsilon/2 argument of the book. The epsilon characterization Look back at how (S2) was verified for (0, 1) in @exm-sup-open-interval. We supposed that some M < 1 was an upper bound and then produced an element of the set above M. Writing M = 1 - \varepsilon, the argument really showed: for every \varepsilon > 0, some element of the set exceeds 1 - \varepsilon. That is a statement about elements of the set, not about upper bounds, and it is exactly equivalent to (S2). A supremum is an upper bound that the set comes arbitrarily close to. [Epsilon Characterization of the Supremum] Let A \subseteq 
R and let s \in 
R be an upper bound of A. Then s = \sup A if and only if for every \varepsilon > 0 there exists a \in A with a > s - \varepsilon. In symbols, for an upper bound s of A: s = \sup A \quad\iff\quad  orall \varepsilon > 0 \ \ \exists a \in A : \ s - \varepsilon < a \ (\le s) . The part in parentheses is automatic, since s is an upper bound; it is written to show where a lies. Draw the band (s - \varepsilon, s] just below s. The theorem says: s is the supremum exactly when every such band, however thin, contains a point of A. (\Rightarrow) The number s - \varepsilon is smaller than s, so it cannot be an upper bound, by (S2). Not being an upper bound means precisely that some element of A lies above it. (\Leftarrow) We need (S2): every upper bound M satisfies s \le M. Suppose some upper bound M lies below s. Then the band between M and s contains no point of A, and the hypothesis says every band does. So the band of width s - M, that is, the hypothesis with \varepsilon = s - M, gives the contradiction. (\Rightarrow) Suppose s = \sup A, and let \varepsilon > 0. Then s - \varepsilon < s by @thm-ordered-field-rules (a).
