If s - \varepsilon were an upper bound of A, then (S2) would give s \le s - \varepsilon, contradicting s - \varepsilon < s by trichotomy. So s - \varepsilon is not an upper bound of A, which means there is a \in A with a > s - \varepsilon. (\Leftarrow) Suppose that for every \varepsilon > 0 there is a \in A with a > s - \varepsilon. Since s is an upper bound of A by hypothesis, (S1) holds, and it remains to check (S2). Let M be an upper bound of A, and suppose, for a contradiction, that M < s. Put \varepsilon \coloneqq s - M, which is positive by @thm-ordered-field-rules (a). By hypothesis there is a \in A with a > s - \varepsilon = M. This contradicts M being an upper bound of A. Hence s \le M by trichotomy, which is (S2). So s = \sup A. The theorem does not use the axiom. It holds in any ordered field, and it recognizes a supremum; the axiom is what guarantees that there is one to recognize. The two halves are used differently. The forward direction is how a known supremum is used: it hands us elements of A as close to \sup A as we like. The backward direction is how a candidate is confirmed: it replaces “every upper bound is at least s” by “every band below s meets A”, which can be checked by writing down an element. The hypothesis “s is an upper bound” cannot be dropped. For A = (0, 1) and s =  rac12, every band ( rac12 - \varepsilon,  rac12] meets A, yet  rac12 is not the supremum. The band condition alone says only that s is not too big; being an upper bound says it is not too small. The element a that the theorem produces depends on \varepsilon, as the order “ orall \varepsilon \ \exists a” allows. For A = (0, 1) and s = 1, the choice a \coloneqq \max \{  rac12, 1 -  rac{\varepsilon}{2} \} works: it lies in (0, 1) and exceeds 1 - \varepsilon. For \varepsilon =  rac1{10} it gives a =  rac{19}{20}; for \varepsilon =  rac1{1000} it must be above  rac{999}{1000}, and  rac{19}{20} no longer works. No single element of (0, 1) works for every \varepsilon. The witness depends on \varepsilon. The theorem gives, for each \varepsilon, some a; it never gives one a that serves every \varepsilon at once. A proof that fixes a first and then says “for every \varepsilon > 0, a > s - \varepsilon” has swapped the quantifiers, and for (0, 1) it asserts something false. When you take a witness from the theorem, write “choose a \in A (depending on \varepsilon) with …”. Let s be an upper bound of a set A \subseteq 
R. Compare 	ext{(i)} \ \  orall \varepsilon > 0 \ \ \exists a \in A : a > s - \varepsilon \qquad	ext{and}\qquad 	ext{(ii)} \ \ \exists a \in A \ \  orall \varepsilon > 0 : a > s - \varepsilon . Statement (i) says s = \sup A. What does (ii) say, and when is it true? Fix a \in A. The condition “a > s - \varepsilon for every \varepsilon > 0” forces a \ge s: if a < s, then \varepsilon \coloneqq s - a > 0 would give a > s - (s - a) = a, which is absurd. Since s is an upper bound, also a \le s, so a = s. Conversely, if s \in A, then a = s satisfies s > s - \varepsilon for every \varepsilon > 0. So (ii) says exactly that s \in A, that is, s is the maximum of A. Swapping the quantifiers turned “supremum” into “maximum”. For A = (0, 1) and s = 1, (i) is true and (ii) is false. Here is the theorem at work on a set where the witness must be found by a short computation. The Idea finds it backwards; the solution writes it forwards. [Confirming a supremum with epsilon] Prove that \sup \{ x^2 : x \in (0, 1) \} = 1. Idea. The upper bound part is easy. For the band condition, fix \varepsilon > 0; we need x \in (0, 1) with x^2 > 1 - \varepsilon. Try x = 1 - h with h > 0 small. Then x^2 = 1 - 2h + h^2 > 1 - 2h, so it suffices that 1 - 2h \ge 1 - \varepsilon, that is, h \le  rac{\varepsilon}{2}. But we also need x \in (0, 1), that is, 0 < h < 1, and  rac{\varepsilon}{2} can be large. Capping it fixes this: take h = \min\{  rac12,  rac{\varepsilon}{2} \}. Proof. Let A = \{ x^2 : x \in (0, 1) \}. For x \in (0, 1), @thm-ordered-field-rules (g) gives x^2 < 1^2 = 1, so 1 is an upper bound of A. Let \varepsilon > 0, and let h \coloneqq \min\{  rac12,  rac{\varepsilon}{2} \}, which depends only on \varepsilon. Then 0 < h \le  rac12, so x \coloneqq 1 - h lies in [ rac12, 1) \subseteq (0, 1), and x^2 \in A. Since h > 0, h^2 > 0, and so x^2 = 1 - 2h + h^2 > 1 - 2h \ge 1 - \varepsilon , where the last step uses h \le  rac{\varepsilon}{2}. By @thm-sup-epsilon, \sup A = 1. The  rac12 in the minimum is arbitrary: any cap below 1 keeps x positive. What matters is that a constraint discovered late in the Idea (here h < 1) is built into the constant from the start of the proof. Sup approximation The forward direction of @thm-sup-epsilon is used so often with \varepsilon =  rac1n that it deserves its own statement. Sup Approximation Let A \subseteq 
R be nonempty and bounded above. For every n \in 
Z_{>0} there is a_n \in A with \sup A -  rac1n < a_n \le \sup A . By @ax-least-upper-bound, \sup A exists. Let n \in 
Z_{>0}. Then n > 0, and  rac1n > 0 by @thm-ordered-field-rules (f). By @thm-sup-epsilon (\Rightarrow) with \varepsilon =  rac1n, there is a_n \in A with a_n > \sup A -  rac1n, and a_n \le \sup A by (S1). The corollary gives, for each n separately, an element a_n. Choosing one for every n at once, so as to form a sequence (a_n), is a use of the axiom of countable choice; we flag it and move on. Once limits are defined in Chapter 2, this says that \sup A is the limit of a sequence from A. We call the move sup approximation: “\sup A -  rac1n is not an upper bound, so some a_n \in A exceeds it.” Monotonicity and scaling We now compute suprema of sets built from other sets. The first rule says that enlarging a set cannot lower its supremum. [Monotonicity of the Supremum] Let A \subseteq B \subseteq 
R, where A is nonempty and B is bounded above. Then \sup A and \sup B exist, and \sup A \le \sup B. Since A is nonempty and A \subseteq B, the set B is nonempty; as it is bounded above, \sup B exists by @ax-least-upper-bound. Every a \in A lies in B, so a \le \sup B by (S1) for B. Hence \sup B is an upper bound of A. So A is nonempty and bounded above, \sup A exists by @ax-least-upper-bound, and \sup A \le \sup B by (S2) for A. Strict inclusion does not give strict inequality: (0, 1) \subsetneq (0, 1], and both have supremum 1. The hypothesis that A is nonempty cannot be dropped, since \emptyset \subseteq B always and \emptyset has no supremum. For scaling we need the scaled set. For A \subseteq 
R and c \in 
R, let cA \coloneqq \{ ca : a \in A \} . For example 2(0, 1] = (0, 2] and (-1)A = -A. [Scaling the Supremum] Let A \subseteq 
R be nonempty and bounded above, and let c \in 
R. 1. If c > 0, then cA is nonempty and bounded above, and \sup(cA) = c \sup A. 2. If c < 0, then cA is nonempty and bounded below, and \inf(cA) = c \sup A. For (a), prove the equality as two inequalities. Multiplying the inequality a \le \sup A by c > 0 shows that c \sup A is an upper bound of cA, which gives \le. For \ge, undo the scaling: dividing by c turns an upper bound of cA into an upper bound of A. No \varepsilon is needed, because multiplication by c > 0 is invertible and preserves order. For (b), a negative factor reverses order, so write c = -\abs{c} and let @thm-inf-neg-sup handle the sign. Let s \coloneqq \sup A, which exists by @ax-least-upper-bound. Since A is nonempty, so is cA. (a) Let c > 0. For every a \in A, a \le s by (S1), so ca \le cs by @thm-ordered-field-rules (c) (or trivially if a = s). Hence cs is an upper bound of cA, so \sup(cA) exists by @ax-least-upper-bound, and t \coloneqq \sup(cA) \le cs by (S2). For the reverse inequality, let a \in A. Then ca \in cA, so ca \le t. Multiplying by  rac1c > 0 (@thm-ordered-field-rules (f) and (c)) gives a \le  rac{t}{c}. Hence  rac tc is an upper bound of A, and (S2) gives s \le  rac tc. Multiplying by c > 0 gives cs \le t. By trichotomy, \sup(cA) = cs. (b) Let c < 0, so -c > 0. The set -(cA) = \{ -ca : a \in A \} equals (-c)A, which by (a) is nonempty and bounded above with \sup((-c)A) = -cs. By @thm-inf-neg-sup (a), cA = -((-c)A) is bounded below, and by @thm-inf-neg-sup, \inf(cA) = -\sup igl( -(cA)  igr) = -\sup igl( (-c)A  igr) = -(-cs) = cs . This proves the theorem. For c = 0 the set cA is \{ 0 \}, and \sup(0A) = 0 = 0 \cdot \sup A as well. Part (a) genuinely needs c > 0: with c = -1 and A = (0, 1], the set cA = [-1, 0) has supremum 0, not c \sup A = -1. Part (b) says what happens instead: a negative factor exchanges supremum and infimum, and indeed \inf [-1, 0) = -1. The supremum of a sum For A, B \subseteq 
R, let A + B \coloneqq \{ a + b : a \in A, \ b \in B \} . For instance (0, 1) + \{ 5 \} = (5, 6) and [0, 1] + [0, 2] = [0, 3]. It is natural to expect \sup(A + B) = \sup A + \sup B. This time the reverse inequality cannot be obtained by undoing an operation: a single element of A + B mixes one element of each set. We need the \varepsilon characterization. [Supremum of a Sum] Let A, B \subseteq 
R be nonempty and bounded above. Then A + B is nonempty and bounded above, and \sup(A + B) = \sup A + \sup B . Try it first (ten minutes): the inequality \le takes one line. Try to prove \ge. The attempt that comes first to mind takes a = \sup A and b = \sup B: then a + b \in A + B, and (S1) for \sup(A + B) gives \ge at once. It fails because a supremum need not belong to its set: for A = B = (0, 1), the number 2 is not in A + B = (0, 2). (The last exercise of this section takes that attempt apart.) The repair is to use elements that are only close to the suprema, which is what @thm-sup-epsilon (\Rightarrow) supplies. So we prove the equality as two inequalities. (\le) Every a + b is at most \sup A + \sup B, so the right side is an upper bound, and the supremum is at most any upper bound. (\ge) Work backwards. To show that \sup(A + B) is at least \sup A + \sup B, it suffices to find, for each \varepsilon > 0, an element of A + B above \sup A + \sup B - \varepsilon. The natural candidate is a + b with a close to \sup A and b close to \sup B. If a falls short of \sup A by less than \varepsilon/2, and b falls short of \sup B by less than \varepsilon/2, the total shortfall is less than \varepsilon. So we split the budget \varepsilon into two halves, one for each set, and ask @thm-sup-epsilon for an element within \varepsilon/2 of each supremum. This is the \varepsilon/2 argument. The number \varepsilon/2 depends only on \varepsilon; the elements a and b depend on \varepsilon. Before reading on: the proof asks for elements within \varepsilon/2 of each supremum. What would it give if it asked for \varepsilon instead, and would that still be enough? By @ax-least-upper-bound, \sup A and \sup B exist. Choosing a_0 \in A and b_0 \in B gives a_0 + b_0 \in A + B, so A + B is nonempty. (\le) Let a \in A and b \in B. By (S1), a \le \sup A and b \le \sup B, so a + b \le \sup A + \sup B by @thm-ordered-field-rules (b). Hence \sup A + \sup B is an upper bound of A + B. By @ax-least-upper-bound, \sup(A + B) exists, and by (S2), \sup(A + B) \le \sup A + \sup B. (\ge) Let \varepsilon > 0. Then  rac{\varepsilon}{2} > 0. By @thm-sup-epsilon (\Rightarrow), there are a \in A and b \in B (both depending on \varepsilon) with a > \sup A - 	frac{\varepsilon}{2} \quad	ext{and}\quad b > \sup B - 	frac{\varepsilon}{2} . Adding, by @thm-ordered-field-rules (b), gives a + b > \sup A + \sup B - \varepsilon. Since a + b \in A + B, (S1) gives \sup(A + B) \ge a + b > \sup A + \sup B - \varepsilon . This holds for every \varepsilon > 0. If we had \sup(A + B) < \sup A + \sup B, then the choice \varepsilon \coloneqq \sup A + \sup B - \sup(A + B) > 0 would give \sup(A + B) > \sup(A + B), which is absurd. Hence \sup(A + B) \ge \sup A + \sup B. The two inequalities and trichotomy give \sup(A + B) = \sup A + \sup B. The answer to the prompt: with \varepsilon in place of \varepsilon/2 the proof gives \sup(A + B) > \sup A + \sup B - 2\varepsilon for every \varepsilon > 0, and that is still enough, since 2\varepsilon runs through all positive numbers as \varepsilon does. Halving is a convenience: it makes the final inequality come out with exactly \varepsilon, which is the form @thm-sup-epsilon (\Leftarrow) asks for. The halves of the proof use the two halves of the definition. The first inequality used only that each supremum is an upper bound (S1) and that \sup(A + B) is least (S2). The second used that each of \sup A and \sup B is least, in its \varepsilon form, and that \sup(A + B) is an upper bound. We call the pattern equality by two inequalities: prove \le by exhibiting an upper bound, and \ge with an \varepsilon. Every hypothesis is needed. If B = \emptyset, then A + B = \emptyset has no supremum. If B is not bounded above, neither is A + B (@exr-epsilon-characterization-c2). And the analogous rule for differences is not \sup(A - B) = \sup A - \sup B: the correct version subtracts an infimum (@exr-epsilon-characterization-b3). Proving one inequality only. Here is a tempting “proof” of @thm-sup-sum: “For a \in A and b \in B, a + b \le \sup A + \sup B. Therefore \sup(A + B) = \sup A + \sup B.” The first sentence proves only that \sup A + \sup B is an upper bound of A + B, which gives \le. It says nothing about being the least one: the same sentence with \sup A + \sup B + 1 is equally true, and would “prove” \sup(A + B) = \sup A + \sup B + 1. Whenever a supremum is claimed to equal something, both (S1) and (S2), or both inequalities, must appear. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Use @thm-sup-epsilon to confirm that \sup [0, 5) = 5. Give the witness a as a formula in \varepsilon. 2. Use @thm-sup-epsilon to confirm that \sup \{ 3 \} = 3. Does your witness depend on \varepsilon? Why not? 3. Use @thm-sup-epsilon to confirm that \sup  igl( (-1, 1) \cup (2, 4)  igr) = 4. 4. Let s be an upper bound of A. Write in symbols, using the \varepsilon characterization, the statement “s is not the supremum of A”. 5. Run the (\ge) half of the proof of @thm-sup-sum on A = (0, 1), B = \{ 5 \}, and \varepsilon =  rac1{10}: give an a and a b the proof could use, and check the inequality it derives. 6. In the proof of @thm-sup-sum, which line can no longer be justified if B is allowed to be empty? (a) 5 is an upper bound of [0, 5). Given \varepsilon > 0, let a \coloneqq \max\{ 0, 5 -  rac{\varepsilon}{2} \}. Then a \ge 0, and a < 5 because both 0 and 5 -  rac{\varepsilon}{2} are less than 5; so a \in [0, 5). Also a \ge 5 -  rac{\varepsilon}{2} > 5 - \varepsilon. By @thm-sup-epsilon, \sup [0, 5) = 5. (b) 3 is an upper bound of \{ 3 \}, and for every \varepsilon > 0 the element a = 3 satisfies 3 > 3 - \varepsilon. The witness does not depend on \varepsilon because 3 belongs to the set: by the Quick check above, a single witness for all \varepsilon exists exactly when the supremum is a maximum. (c) Every element is less than 4, so 4 is an upper bound. Given \varepsilon > 0, let a \coloneqq \max\{ 3, 4 -  rac{\varepsilon}{2} \}. Then 3 \le a < 4, so a \in (2, 4), and a \ge 4 -  rac{\varepsilon}{2} > 4 - \varepsilon. By @thm-sup-epsilon the supremum is 4. (d) \exists \varepsilon > 0 \ \  orall a \in A : a \le s - \varepsilon. In words: some band below s contains no point of A, so s - \varepsilon is a smaller upper bound. (e) Here \sup A = 1, \sup B = 5, and  rac{\varepsilon}{2} =  rac1{20}. The proof needs a \in (0, 1) with a > 1 -  rac1{20} =  rac{19}{20}, for instance a =  rac{24}{25}, and b \in B with b > 5 -  rac1{20}, which forces b = 5. Then a + b =  rac{149}{25} = 5.96 > 5.9 = \sup A + \sup B - \varepsilon. Any a \in ( rac{19}{20}, 1) works; the one b works for every \varepsilon because 5 is the maximum of B. (f) The first line, “By @ax-least-upper-bound, \sup A and \sup B exist”. The axiom needs B nonempty, and \emptyset has no supremum. The line that chooses b \in B in the (\ge) half fails too, since there is nothing to choose. B. Practice [B1: A computed supremum] Prove that \sup \{ x^2 : x \in (-1, 2) \} = 4. Hence show that the set has no maximum. Let A = \{ x^2 : x \in (-1, 2) \}. Upper bound. Let x \in (-1, 2). If x \ge 0, then x < 2 gives x^2 < 4 by @thm-ordered-field-rules (g). If -1 < x < 0, then \abs{x} < 1 by @prp-absolute-value-rules (d), so x^2 = \abs{x}^2 < 1 < 4 by @thm-ordered-field-rules (g). So 4 is an upper bound, and 4 
otin A. Band condition. Working backwards as in @exm-sup-squares-epsilon: with x = 2 - h we have x^2 = 4 - 4h + h^2 > 4 - 4h, so h \le  rac{\varepsilon}{4} suffices, provided 0 < h < 3 to keep x \in (-1, 2). So let \varepsilon > 0 and h \coloneqq \min\{ 1,  rac{\varepsilon}{4} \}, which depends only on \varepsilon. Then 0 < h \le 1, so x \coloneqq 2 - h \in [1, 2) \subseteq (-1, 2), and since h^2 > 0, x^2 = 4 - 4h + h^2 > 4 - 4h \ge 4 - \varepsilon . By @thm-sup-epsilon, \sup A = 4. Since 4 
otin A, the set has no maximum, by @exr-suprema-b1 (a). [B2: Supremum of a union] Let A, B \subseteq 
R be nonempty and bounded above. Prove that A \cup B is bounded above and \sup(A \cup B) = \max\{ \sup A, \sup B \}. Let m \coloneqq \max\{ \sup A, \sup B \}; both suprema exist by @ax-least-upper-bound. If x \in A \cup B, then x \le \sup A \le m or x \le \sup B \le m, so m is an upper bound of A \cup B, which is nonempty. By symmetry we may assume m = \sup A. Given \varepsilon > 0, @thm-sup-epsilon (\Rightarrow) gives a \in A with a > \sup A - \varepsilon = m - \varepsilon, and a \in A \cup B. By @thm-sup-epsilon (\Leftarrow), \sup(A \cup B) = m. [B3: Supremum of a difference] Let A \subseteq 
R be nonempty and bounded above, and B \subseteq 
R nonempty and bounded below. Prove that \sup \{ a - b : a \in A, \ b \in B \} = \sup A - \inf B . Give an example showing that the right side cannot be replaced by \sup A - \sup B. The set in question is A + (-B). By @thm-inf-neg-sup (a), -B is bounded above, and it is nonempty. By @thm-greatest-lower-bound, \inf B = -\sup(-B), that is, \sup(-B) = -\inf B. So @thm-sup-sum applies to A and -B: \sup igl( A + (-B)  igr) = \sup A + \sup(-B) = \sup A - \inf B . For the example, take A = \{ 0 \} and B = [0, 1]. The differences 0 - b fill [-1, 0], whose supremum is 0 = \sup A - \inf B, whereas \sup A - \sup B = -1. C. Going deeper [C1: Products of sets] For A, B \subseteq 
R let AB \coloneqq \{ ab : a \in A, \ b \in B \}. 1. Show that \sup(AB) = \sup A \cdot \sup B can fail for nonempty bounded sets A, B. 2. Prove that it holds when A and B are nonempty, bounded above, and contained in (0, \infty). [Hint 1] For (a), try sets of negative numbers. For (b), the inequality \le is routine; for \ge, fix one element b \in B and compare the set bA with AB. [Hint 2] For \ge in (b): fix b \in B. Which theorem computes \sup(bA), and which compares the suprema of two sets, one inside the other? What does the inequality you get say about b, once b varies? (a) Take A = B = [-2, -1]. Then \sup A \cdot \sup B = (-1)(-1) = 1, but 4 = (-2)(-2) \in AB, so \sup(AB) \ge 4 
e 1 by (S1). (b) Let s \coloneqq \sup A and t \coloneqq \sup B, which exist by @ax-least-upper-bound. Since A contains a positive element and s is an upper bound, s > 0; likewise t > 0. (\le) For a \in A and b \in B, we have 0 < a \le s and 0 < b \le t, so ab \le sb \le st by @thm-ordered-field-rules (c) (with trivial equality cases). So st is an upper bound of the nonempty set AB, \sup(AB) exists, and \sup(AB) \le st by (S2). (\ge) Fix b \in B. Then bA \subseteq AB and b > 0, so @thm-sup-scaling and @thm-sup-monotone give bs = \sup(bA) \le \sup(AB). Multiplying by  rac1s > 0 gives b \le  rac{\sup(AB)}{s}. As b \in B was arbitrary,  rac{\sup(AB)}{s} is an upper bound of B, so t \le  rac{\sup(AB)}{s} by (S2), that is, st \le \sup(AB). By trichotomy, \sup(AB) = st. Positivity was used in (\le), to multiply inequalities, and in (\ge), to scale by b and divide by s; part (a) shows it cannot be dropped. [C2: Exit check: sums of sets] Let A, B \subseteq 
R be nonempty. 1. Assume A and B are bounded above. Without looking back, prove \sup(A + B) = \sup A + \sup B. This time, instead of proving \ge separately, show that \sup A + \sup B satisfies both hypotheses of @thm-sup-epsilon for the set A + B. 2. Assume A and B are bounded below. State and prove the corresponding formula for \inf(A + B). 3. Show that if B is not bounded above, then neither is A + B. (a) Let s \coloneqq \sup A + \sup B, where both suprema exist by @ax-least-upper-bound. Upper bound: for a \in A, b \in B, (S1) and @thm-ordered-field-rules (b) give a + b \le s. Band condition: let \varepsilon > 0; then  rac{\varepsilon}{2} > 0, and @thm-sup-epsilon (\Rightarrow) gives a \in A and b \in B, depending on \varepsilon, with a > \sup A -  rac{\varepsilon}{2} and b > \sup B -  rac{\varepsilon}{2}. Adding, a + b > s - \varepsilon, and a + b \in A + B. By @thm-sup-epsilon (\Leftarrow), s = \sup(A + B). (b) \inf(A + B) = \inf A + \inf B. Indeed -(A + B) = (-A) + (-B), since -(a + b) = (-a) + (-b). By @thm-inf-neg-sup (a), -A and -B are nonempty and bounded above, so (a) and @thm-greatest-lower-bound give  egin{aligned} \inf(A + B) &= -\sup igl( (-A) + (-B)  igr) \ &= -\sup(-A) - \sup(-B) = \inf A + \inf B . \end{aligned} Here A + B is bounded below because -(A + B) is bounded above, by (a) and @thm-inf-neg-sup (a). (c) Fix a_0 \in A and let M \in 
R. Since B is not bounded above, M - a_0 is not an upper bound of B, so some b \in B has b > M - a_0. Then a_0 + b \in A + B and a_0 + b > M. As M was arbitrary, A + B is not bounded above. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 1: (a) says why \sup A, \sup B exist and why A + B is nonempty. - 2: (a) shows \sup A + \sup B is an upper bound of A + B, adding the two (S1) inequalities. - 3: (a) fixes an arbitrary \varepsilon > 0, obtains a \in A and b \in B, depending on \varepsilon, within \varepsilon/2 of their suprema, and concludes with @thm-sup-epsilon (\Leftarrow). - 2: (b) reduces to (a) through -(A + B) = (-A) + (-B) and @thm-greatest-lower-bound, including why A + B is bounded below. - 2: (c) produces, for an arbitrary M, an element of A + B above M. Fatal errors (0 for the step): taking a = \sup A \in A; choosing one a before \varepsilon is fixed; proving only \le in (a). A solution of (a) that proves \le and \ge separately, as in @thm-sup-sum, earns the 5 points of the second and third lines if the \ge half is complete. A solution of (b) that repeats the argument of (a) with lower bounds earns the (b) points. [C3: Find the wrong line] Each “proof” below contains a line that is false in general. Find it, give a set for which it fails, and decide whether the claim itself is true. 1. Claim. If A \subseteq 
R is nonempty and bounded above and a < 1 for every a \in A, then \sup A < 1. “Proof.” (1) Let s = \sup A. (2) Since s \in A, the hypothesis gives s < 1. (3) Hence \sup A < 1. 2. Claim. If A, B \subseteq 
R are nonempty and bounded above, then \sup(A + B) \ge \sup A + \sup B. “Proof.” (1) Let a = \sup A and b = \sup B. (2) Then a \in A and b \in B, so a + b \in A + B. (3) By (S1), a + b \le \sup(A + B), which is the claim. (a) Line (2) is wrong: it assumes \sup A \in A, which fails for A = (0, 1), where \sup A = 1 
otin A. For that set the claim is false: every element is less than 1, and \sup A = 1 
ot< 1. The correct conclusion is \sup A \le 1, which follows from (S2) because 1 is an upper bound. (b) Line (2) is wrong for the same reason: for A = B = (0, 1), neither supremum belongs to its set, so a + b = 2 need not lie in A + B = (0, 2), and here it does not. The claim is true, since it is half of @thm-sup-sum, but this argument does not prove it; a correct argument for this inequality is the \varepsilon/2 argument in the proof of @thm-sup-sum. The flawed line is valid exactly when A and B have maxima, which is the situation the author of the “proof” silently imagined.

title: 1.5 The Archimedean Property
content:
The Archimedean Property We now have the least upper bound axiom (@ax-least-upper-bound) and a way to use it, the characterization of the supremum by \varepsilon (@thm-sup-epsilon). This section draws the first consequence, one that looks too obvious to need proof: the natural numbers eventually pass every real number. When we first met suprema, we claimed that \sup \{ 1 - 1/n : n \in 
Z_{>0} \} = 1 and postponed the proof, because it needs exactly this fact. Here we prove the fact from the axiom, pay off that claim, and then meet an ordered field where the fact is false, so that we can see which line of the proof the axiom is holding up. Where the natural numbers live So far 
R is an ordered field satisfying one extra axiom. The numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, \dots are in it, since 2 is 1 + 1, 3 is 2 + 1, and so on. But “and so on” is not a definition. We want the set you get by starting at 0 and adding 1 again and again, and nothing else. The first half of that description is easy to state as a property of a set. [Inductive set] A subset S \subseteq 
R is inductive if 1. 0 \in S, and 2. for every x \in S, also x + 1 \in S. In words: an inductive set contains 0, and it is closed under the step “add one”. Nothing stops it from containing other numbers as well. Some examples, checked clause by clause. - 
R itself is inductive: it contains 0, and x + 1 is a real number whenever x is. - [0, \infty) = \{ x \in 
R : x \ge 0 \} is inductive: 0 \ge 0, and x \ge 0 gives x + 1 \ge 0 + 1 > 0. - \{ 0 \} \cup [1, \infty) is inductive. From 0 we step to 1, which is in [1, \infty), and [1, \infty) is closed under adding 1. A nonexample by minimal change: [0, 5] contains 0, so (N1) holds, but 4.5 \in [0, 5] and 5.5 
otin [0, 5], so (N2) fails. Chopping the top off [0, \infty) destroys closure under the step. The inductive sets above are too big: [0, \infty) contains 1.5 and 4.7. What we want is the smallest one. Intersecting all of them throws away everything that some inductive set can do without. The set of natural numbers is 
N \coloneqq \{ x \in 
R : x \in S 	ext{ for every inductive set } S \subseteq 
R \}, that is, the real numbers that belong to every inductive subset of 
R. Two things are true of 
N, and both follow at once from the definition. - 
N is inductive. Every inductive set contains 0, so 0 \in 
N. If x \in 
N, then x lies in every inductive set S, and each such S then contains x + 1 by (N2); so x + 1 \in 
N. - 
N is contained in every inductive set, since it is their intersection. The second property is the principle of induction (@fd1:ax-induction) in disguise. To prove that a statement P(n) holds for every n \in 
N, let S \coloneqq \{ n \in 
N : P(n) \}. If P(0) holds and P(n) implies P(n + 1), then S is inductive, so 
N \subseteq S, and P(n) holds for all n \in 
N. [Every nonzero natural number is at least 1] Show that n \ge 1 for every n \in 
N with n 
e 0, and deduce that for such n, 1/n is defined and 0 < 1/n \le 1. The set \{ 0 \} \cup [1, \infty) is inductive, as checked above. Since 
N is contained in every inductive set, 
N \subseteq \{ 0 \} \cup [1, \infty), that is, n \ge 1 for every n \in 
N with n 
e 0. In particular such an n is positive, so 1/n is defined. From 0 < 1 \le n @thm-ordered-field-rules (f) gives 0 < 1/n \le 1/1 = 1. The proof never mentioned a single natural number by name. It found an inductive set containing the property we wanted, and let the definition of 
N do the rest. That is the whole technique. The nonzero natural numbers are the positive integers, 
Z_{>0} \coloneqq \{ n \in 
N : n 
e 0 \} = \{ n \in 
N : n \ge 1 \}, the two descriptions agreeing by @exm-naturals-at-least-one. This is the set \{ 1, 2, 3, \dots \} that indexed our examples informally before; from here on it is a defined subset of 
R, and 1/n is defined and positive for every n \in 
Z_{>0}. Logic and Proof, Chapter 3 takes induction as a basic property of 
N (@fd1:ax-induction), and Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 2 proves well-ordering and the arithmetic below from it. The set defined here is that same 
N, now located inside 
R; it is also the copy 0, 1, 1 + 1, 1 + 1 + 1, \dots that every ordered field contains (@exr-ordered-fields-c1), and “
N is the smallest inductive set” is exactly the induction principle of Logic and Proof, Chapter 3, in the form “every inductive subset of 
N is all of 
N”. From now on we use the familiar arithmetic of 
N, each item proved by induction in Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 2: sums and products of natural numbers are natural numbers; if n \in 
N and n \ge 1, then n - 1 \in 
N; no natural number lies strictly between n and n + 1; and every nonempty subset of 
N has a least element (well-ordering). The integers are 
Z \coloneqq 
N \cup \{ -n : n \in 
N \}, and the rationals are 
Q \coloneqq \{ m/n : m \in 
Z, \ n \in 
Z_{>0} \}, with 
Z_{>0} the positive integers defined above. We also use, again from Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 2, that sums, differences, and products of integers are integers. The integers n > 0 are exactly the elements of 
Z_{>0}: such an integer is not -m with m \in 
N, since -m \le 0, so it is a nonzero natural number; conversely, a nonzero natural number is > 0 by @exm-naturals-at-least-one. So 
Z_{>0} = \{ n \in 
Z : n > 0 \}. The natural numbers are not bounded Is 
N bounded above in 
R? Everyone’s picture of the number line says no: the marks 1, 2, 3, \dots march off to the right forever. But a picture is not a proof, and here the picture hides something. Nothing in the ordered-field axioms (@def-ordered-field) forbids a number larger than every natural number. At the end of this section we build an ordered field that contains one. So if 
R has no such number, the reason must be the one axiom that 
R has and that field lacks. [Archimedean Property] The set 
N is not bounded above in 
R; in other words, every real number x is exceeded by some n \in 
N. Suppose 
N had an upper bound. Then the axiom hands us the least one, s = \sup 
N. Every natural number n has a successor n + 1 that is still a natural number, and so still at most s. Moving back one step, n \le s - 1 for every n: the smaller number s - 1 is an upper bound too. A least upper bound with a smaller upper bound below it is absurd. Suppose, for contradiction, that 
N is bounded above. The set 
N is nonempty, since 0 \in 
N. By @ax-least-upper-bound, 
N has a supremum s \coloneqq \sup 
N \in 
R. Let n \in 
N. Since 
N is inductive, n + 1 \in 
N, and since s is an upper bound of 
N, n + 1 \le s, that is, n \le s - 1. As n was arbitrary, s - 1 is an upper bound of 
N. Property (S2) of the supremum (@def-supremum) now gives s \le s - 1, that is, 1 \le 0, which contradicts 0 < 1. Therefore 
N is not bounded above. Unwinding the definition (@def-bounded-above), no x \in 
R is an upper bound of 
N: for every x \in 
R it is false that n \le x for all n \in 
N. So for every x some n \in 
N has n 
ot\le x, that is, n > x by trichotomy. This proves the theorem. Each hypothesis of the axiom was used and named: “nonempty” through 0 \in 
N, “bounded above” through the assumption for contradiction. The inductive property of 
N supplied the jump n \mapsto n + 1. The contradiction step is ulename{
eg I} (@fd1:def-rules-negation), not ulename{RAA} (@fd1:def-rule-raa), the classical rule of proof by contradiction: we assumed “
N is bounded above”, reached a contradiction, and concluded its negation. Inside that box every step is direct. The proof shows that s - 1 is an upper bound; it does not argue “s - 1 is not an upper bound, so some n exceeds s - 1”, a step that would itself need the classical law described next. The proof’s one classical step comes after the ulename{
eg I}, in its last paragraph. Passing from “not every n satisfies n \le x” to “some n satisfies n > x” is the quantifier law “not all” gives “some not” of Logic and Proof, Chapter 4, and that law is derived there with ulename{RAA}. The form we will use most often puts a small number, not a large one, in the role of x. For every \varepsilon > 0 there is n \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/n < \varepsilon. In symbols, ( orall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists n \in 
Z_{>0}) \quad  rac{1}{n} < \varepsilon . Moreover, every m \in 
Z_{>0} with m \ge n then also satisfies 1/m < \varepsilon. Let \varepsilon > 0. Then 1/\varepsilon is defined and positive. By @thm-naturals-unbounded applied to x = 1/\varepsilon, there is n \in 
N with n > 1/\varepsilon > 0; so n \in 
Z_{>0}. Taking reciprocals reverses a strict inequality between positive numbers (@thm-ordered-field-rules (f)), so 1/n < \varepsilon. If m \ge n, then 1/m \le 1/n < \varepsilon by the same rule. Read the quantifiers in order. The \varepsilon is given first and the n is found afterwards, so n depends on \varepsilon: the proof chose n > 1/\varepsilon, and a smaller \varepsilon forces a larger n. Swapping the quantifiers gives a false statement. “There is n \in 
Z_{>0} such that 1/n < \varepsilon for every \varepsilon > 0” would make 1/n smaller than every positive number. Since 1/n > 0 (@exm-naturals-at-least-one), we could take \varepsilon = 1/n itself and get 1/n < 1/n, which is absurd. The “moreover” clause says that once one n works, every later one works too. Chapter 2 turns this “from some point on” into the definition of a limit. Find the least n \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/n < 0.003. Then do the same for \varepsilon = 0.0003. What does the comparison say about the dependence of n on \varepsilon? For positive n, 1/n < 0.003 is equivalent to n > 1/0.003 = 333.\overline{3}. The least positive integer with this property is n = 334; indeed 1/333 = 0.003003\ldots is too big. For \varepsilon = 0.0003 the condition is n > 3333.\overline{3}, so the least n is 3334. Dividing \varepsilon by 10 multiplied the least n by about 10. No single n serves every \varepsilon, which is why the quantifiers read “for every \varepsilon there is n” and not the other way round. Paying an old debt In @exm-sup-one-minus-reciprocal we showed that 1 is an upper bound of A = \{ 1 - 1/n : n \in 
Z_{>0} \} and that A has no maximum. We stopped short of \sup A = 1, because (S2) needed an n with 1/n below a given positive number. That is exactly what @cor-archimedean-epsilon supplies, and the \varepsilon-characterization tells us what remains to be shown. [The supremum is 1] Let A \coloneqq \{ 1 - 1/n : n \in 
Z_{>0} \}. Prove that \sup A = 1. The set A is nonempty, since 0 = 1 - 1/1 \in A. Upper bound. For every n \in 
Z_{>0} we have 1/n > 0 (@exm-naturals-at-least-one), so 1 - 1/n < 1. Hence 1 is an upper bound of A. An element in every band below 1. Let \varepsilon > 0. By @cor-archimedean-epsilon there is n \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/n < \varepsilon; this n depends on \varepsilon. Then a \coloneqq 1 - 1/n \in A and a > 1 - \varepsilon. Since 1 is an upper bound of A and every band (1 - \varepsilon, 1] contains an element of A, @thm-sup-epsilon gives \sup A = 1. For a concrete instance, \varepsilon = 0.01 needs n > 100, and n = 101 gives the element 1 - 1/101 = 100/101 > 0.99. Together with @exm-sup-one-minus-reciprocal, A is a set whose supremum 1 is not attained. The pattern of this example, “upper bound, then an element in every band below it”, is the one every supremum computation in this book follows. The only new input here was @cor-archimedean-epsilon, which turns “1/n is small” into a precise choice of n. An ordered field without the Archimedean property We claimed that the Archimedean property does not follow from the ordered-field axioms alone. Now we back that up with a concrete field containing an element larger than every natural number. The field is made of fractions of polynomials, and the element is the variable x itself. A rational function is a quotient p/q of real polynomials p and q with q not the zero polynomial. Two quotients p/q and p'/q' are the same element when p q' = p' q, exactly as for fractions of integers. With the usual addition and multiplication of fractions, the rational functions form a field, written 
R(x). This is the same construction that builds 
Q out of 
Z, applied to polynomials; it is algebra, and we take it as known without proof here. The real numbers sit inside 
R(x) as the constant functions. The leading coefficient of a nonzero polynomial is the coefficient of its highest power of x. For instance, the leading coefficient of 3 - 2x^2 is -2. Call a nonzero p/q \in 
R(x) positive if the leading coefficients of p and q are both positive or both negative, and write f < g when g - f is positive. Here is the picture behind this definition. For large real t, the value p(t)/q(t) has the sign of the product of the two leading coefficients, because the top powers dominate. So “f > 0” means “f(t) > 0 for all sufficiently large t”, and f < g means that the graph of g eventually lies above the graph of f. This is only a picture: the definition uses leading coefficients and nothing else. Positivity does not depend on how the fraction is written. Suppose p/q = p'/q', so that p q' = p' q, and let \alpha,  eta, \alpha',  eta' be the leading coefficients of p, q, p', q'. The leading coefficient of a product of polynomials is the product of their leading coefficients, so \alpha  eta' = \alpha'  eta. Multiplying both sides by  eta  eta' gives \alpha eta \cdot  eta'^2 = \alpha' eta' \cdot  eta^2, and  eta^2,  eta'^2 > 0. Hence \alpha eta and \alpha' eta' have the same sign: p/q is positive exactly when p'/q' is. With this order 
R(x) is an ordered field. The key facts are that sums and products of positive elements are positive, and that for each nonzero f exactly one of f and -f is positive. Checking these is routine, and @exr-archimedean-property-c2 walks through them. On the constants, the new order is the old one: the constant c is positive exactly when c > 0. The example below uses that 
R(x) is an ordered field, and with it the rules of @thm-ordered-field-rules, which hold in every ordered field; so it rests on @exr-archimedean-property-c2, where that is proved. The natural numbers of 
R(x), the smallest inductive subset in the sense of @def-inductive-set, are the constants 0, 1, 2, 3, \dots. Indeed, the constant functions n with n \in 
N form an inductive subset of 
R(x): it contains the constant 0, and the constant n plus 1 is the constant n + 1. So every natural number of 
R(x) is such a constant. Conversely, let I be an inductive subset of 
R(x). The set of n \in 
N whose constant lies in I contains 0 and passes from n to n + 1, so it is an inductive subset of 
R and contains all of 
N. So every constant n lies in every inductive subset of 
R(x). [A non-Archimedean field] In 
R(x) with the order just described, show that n < x for every n \in 
N. Deduce that 
N is bounded above in 
R(x), and that @cor-archimedean-epsilon fails in 
R(x). Let n \in 
N. Then x - n = (x - n)/1. The numerator x - n has leading coefficient 1 and the denominator 1 has leading coefficient 1. They have the same sign, so x - n is positive, that is, n < x. Hence x is an upper bound of 
N in 
R(x), and 
N is bounded above there. So the conclusion of @thm-naturals-unbounded is false in 
R(x). Now take \varepsilon \coloneqq 1/x. It is positive: numerator 1 and denominator x both have leading coefficient 1. For each n \in 
Z_{>0} we have 0 < n < x, so taking reciprocals gives 1/x < 1/n. No positive integer n satisfies 1/n < \varepsilon, and @cor-archimedean-epsilon fails. The element 1/x is positive yet smaller than every 1/n: an “infinitely small” number. The real line has none, and that is exactly what @cor-archimedean-epsilon says. The line of the proof that fails Every step in the proof of @thm-naturals-unbounded, except one, is valid in any ordered field. So let us run the proof in 
R(x) and watch where it breaks. - “Suppose 
N is bounded above.” In 
R(x) this is true, with upper bound x. - “
N is nonempty.” True. - “By @ax-least-upper-bound, 
N has a supremum s.” This is the line that fails. In 
R(x), 
N has no least upper bound at all. Indeed, let M be any upper bound of 
N in 
R(x). For each n \in 
N, also n + 1 \in 
N, so n + 1 \le M, that is, n \le M - 1. Hence M - 1 is also an upper bound, and it is strictly smaller than M. No upper bound is the least one. - The remaining lines, “n + 1 \le s for every n \in 
N, so s - 1 is an upper bound, and (S2) gives s \le s - 1”, use only the ordered-field axioms and the fact that 
N is inductive. They would go through in 
R(x) if there were an s to apply them to. The argument that shows 
N has no supremum in 
R(x) is the middle paragraph of the proof of @thm-naturals-unbounded, with M in place of s. That proof showed that a supremum of 
N cannot exist in any ordered field; the axiom then says that, in 
R, a bounded 
N would have to have one. In 
R(x) there is no axiom to force it, so no contradiction arises. Two conclusions follow: - 
R(x) is an ordered field in which @ax-least-upper-bound fails, with witness the nonempty, bounded-above set 
N. - In any ordered field, the least upper bound axiom implies the Archimedean property. That is precisely what our proof showed. The Archimedean property is not “obvious”, and it is not a consequence of the ordered-field axioms. It is exactly what 
R(x) lacks, where x exceeds every natural number. In 
R it holds only because of the least upper bound axiom. A proof that says “choose an integer larger than x” is using @thm-naturals-unbounded, and should cite it. The converse fails: an ordered field can be Archimedean without satisfying the axiom. The field 
Q is one (@exr-archimedean-property-c3), and it fails the axiom by @thm-no-rational-sup-sqrt2. So the Archimedean property is strictly weaker than the axiom. Chapter 11 shows which properties, added to the Archimedean property, bring back the full axiom. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Write the Archimedean property “for every x \in 
R there is n \in 
N with n > x” in symbols, and write its negation in symbols. 2. Which of the following subsets of 
R are inductive: [	frac12, \infty), [0, 10], 
N \cup \{ 	frac12 \}, 
Z? Name the failing clause for each one that is not. 3. True or false, with a reason: in @cor-archimedean-epsilon, one n can be chosen that works for every \varepsilon > 0. 4. In the proof of @thm-naturals-unbounded, which line uses the least upper bound axiom, and which line uses that 
N is inductive? (a) The property is ( orall x \in 
R)(\exists n \in 
N)\ n > x. Its negation is (\exists x \in 
R)( orall n \in 
N)\ n \le x: some real number is an upper bound of 
N. (b) [	frac12, \infty) is not: 0 
otin [	frac12, \infty), so (N1) fails, although x \ge 	frac12 gives x + 1 \ge 	frac32 \ge 	frac12, so (N2) holds. [0, 10] is not: it contains 0, but 10 \in [0, 10] and 11 
otin [0, 10], so (N2) fails. 
N \cup \{ 	frac12 \} is not: 	frac12 is in it but 	frac32 is not, since 	frac32 lies strictly between the natural numbers 1 and 2; so (N2) fails. 
Z is inductive: 0 \in 
Z, and k + 1 \in 
Z for every integer k. (c) False. Such an n would satisfy 1/n < \varepsilon for every \varepsilon > 0. But 1/n > 0 by @exm-naturals-at-least-one, so \varepsilon = 1/n is allowed, and it gives 1/n < 1/n, which is absurd. The n must depend on \varepsilon. (d) The axiom is used in “
N has a supremum s”. That 
N is inductive is used in “n + 1 \in 
N”. B. Practice [B1: An infimum] Prove that \inf \{ 1/n : n \in 
Z_{>0} \} = 0, and that the set has no minimum. Let B \coloneqq \{ 1/n : n \in 
Z_{>0} \}; it is nonempty, since 1 \in B. By @exm-naturals-at-least-one, 1/n > 0 for every n, so 0 is a lower bound of B. Let L be any lower bound of B; we show L \le 0. Suppose instead L > 0. By @cor-archimedean-epsilon with \varepsilon = L, there is n \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/n < L. This contradicts L being a lower bound of B. Hence L \le 0. So 0 is a lower bound that is greater than or equal to every lower bound, that is, \inf B = 0 (@def-infimum). Since 0 
otin B (every element is positive), the infimum is not attained, and B has no minimum. [B2: Scaled Archimedes] Let a > 0 and y \in 
R. Prove that there is n \in 
N with n a > y. What does this say when a is the length of a measuring stick? Since a > 0, the number y/a is defined. By @thm-naturals-unbounded there is n \in 
N with n > y/a; the n depends on y and a. Multiplying by a > 0 preserves the strict inequality (@thm-ordered-field-rules (c)), so n a > y. In words: laying a stick of length a, however short, end to end enough times carries you past any given point y, however far away. This is the form in which Archimedes used the property. [B3: Smaller than every 1/n] Let x \in 
R with 0 \le x < 1/n for every n \in 
Z_{>0}. Prove that x = 0. Then deduce: if a, b \in 
R satisfy \abs{a - b} < 1/n for every n \in 
Z_{>0}, then a = b. Suppose x 
e 0. Since x \ge 0, we get x > 0. By @cor-archimedean-epsilon with \varepsilon = x, there is n \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/n < x, contradicting the hypothesis x < 1/n. Hence x = 0. For the second statement, put x \coloneqq \abs{a - b}. Then 0 \le x < 1/n for every n, so x = 0 by the first part, that is, a = b. This is how equality is proved in analysis over and over: show that the distance is nonnegative and smaller than every 1/n. [B4: Putting a proof in order] Here are nine lines. Seven of them, in a suitable order, prove that \sup A = 1 for A \coloneqq \{  rac{n}{n + 1} : n \in 
N \}. Give an admissible order. Then say why each of the other two lines cannot be used. 1. Let \varepsilon > 0. 2. Hence a \coloneqq  rac{n}{n + 1} is an element of A with a > 1 - \varepsilon. 3. For every n \in 
N, n < n + 1 and n + 1 > 0, so  rac{n}{n + 1} < 1. Hence 1 is an upper bound of A. 4. By @cor-archimedean-epsilon there is n \in 
Z_{>0}, depending on \varepsilon, with  rac1n < \varepsilon. 5. Choose n \in 
Z_{>0} such that  rac1n < \varepsilon for every \varepsilon > 0. 6. Since \varepsilon > 0 was arbitrary, every band (1 - \varepsilon, 1] contains an element of A. 7. Then  rac{n}{n + 1} = 1 -  rac1{n + 1}, and  rac1{n + 1} <  rac1n < \varepsilon. 8. By @thm-sup-epsilon, \sup A = 1. 9. Fix n \in 
Z_{>0} and let \varepsilon \coloneqq  rac1n; then  rac{n}{n + 1} = 1 -  rac1{n + 1} > 1 - \varepsilon. An admissible order is (iii), (i), (iv), (vii), (ii), (vi), (viii). The line (iii) may stand anywhere before (viii), since it uses nothing but the definition of A. The other lines admit only this order. Inside the block that starts with (i), line (iv) needs the \varepsilon of (i), line (vii) needs the n of (iv), line (ii) needs (vii), and (vi) records that \varepsilon was arbitrary. Line (viii) needs both (iii) and (vi), the two hypotheses of @thm-sup-epsilon. Line (v) has the quantifiers in the wrong order. It asks for one n that works for every \varepsilon, and there is none: \varepsilon =  rac1n itself would give  rac1n <  rac1n. @cor-archimedean-epsilon gives an n for each \varepsilon. Line (ix) is true, but its \varepsilon is of the wrong kind: it is chosen to fit n, instead of being given first. It shows only that the bands of the special widths  rac1n meet A, while @thm-sup-epsilon needs every band, of every width \varepsilon > 0. Passing from the special widths to all widths is exactly the work of lines (iv) and (vii), which (ix) skips. C. Going deeper [C1: Exit check: the Archimedean property, and a circular proof] 1. Without looking back, prove the Archimedean property from the least upper bound axiom. Mark the line that uses the axiom, and explain why that line fails in 
R(x). 2. A student offers the following proof. “Let x \in 
R. Let n \coloneqq \ceil{x} + 1, where \ceil{x} is the least integer that is greater than or equal to x. Then n > x.” Find the gap. Show that in 
R(x) the element x has no “least integer greater than or equal to it”. (a) Suppose 
N is bounded above in 
R. Since 0 \in 
N, the set is nonempty, so by @ax-least-upper-bound it has a supremum s (this line uses the axiom). For every n \in 
N, also n + 1 \in 
N, since 
N is inductive, so n + 1 \le s by (S1), that is, n \le s - 1. Hence s - 1 is an upper bound of 
N, and (S2) gives s \le s - 1, which is false. So 
N is not bounded above, which means that every x \in 
R is exceeded by some n \in 
N. In 
R(x) the set 
N is nonempty and bounded above by x (@exm-nonarchimedean-field), but it has no supremum. Any upper bound M gives a smaller one, M - 1, because n + 1 \le M for every n \in 
N forces n \le M - 1. So the marked line has nothing to produce, and there the proof stops. (b) The gap is the existence of \ceil{x}. The set \{ k \in 
Z : k \ge x \} has a least element only if it is nonempty, and it is nonempty exactly when some integer is at least x. That is (a form of) the Archimedean property, the statement being proved. The proof is circular. In 
R(x), take the element x and suppose k \in 
Z satisfies k \ge x. If k \le 0, then k \le 0 < 1 < x. If k \ge 1, then k \in 
N and k < x by @exm-nonarchimedean-field. Either way k < x, a contradiction. So no integer is greater than or equal to x, and \ceil{x} does not exist. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 1: (a) supposes, for a contradiction, that 
N is bounded above, and notes 0 \in 
N. - 2: (a) obtains s = \sup 
N from @ax-least-upper-bound, with both hypotheses checked, and marks this line. - 2: (a) shows that s - 1 is an upper bound of 
N: n + 1 \in 
N because 
N is inductive, so n + 1 \le s by (S1), that is, n \le s - 1, for every n \in 
N. - 1: (a) applies the “least” property (S2) to the upper bound s - 1, reaches s \le s - 1, a contradiction, and concludes. - 1: (a) explains why the marked line fails in 
R(x): every upper bound M of 
N there has the smaller upper bound M - 1. - 2: (b) names the existence of \ceil{x} as the gap, and says it already needs an integer at least x, which is what is being proved. - 1: (b) shows that no integer is at least x in 
R(x). Fatal errors (0 for the step): taking s to be a natural number, or the maximum of 
N; omitting “for every n” (one n with n \le s - 1 does not make s - 1 an upper bound); using \ceil{x},  loor{x}, or the Archimedean property inside (a). A proof of (a) that argues “by (S2), or @thm-sup-epsilon with \varepsilon = 1, s - 1 is not an upper bound, so some n > s - 1, and then n + 1 > s” is also correct and earns the same 3 points for those steps; it uses one more classical step, inside the box (the remark after @thm-naturals-unbounded). A proof of (a) that applies the axiom to a bounded set of the form \{ n \in 
N : n \le x \} instead earns full marks for (a) if it reaches a contradiction from the supremum in the same way. [C2: The order on the rational functions] Let P \subseteq 
R(x) be the set of positive elements defined in this section, and let f < g mean g - f \in P. 1. Show that every nonzero f \in 
R(x) can be written as p/q with the leading coefficient of q positive, and that then f \in P if and only if the leading coefficient of p is positive. 2. Show that for every nonzero f, exactly one of f \in P and -f \in P holds. 3. Show that if f, g \in P, then f g \in P and f + g \in P. 4. Deduce the order axioms of @def-ordered-field for <: trichotomy, transitivity, f < g \Rightarrow f + h < g + h, and f, g > 0 \Rightarrow f g > 0. [Hint 1] Choose good representatives first. Every fraction can be rewritten so that its denominator has positive leading coefficient, and after that only the numerator decides positivity. [Hint 2] For the sum in (c), with both denominators normalized, write f + g = (p_1 q_2 + p_2 q_1)/(q_1 q_2) and split into two cases: the two terms of the numerator have different degrees, or the same degree. Write \operatorname{lc}(p) for the leading coefficient of a nonzero polynomial p. Recall that \operatorname{lc}(pq) = \operatorname{lc}(p)\operatorname{lc}(q), since the top powers multiply. (a) Let f = p/q. If \operatorname{lc}(q) < 0, then f = (-p)/(-q) and \operatorname{lc}(-q) = -\operatorname{lc}(q) > 0. So we may assume \operatorname{lc}(q) > 0. Then “\operatorname{lc}(p) and \operatorname{lc}(q) have the same sign” means exactly \operatorname{lc}(p) > 0. By the well-definedness shown in the section, this does not depend on the chosen representation. (b) Write f = p/q with \operatorname{lc}(q) > 0, as in (a). Then -f = (-p)/q and \operatorname{lc}(-p) = -\operatorname{lc}(p). Since p 
e 0, \operatorname{lc}(p) is a nonzero real number, so by trichotomy in 
R exactly one of \operatorname{lc}(p) > 0 and -\operatorname{lc}(p) > 0 holds. By (a), exactly one of f \in P and -f \in P holds. (c) Write f = p_1/q_1 and g = p_2/q_2 with all four leading coefficients positive, using (a). The product is f g = (p_1 p_2)/(q_1 q_2) with \operatorname{lc}(p_1 p_2) = \operatorname{lc}(p_1)\operatorname{lc}(p_2) > 0 and \operatorname{lc}(q_1 q_2) > 0, so f g \in P. The sum is f + g =  rac{p_1 q_2 + p_2 q_1}{q_1 q_2}. Both p_1 q_2 and p_2 q_1 have positive leading coefficient. If their degrees differ, the leading coefficient of the sum is that of the term of higher degree, which is positive. If their degrees agree, it is the sum of the two leading coefficients, which is positive. In both cases the numerator is nonzero with positive leading coefficient, and \operatorname{lc}(q_1 q_2) > 0, so f + g \in P. (d) Trichotomy. Given f, g, either g - f = 0, or g - f 
e 0 and by (b) exactly one of g - f \in P and f - g = -(g - f) \in P holds. So exactly one of f = g, f < g, g < f holds. Transitivity. If f < g and g < h, then g - f \in P and h - g \in P, so h - f = (h - g) + (g - f) \in P by (c); that is, f < h. Addition. If f < g, then (g + h) - (f + h) = g - f \in P, so f + h < g + h. Products. If f > 0 and g > 0, then f = f - 0 \in P and g \in P, so f g \in P by (c); that is, f g > 0. [C3: Archimedean without the axiom] 1. Prove, without using @ax-least-upper-bound, that for every r \in 
Q there is n \in 
N with n > r. 2. Deduce that the Archimedean property does not imply the least upper bound axiom in an ordered field. (a) Write r = m/k with m \in 
Z and k \in 
Z_{>0}. If m \le 0, then r \le 0 < 1, and n = 1 works. If m \ge 1, then m \in 
N. Since k \ge 1 (@exm-naturals-at-least-one) and m > 0, we get r = m/k \le m < m + 1, and n \coloneqq m + 1 \in 
N works. No supremum was used: only the arithmetic of integers and the ordered-field rules. (b) By (a), 
Q is an ordered field in which 
N is not bounded above, so 
Q has the Archimedean property. By @thm-no-rational-sup-sqrt2, the nonempty set \{ x \in 
Q : x > 0, \ x^2 < 2 \}, which is bounded above by 2, has no supremum in 
Q. So 
Q is Archimedean and fails the least upper bound axiom, and the Archimedean property cannot imply the axiom.

title: 1.6 Density of the Rationals and the Existence of Roots
content:
Density of the Rationals and the Existence of Roots When we first met suprema, @thm-no-rational-sup-sqrt2 showed that the set of positive rationals whose square is less than 2 has no supremum in 
Q. In 
R the axiom gives that set a supremum. This section finds out what the supremum is: a positive number whose square is exactly 2. The same template produces every root a^{1/n}. With roots in hand, and with the Archimedean property of the previous section, we then answer a question about arrangement: the rationals and the irrationals are both spread through every interval of the line, however short. Constructing a point as a supremum Logic and Proof, Chapter 2 showed that no rational number squares to 2 (@fd1:thm-sqrt2-irrational). Nothing so far says that any real number does. The ordered-field axioms cannot say it, since 
Q satisfies them all. So if a square root of 2 exists in 
R, the least upper bound axiom must produce it. [The Square Root of Two Exists] There is exactly one real number s > 0 with s^2 = 2. Try it first (ten minutes): the axiom is the only statement we have that produces a real number. To which set would you apply it, and what would you then have to show? The obvious attempts do not get started. There is no formula for \sqrt 2 in terms of rationals, and the decimals 1, 1.4, 1.41, \dots of the chapter’s introduction would need a limit, which we do not have yet. The only statement that produces a real number is @ax-least-upper-bound, so \sqrt 2 will have to be a supremum, and @thm-no-rational-sup-sqrt2 suggests which one. Collect the positive reals whose square is below 2 into a set S. The candidate is s = \sup S. The plan has three steps: ① check that S is nonempty and bounded above, so the axiom supplies s; ② rule out s^2 < 2; ③ rule out s^2 > 2. Trichotomy then leaves s^2 = 2. Each case is ruled out by nudging s. If s^2 < 2, there is still room below 2, so a slightly larger number s + h is still in S. That is impossible for an upper bound. If s^2 > 2, a slightly smaller number s - h still has square above 2, and is therefore still an upper bound. That is impossible for the least upper bound. The nudges are the ones found in @thm-no-rational-sup-sqrt2, where they were derived backwards from the goal. To recall the first: we want (s + h)^2 = s^2 + 2sh + h^2 < 2. If h \le 1, then h^2 \le h, so (s + h)^2 \le s^2 + (2s + 1)h. Letting (2s + 1)h use half of the room 2 - s^2 gives h = (2 - s^2)/(4s + 2), and we must then check h \le 1. For the second nudge, (s - h)^2 > s^2 - 2sh, and the right side is 2 exactly when h = (s^2 - 2)/(2s). None of this used rationality. What is new is only that s now exists. Before reading on: which line of the proof uses the axiom, and what would that line say over 
Q? Let S \coloneqq \{ x \in 
R : x > 0, \ x^2 < 2 \}. By @exm-lub-first-use, S is nonempty (it contains 1) and bounded above by 2, so by @ax-least-upper-bound its supremum s \coloneqq \sup S exists, and 1 \le s \le 2. In particular s > 0 and s^2 \ge 1. Throughout we use @thm-ordered-field-rules (g): for u, v \ge 0, u < v if and only if u^2 < v^2. Case 1: s^2 < 2. Let h \coloneqq  rac{2 - s^2}{4s + 2}, which depends only on s. Then h > 0, because 2 - s^2 > 0 and 4s + 2 > 0. Also h \le 	frac16, because 2 - s^2 \le 1 and 4s + 2 \ge 6. Hence h \le 1, and multiplying by h > 0 gives h^2 \le h. Therefore  egin{aligned} (s + h)^2 &= s^2 + 2sh + h^2 \le s^2 + (2s + 1)h \ &= s^2 + 	frac{2 - s^2}{2} = 1 + 	frac{s^2}{2} < 2, \end{aligned} where the last inequality holds because s^2 < 2. Also s + h > 0. Hence s + h \in S. But s + h > s, which contradicts (S1), that s is an upper bound of S. So Case 1 is impossible. Case 2: s^2 > 2. Let h \coloneqq  rac{s^2 - 2}{2s}, which is defined and positive because s > 0 and s^2 > 2. Then s - h = (s^2 + 2)/(2s) > 0, and (s - h)^2 = s^2 - 2sh + h^2 = 2 + h^2 > 2 . We claim that s - h is an upper bound of S. Let x \in S and suppose x > s - h. Since s - h > 0, we get x^2 > (s - h)^2 > 2, contradicting x^2 < 2. Hence x \le s - h for every x \in S. Then (S2) gives s \le s - h, which is false since h > 0. So Case 2 is impossible. By trichotomy, s^2 = 2. For uniqueness, let t > 0 with t^2 = 2. If t < s, then t^2 < s^2, and if s < t, then s^2 < t^2; both contradict t^2 = 2 = s^2. Hence t = s. This proves the theorem. We write \sqrt{2} for this number. By @fd1:thm-sqrt2-irrational it is not rational, so 
R 
e 
Q: irrational numbers exist. Compare this proof with the one of @thm-no-rational-sup-sqrt2. The two computations with h are the same, word for word: they are ordered-field algebra, and for a rational s both values of h are rational. What changed is a single line. In 
Q there was no s to start from: the argument showed that no rational number can be the supremum, since its square cannot be less than 2, more than 2, or equal to 2. In 
R the axiom supplies s, and the very same argument now shows that its square can only be 2. The proof is an instance of a move this book uses again and again. To construct a point: collect the points where “things are still fine” into a set, take its supremum, and rule out each way the supremum could fail to be the point you want. Here “things are still fine” meant x^2 < 2. The exercises of this section and of the last section of the chapter ask you to run the move yourself, with less and less of the proof given. In Chapter 6 the Intermediate Value Theorem is proved the same way: the point where a continuous function crosses zero is the supremum of the points where it is still negative. In Chapter 4 the Heine–Borel theorem takes the supremum of the points x for which [a, x] is still covered by finitely many of the given open sets. Roots of every order The template does not care that the exponent is 2 or that the number is 2. Only the choice of h needs new work. [Existence of Roots] Let a > 0 and n \in 
Z_{>0}. There is exactly one real number s > 0 with s^n = a. We write this number a^{1/n}, or \sqrt[n]{a}. For a = 0 the only real s \ge 0 with s^n = 0 is s = 0 (a product of positive numbers is positive), so we also set \sqrt[n]{0} \coloneqq 0; every a \ge 0 then has exactly one nonnegative n-th root. Take S = \{ x > 0 : x^n < a \} and s = \sup S, as before, and rule out s^n < a and s^n > a. The new difficulty is the estimate. For n = 2 we expanded (s + h)^2 and bounded h^2 by h. For general n, expanding (s + h)^n is messy. We work backwards from what we need instead. We need (s + h)^n - s^n < a - s^n. A difference of n-th powers factors: y^n - x^n = (y - x) igl( y^{n-1} + y^{n-2} x + \dots + x^{n-1}  igr). With y = s + h and x = s, the first factor is h, which we control. The second factor is a sum of n terms, each at most (s + h)^{n-1}. That still depends on h, and we cannot solve for h while h is on both sides. So we bound it by something a little bigger: if h < 1, each term is at most (s + 1)^{n-1}. This gives (s + h)^n - s^n \le h \cdot C, \qquad C \coloneqq n (s + 1)^{n-1} . The point is that C depends only on n and s, and not on h. Now it suffices to have hC < a - s^n, and h = (a - s^n)/(2C) does it, with a factor 	frac12 to make the inequality strict. We needed h < 1 along the way, so we cap h at 	frac12. For s - h the same factorization gives s^n - (s - h)^n \le h \cdot n s^{n-1} \le hC, so the same C, and the same h, serve both cases. We first prove a power estimate. Let 0 \le x < y and k \in 
Z_{>0}. Then x^k < y^k: the map x \mapsto x^k is strictly increasing on [0, \infty). Consequently x^m \le y^m for every integer m \ge 0, where u^0 \coloneqq 1. Moreover 0 < y^k - x^k \le k y^{k-1} (y - x). Powers are defined by recursion (Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 2): u^0 \coloneqq 1 and u^{k+1} \coloneqq u^k u, so that u^1 = u; here only k \ge 1 is needed. We first show 0 \le x^k < y^k by induction on k. For k = 1 this is the hypothesis. If 0 \le x^k < y^k, then x^{k+1} = x^k x \ge 0, and x^{k+1} = x^k x \le x^k y < y^k y = y^{k+1}, where the first step multiplies x < y by x^k \ge 0 (@thm-ordered-field-rules (c), or equality if x^k = 0) and the second multiplies x^k < y^k by y > 0. This proves the first statement, and the second follows, since for m = 0 both sides are 1. For the estimate, write \Sigma \coloneqq \sum_{j=0}^{k-1} y^j x^{k-1-j}. Multiplying out,  egin{aligned} (y - x)\Sigma &= \sum_{j=0}^{k-1} y^{j+1} x^{k-1-j} - \sum_{j=0}^{k-1} y^j x^{k-j} \ &= y^k - x^k, \end{aligned} since every other term appears once in each sum and cancels. Each term of \Sigma satisfies 0 \le y^j x^{k-1-j} \le y^j y^{k-1-j} = y^{k-1}, by the second statement with m = k - 1 - j, multiplied by y^j > 0; and the term with j = k - 1 equals y^{k-1} > 0. Hence 0 < \Sigma \le k y^{k-1}. Multiplying by y - x > 0 gives the claim. Let S \coloneqq \{ x \in 
R : x > 0, \ x^n < a \}. S is nonempty. Let x_0 \coloneqq a/(1 + a). Then 0 < x_0 < 1 and x_0 < a. Since 0 < x_0 < 1, multiplying by x_0 repeatedly gives x_0^n \le x_0 (by induction on n). Hence x_0^n \le x_0 < a, and x_0 \in S. S is bounded above by 1 + a. If x \ge 1 + a, then x \ge 1, so x^n \ge x (again by induction on n), and x^n \ge 1 + a > a. So x 
otin S. By @ax-least-upper-bound, s \coloneqq \sup S exists, and s \ge x_0 > 0. Let C \coloneqq n (s + 1)^{n-1}, which depends only on n and s. Suppose s^n 
e a, and let h \coloneqq \min\Bigl\{  rac12, \  rac{\abs{s^n - a}}{2C} \Bigr\} > 0 . Then hC \le 	frac12 \abs{s^n - a} < \abs{s^n - a}. Case 1: s^n < a. Apply the claim with k = n, x = s, and y = s + h. Since s + h < s + 1, the claim with m = n - 1 gives (s + h)^{n-1} \le (s + 1)^{n-1} (both sides are 1 when n = 1). Therefore (s + h)^n - s^n \le n (s + h)^{n-1} h \le C h < a - s^n , so (s + h)^n < a. Hence s + h \in S, although s + h > s. This contradicts that s is an upper bound of S. Case 2: s^n > a. First, s - h > 0. Indeed (s + 1)^{n-1} \ge s^{n-1} by the claim with m = n - 1 (both sides are 1 when n = 1), so h \le  rac{s^n - a}{2C} <  rac{s^n}{2C} \le  rac{s^n}{2 n s^{n-1}} =  rac{s}{2n} < s . Apply the claim with k = n, x = s - h, and y = s: s^n - (s - h)^n \le n s^{n-1} h \le C h < s^n - a , so (s - h)^n > a. Now s - h is an upper bound of S: if x \in S had x > s - h, the claim would give x^n > (s - h)^n > a, contradicting x \in S. But s - h < s, which contradicts that s is the least upper bound. Both cases are impossible, so s^n = a by trichotomy. If also t > 0 and t^n = a, then t = s, since t < s or s < t would give t^n 
e s^n by the claim. This proves the theorem. For n = 2 and a = 2 the constant is C = 2(s + 1), slightly larger than the 2s + 1 that the direct expansion gave. The general proof pays for its generality with a cruder bound. We never needed a good bound, only one that does not depend on h. [Locating a cube root] Show that 1.25 < \sqrt[3]{2} < 1.26. By @thm-nth-root, s \coloneqq \sqrt[3]{2} exists and s^3 = 2. Exact arithmetic gives 1.25^3 = 1.953125 < 2 < 2.000376 = 1.26^3 . The claim in the proof of @thm-nth-root says that x \mapsto x^3 is strictly increasing on [0, \infty). If s \le 1.25, then s^3 \le 1.25^3 < 2; and if s \ge 1.26, then s^3 \ge 1.26^3 > 2. Both contradict s^3 = 2, so 1.25 < s < 1.26. With n-th roots we can define a^{m/n} \coloneqq (a^{1/n})^m for a > 0, and check that the usual exponent laws hold for rational exponents. The powers a^x with irrational x wait for the exponential function, which Chapter 10 builds from power series. The integer part of a real number Before asking where the rationals are, we need to locate every real number between two consecutive integers. This sounds like school arithmetic, and it is. But its proof uses both the Archimedean property and well-ordering, and in 
R(x) it fails for the element x (@exr-archimedean-property-c1). [Integer Part] For every y \in 
R there is exactly one integer m with m \le y < m + 1. This integer is the integer part or floor of y, written  loor{y}. For instance  loor{2.7} = 2 and  loor{-2.7} = -3. Picture the integers as marks spaced 1 apart. The Archimedean property puts a mark to the right of y, and a mark to the left of y. Among the marks to the right, well-ordering picks out the first one; the mark just before it is  loor{y}. Well-ordering is a statement about subsets of 
N, so we shift the marks so that they start at 0. Existence. Let y \in 
R. By @thm-naturals-unbounded, there is p \in 
N with p > -y, and there is j \in 
N with j > y + p. Hence the set T \coloneqq \{ j \in 
N : j - p > y \} is nonempty. By well-ordering (Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 2), T has a least element j_0. Let m \coloneqq j_0 - p - 1, an integer because differences of integers are integers (the remark on 
N in the previous section). Then m + 1 = j_0 - p > y, since j_0 \in T. It remains to show m \le y. First, 0 - p = -p < y by the choice of p, so 0 
otin T and j_0 
e 0. Hence j_0 \ge 1 (@exm-naturals-at-least-one), so j_0 - 1 \in 
N (again from that remark), and j_0 - 1 
otin T because it is smaller than the least element of T. So (j_0 - 1) - p \le y, that is, m \le y. Uniqueness. Suppose m and m' are integers with m \le y < m + 1 and m' \le y < m' + 1, and suppose m < m'. Then m' - m is a positive integer, hence a nonzero natural number (the remark on 
N in the previous section), so m' - m \ge 1 by @exm-naturals-at-least-one; that is, m' \ge m + 1. Hence y \ge m' \ge m + 1 > y, a contradiction. By symmetry m' < m is impossible too, so m = m'. The rationals are dense We know now that irrational numbers exist. How are they arranged among the rationals? Could there be a whole interval with no rational number in it? No: every interval, however short, contains a rational. [Density of the Rationals] Let x, y \in 
R with x < y. There is q \in 
Q with x < q < y. Think of a ruler whose marks are the fractions k/n, spaced 1/n apart. If the spacing is smaller than the gap y - x, the ruler cannot jump over the interval (x, y): the first mark to the right of x is at most one step past x, and so it lands before y. The plan: ① choose n with 1/n < y - x, by the Archimedean property; ② let m/n be the first mark strictly to the right of x, that is, m =  loor{nx} + 1; ③ check that m/n < y. Let x < y. Then y - x > 0, so by @cor-archimedean-epsilon there is n \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/n < y - x; the n depends on x and y, through y - x. By @lem-integer-part, let m \coloneqq  loor{nx} + 1, an integer, since sums of integers are integers (the remark on 
N in the previous section). Then m - 1 \le nx < m. Therefore nx < m \le nx + 1 < nx + n(y - x) = ny , where the last inequality uses 1 < n(y - x), which is 1/n < y - x multiplied by n > 0. Dividing by n > 0 gives x < m/n < y. Since m \in 
Z and n \in 
Z_{>0}, q \coloneqq m/n is rational. This proves the theorem. [Running the proof] Follow the proof of @thm-rationals-dense to find a rational number between \sqrt{2} and 	frac32. Step ①: the spacing. We need 1/n < 	frac32 - \sqrt{2}, that is, \sqrt{2} < 	frac32 - 	frac1n. By @thm-ordered-field-rules (g), applied to the positive numbers \sqrt{2} and 	frac32 - 	frac1n, this holds exactly when 2 < (	frac32 - 	frac1n)^2. For n = 12, 	frac32 - 	frac1{12} = 	frac{17}{12} and (	frac{17}{12})^2 = 	frac{289}{144} > 	frac{288}{144} = 2, so n = 12 works. (For n = 11, (	frac{31}{22})^2 = 	frac{961}{484} < 2, so 12 is the least n that works, but any n \ge 12 would do.) Step ②: the first mark past x. We need  loor{12\sqrt{2}}. Since 16^2 = 256 \le 288 = (12\sqrt{2})^2 < 289 = 17^2, @thm-ordered-field-rules (g) gives 16 \le 12\sqrt{2} < 17, so  loor{12\sqrt{2}} = 16 and m = 17. Step ③: the answer. The proof guarantees \sqrt{2} < 	frac{17}{12} < 	frac32. Directly: (	frac{17}{12})^2 = 	frac{289}{144} > 2 gives the left inequality, and 	frac{17}{12} < 	frac{18}{12} gives the right one. The irrationals are just as widely spread. The trick is to shift the rationals by \sqrt{2}. Let x, y \in 
R with x < y. There is an irrational number z with x < z < y. Since x - \sqrt{2} < y - \sqrt{2}, @thm-rationals-dense gives q \in 
Q with x - \sqrt{2} < q < y - \sqrt{2}. Let z \coloneqq q + \sqrt{2}. Then x < z < y. If z were rational, then \sqrt{2} = z - q would be a difference of rationals, hence rational, contradicting @fd1:thm-sqrt2-irrational. So z is irrational. This is why the existence of \sqrt{2} came first in this section: the proof of @cor-irrationals-dense needs one irrational number to shift by, and @thm-sqrt2-exists supplies it. Name a rational number between \sqrt{2} and 1.415, and an irrational number between 0 and 10^{-6}. Justify both. Rational: 1.4143. Its square is 2.00024449 > 2, so 1.4143 > \sqrt{2} by @thm-ordered-field-rules (g), and 1.4143 < 1.415. Irrational: z \coloneqq \sqrt{2} \cdot 10^{-7}. Since 1 < \sqrt{2} < 2, we get 0 < z < 2 \cdot 10^{-7} < 10^{-6}. If z were rational, then \sqrt{2} = 10^7 z would be rational, contradicting @fd1:thm-sqrt2-irrational. “Dense” does not mean “next to each other”. There is no smallest positive rational number and no “next rational after 0”: if q > 0 is rational, then q/2 is a smaller positive rational. The same holds for irrationals: if z > 0 is irrational, so is z/2, and it is smaller. Between any two distinct rationals there are infinitely many more, and between any two distinct reals there are rationals and irrationals alike. Density is what makes decimals, and more generally rational approximation, possible. Every real number can be pinned down by rationals from below as closely as we like (@exr-density-and-roots-b1). In Metric and Topological Spaces the word dense becomes a notion in any metric space: a set that meets every ball. The rationals in the real line are the model example. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] True or false? Give a reason or a counterexample for each. 1. There is a least positive irrational number. 2. Between any two distinct rational numbers there is an irrational number. 3. Between any two distinct irrational numbers there is a rational number. 4. Every nonempty set of rationals that is bounded above has a supremum in 
R, and that supremum is rational. 5. In the proof of @thm-nth-root, the constant C depends on h. 6. Run Case 1 of the proof of @thm-sqrt2-exists with the value  rac75 in place of s (so s^2 =  rac{49}{25} < 2): compute h, and check that (s + h)^2 < 2. Which property of a supremum does this show  rac75 lacks? (a) False. If z > 0 is irrational, then z/2 is positive, smaller than z, and irrational (if z/2 were rational, so would be z = 2 \cdot (z/2)). (b) True, by @cor-irrationals-dense applied to the two rationals. (c) True, by @thm-rationals-dense applied to the two irrationals. (d) False. The set A \coloneqq \{ x \in 
Q : x > 0, \ x^2 < 2 \} is nonempty and bounded above by 2, so it has a supremum s \in 
R by @ax-least-upper-bound. If s were rational, it would be a rational upper bound of A that is at most every real upper bound, and in particular at most every rational one. So s would be a supremum of A in 
Q, contradicting @thm-no-rational-sup-sqrt2. (In fact s = \sqrt{2}.) (e) False. C = n(s + 1)^{n-1} depends only on n and s. It has to be independent of h, because h is then chosen in terms of C. (f) Here 2 - s^2 =  rac1{25} and 4s + 2 =  rac{38}{5}, so h =  rac{1/25}{38/5} =  rac1{190} and s + h =  rac{267}{190}. Then \Bigl(  rac{267}{190} \Bigr)^2 =  rac{71289}{36100} <  rac{72200}{36100} = 2 , and the proof’s bound gives the same: (s + h)^2 \le 1 +  rac{s^2}{2} =  rac{99}{50} < 2. So  rac{267}{190} \in S and  rac{267}{190} >  rac75: the number  rac75 is not an upper bound of S, so it fails (S1). This is no contradiction, because nothing said that  rac75 was the supremum. In the proof the same computation contradicts (S1) for s = \sup S. B. Practice [B1: Every real number is a supremum of rationals] Let x \in 
R. Prove that x = \sup \{ q \in 
Q : q < x \}. Let A \coloneqq \{ q \in 
Q : q < x \}. By @thm-rationals-dense applied to x - 1 < x, there is a rational in (x - 1, x), so A is nonempty. By definition every element of A is less than x, so x is an upper bound of A. Let \varepsilon > 0. By @thm-rationals-dense applied to x - \varepsilon < x, there is q \in 
Q with x - \varepsilon < q < x. Then q \in A and q > x - \varepsilon. By @thm-sup-epsilon, x = \sup A. [B2: The square root of three, finished] Here is the start of a proof that there is exactly one real s > 0 with s^2 = 3. Let S \coloneqq \{ x \in 
R : x > 0, \ x^2 < 3 \}. Then 1 \in S, and if x \ge 2, then x^2 \ge 4 > 3; so S is nonempty and bounded above by 2. By @ax-least-upper-bound, s \coloneqq \sup S exists, and s \ge 1. Case s^2 < 3. Let h \coloneqq (3 - s^2)/(4s + 2). Then h > 0. Since 3 - s^2 \le 2 and 4s + 2 \ge 6, we have h \le  rac13, so h^2 \le h, and (s + h)^2 \le s^2 + (2s + 1)h =  rac{3 + s^2}{2} < 3. Hence s + h \in S, and s + h > s contradicts (S1). Case s^2 > 3. \ldots Name the move, then complete it. Give an explicit h for the second case and check that it works; then finish the proof, including uniqueness. The move is construct a point as a supremum: the points where “things are still fine” (x^2 < 3) form S, the axiom supplies s = \sup S, and each way s could fail (s^2 < 3, s^2 > 3) is ruled out. The given text rules out the first; the missing step rules out the second, against (S2) this time. Case s^2 > 3. Let h \coloneqq (s^2 - 3)/(2s), which is defined and positive because s \ge 1 and s^2 > 3. Then s - h = (s^2 + 3)/(2s) > 0 and (s - h)^2 = s^2 - 2sh + h^2 = 3 + h^2 > 3 . If some x \in S had x > s - h, then, as s - h > 0, @thm-ordered-field-rules (g) would give x^2 > (s - h)^2 > 3, which is impossible for x \in S. So s - h is an upper bound of S, and (S2) gives s \le s - h, which is false since h > 0. Both cases are impossible, so s^2 = 3 by trichotomy. For uniqueness, let t > 0 with t^2 = 3. If t < s or s < t, then @thm-ordered-field-rules (g) gives t^2 < s^2 or s^2 < t^2, contradicting t^2 = 3 = s^2. Hence t = s. [B3: The cube root of five] Prove that there is exactly one real s > 0 with s^3 = 5. Hence show that 1.70 < s < 1.71. By @thm-nth-root with a = 5 and n = 3, there is exactly one s > 0 with s^3 = 5. Exact arithmetic gives 1.70^3 = 4.913 < 5 and 1.71^3 = 5.000211 > 5. By the claim in the proof of @thm-nth-root, x \mapsto x^3 is strictly increasing on [0, \infty). If s \le 1.70, then s^3 \le 4.913 < 5; if s \ge 1.71, then s^3 \ge 5.000211 > 5. Both contradict s^3 = 5, so 1.70 < s < 1.71. C. Going deeper [C1: Exit check: the square root of two, in both fields] 1. Prove that there is a real number s > 0 with s^2 = 2. 2. Prove that the set \{ x \in 
Q : x > 0, \ x^2 < 2 \} has no supremum in 
Q. 3. Both proofs use the same two values of h. Explain in two or three sentences why the same computation yields an existence theorem in 
R and a nonexistence theorem in 
Q. (a) This is @thm-sqrt2-exists. Let S \coloneqq \{ x \in 
R : x > 0, \ x^2 < 2 \}; it contains 1 and is bounded above by 2, so s \coloneqq \sup S exists by @ax-least-upper-bound, and s \ge 1. If s^2 < 2, then h \coloneqq (2 - s^2)/(4s + 2) satisfies 0 < h \le 	frac16, so h^2 \le h and (s + h)^2 \le s^2 + (2s + 1)h = 1 + s^2/2 < 2, and s + h \in S exceeds the upper bound s: impossible. If s^2 > 2, then h \coloneqq (s^2 - 2)/(2s) satisfies s - h = (s^2 + 2)/(2s) > 0 and (s - h)^2 = 2 + h^2 > 2; every x \in S then satisfies x \le s - h, since x > s - h would give x^2 > 2. So s - h < s is an upper bound, contradicting (S2). By trichotomy s^2 = 2. (b) Let A \coloneqq \{ x \in 
Q : x > 0, \ x^2 < 2 \}, and suppose r \in 
Q is a supremum of A in 
Q, that is, a rational upper bound of A that is at most every rational upper bound. As 1 \in A, r \ge 1. By @fd1:thm-sqrt2-irrational, r^2 
e 2. If r^2 < 2, let h \coloneqq (2 - r^2)/(4r + 2). This is rational, and the computation of (a) gives (r + h)^2 < 2. So r + h \in A and r + h > r, contradicting that r is an upper bound. If r^2 > 2, let h \coloneqq (r^2 - 2)/(2r). Then r - h = (r^2 + 2)/(2r) is rational and positive, with (r - h)^2 = 2 + h^2 > 2. As in (a), every x \in A satisfies x \le r - h, so r - h is a rational upper bound of A smaller than r, contradicting the choice of r. Both cases are impossible, so A has no supremum in 
Q. (c) The computation shows, in any ordered field, that a supremum of the set cannot have square less than 2 or greater than 2. In 
R the axiom guarantees that a supremum exists, so its square must be 2: existence. In 
Q no element has square 2 (@fd1:thm-sqrt2-irrational), so no case is left, and no supremum can exist. For rational r the values of h are rational, which is why the argument stays inside 
Q. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 1: (a) defines S, checks that it is nonempty and bounded above, and takes s = \sup S from @ax-least-upper-bound. - 2: (a) rules out s^2 < 2 with an explicit h > 0, verifying (s + h)^2 < 2 including any side condition such as h \le 1, and contradicts (S1). - 2: (a) rules out s^2 > 2 with an explicit h > 0, verifying s - h > 0 and that s - h is an upper bound, and contradicts (S2). - 1: (b) supposes a rational supremum r and excludes r^2 = 2 by @fd1:thm-sqrt2-irrational. - 2: (b) in each case checks that the new number is rational and derives the contradiction with “upper bound in 
Q” or “least among rational upper bounds”. - 2: (c) says that the computation excludes s^2 < 2 and s^2 > 2 in any ordered field, that in 
R the axiom supplies s so s^2 = 2 remains, and that in 
Q nothing remains.
