Fatal errors (0 for the step): using \sqrt 2 to define S or h; asserting s + h \in S or (s - h)^2 > 2 without the computation; an h that depends on an element of S rather than on s alone. A proof with a different h (for instance h = \min\{ 1, (2 - s^2)/6 \} in Case 1, using 2s + 1 \le 5) earns full marks if its bound is verified. [C2: Dyadic rationals] A dyadic rational is a number of the form m/2^k with m \in 
Z and k \in 
N. Prove that between any two real numbers x < y there is a dyadic rational. Hint: compare 2^k with k. First, 2^k > k for every k \in 
N, by induction (@fd1:ax-induction; @fd1:exr-induction-b1 even gives 2^k \ge k + 1): 2^0 = 1 > 0, and if 2^k > k, then 2^{k+1} = 2^k + 2^k > k + 1, since 2^k \ge 1. Let x < y. By @cor-archimedean-epsilon there is k \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/k < y - x; the k depends on y - x. Then 1/2^k < 1/k < y - x. By @lem-integer-part, let m \coloneqq  loor{2^k x} + 1. Then m - 1 \le 2^k x < m, and 2^k x < m \le 2^k x + 1 < 2^k x + 2^k (y - x) = 2^k y , using 1 < 2^k (y - x). Dividing by 2^k > 0 gives x < m/2^k < y. The proof is that of @thm-rationals-dense with the ruler of step 1/n replaced by one of step 1/2^k. Only the choice of step size changed; any family of steps that can be made smaller than every \varepsilon > 0 would do. [C3: Find the faulty line] A student proves @thm-rationals-dense as follows. Let x < y. 1. Let R \coloneqq \{ r \in 
Q : r > x \}. By @thm-naturals-unbounded some natural number exceeds x, so R is nonempty. 2. By well-ordering, R has a least element q. 3. By @cor-archimedean-epsilon, choose n \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/n < y - x. 4. Since q - 1/n is rational and smaller than the least element q of R, it is not in R. So q - 1/n \le x, and hence q \le x + 1/n < y. 5. Therefore q \in 
Q and x < q < y. Is the statement the student is proving true? Does the argument prove it? Find the line that fails and say why. Show that for x = 0 the set R has no least element. Then repair the proof by changing R so that the faulty line becomes correct. The statement is true: it is @thm-rationals-dense. So there is no counterexample to the conclusion, and the only question is whether the argument proves it. It does not. Line (2) fails. Well-ordering says that a nonempty subset of 
N has a least element. The set R is a set of rationals, not of natural numbers, and it need not have a least element. For x = 0, R is the set of positive rationals; if q \in R, then q/2 \in R and q/2 < q. So no element of R is least. Lines (3)–(5) are correct once a least element is available. Repair. Fix n first, as in line (3), and replace R by a set of integers: R_n \coloneqq \{ m \in 
Z : m/n > x \}. By @lem-integer-part, its least element is m \coloneqq  loor{nx} + 1: indeed m/n > x, while (m - 1)/n \le x. Now line (4) holds with q \coloneqq m/n: since (m - 1)/n = q - 1/n \le x, we get q \le x + 1/n < y. This is the proof of @thm-rationals-dense. The point is that the step 1/n is fixed first, so the candidates m/n form a copy of the integers, where “least” makes sense.

title: 1.7 Nested Intervals and the Uncountability of the Reals
content:
Nested Intervals and the Uncountability of the Reals Each point we have built so far was a single supremum: the supremum of a set that “reaches toward” the point we want. This section builds points from a different kind of data, a sequence of closed intervals, each inside the one before. We prove that such intervals always have a point in common. In 
Q this fails, and so it is one more way of saying that 
R has no gaps. The payoff is a proof that the real numbers cannot be listed, one that uses no decimal expansions, only the axiom. Trapping a point Here is a way to hunt for \sqrt{2} using nothing but rational arithmetic. Start with the interval [1, 2]; since 1^2 < 2 < 2^2, the number we are after is in there. Cut the interval at its midpoint 	frac32. Since (	frac32)^2 = 	frac94 > 2, keep the left half [1, 	frac32]. Cut again at 	frac54: since (	frac54)^2 = 	frac{25}{16} < 2, keep the right half. Continuing, we get  egin{aligned} [1, 2] &\supseteq  igl[ 1, 	frac32  igr] \supseteq  igl[ 	frac54, 	frac32  igr] \ &\supseteq  igl[ 	frac{11}8, 	frac32  igr] \supseteq  igl[ 	frac{11}8, 	frac{23}{16}  igr] \supseteq \cdots, \end{aligned} each interval half as long as the one before, each with rational endpoints, and each containing \sqrt{2}. Is there a number lying in all of them? In 
R the answer should be “yes, \sqrt{2}”. In 
Q the answer is “no”: the only candidate is \sqrt{2}, and it is not rational. We make both answers precise below. First, a name for the shape of this data. A family of sets I_1, I_2, I_3, \dots is nested if I_{n+1} \subseteq I_n for every n \ge 1. [Nested Interval Theorem] For each n \ge 1, let I_n = [a_n, b_n] be a closed bounded interval with a_n \le b_n, and suppose the family is nested: I_{n+1} \subseteq I_n for every n \ge 1. Then  igcap_{n \ge 1} I_n 
e \emptyset. More precisely, \alpha \coloneqq \sup \{ a_n : n \ge 1 \} exists and lies in every I_n. If moreover for every \varepsilon > 0 there is n \ge 1 with b_n - a_n < \varepsilon, then  igcap_{n \ge 1} I_n = \{ \alpha \}. Picture the intervals on the line. As n grows, the left endpoints move right (or stay), the right endpoints move left (or stay), and they never cross: every left endpoint lies below every right endpoint, even for different indices. So the set of left endpoints is bounded above by each b_n. Its supremum \alpha is at least every a_n, because it is an upper bound. It is at most every b_n, because it is the least upper bound and each b_n is an upper bound. Hence \alpha \in [a_n, b_n] for every n. For uniqueness: two different common points x < y would force every interval to have length at least y - x, and the shrinking hypothesis with \varepsilon = y - x forbids that. We first compare endpoints with different indices. a_m \le b_n for all m, n \ge 1. From I_{j+1} \subseteq I_j for every j, induction on k - m gives I_k \subseteq I_m whenever m \le k. Let m, n \ge 1 and k \coloneqq \max\{ m, n \}. Then I_k \subseteq I_m and I_k \subseteq I_n. Since a_k \in I_k \subseteq I_m, we have a_m \le a_k. Since b_k \in I_k \subseteq I_n, we have b_k \le b_n. Hence a_m \le a_k \le b_k \le b_n. Let A \coloneqq \{ a_n : n \ge 1 \}. It is nonempty, since a_1 \in A, and by the claim it is bounded above by b_1. By @ax-least-upper-bound, \alpha \coloneqq \sup A exists. Fix n \ge 1. Since \alpha is an upper bound of A, a_n \le \alpha. By the claim, b_n is an upper bound of A, so (S2) of @def-supremum gives \alpha \le b_n. Hence \alpha \in [a_n, b_n] = I_n. As n was arbitrary, \alpha \in  igcap_{n} I_n, and the intersection is nonempty. Now assume the shrinking hypothesis, and let x \in  igcap_n I_n. Suppose x 
e \alpha, and let u \coloneqq \min\{ x, \alpha \} and v \coloneqq \max\{ x, \alpha \}, so u < v and both lie in every I_n. For every n, a_n \le u < v \le b_n, so b_n - a_n \ge v - u. But \varepsilon \coloneqq v - u > 0, and by hypothesis some n has b_n - a_n < v - u. This is a contradiction, so x = \alpha. Hence  igcap_n I_n = \{ \alpha \}. Closedness is what lets \alpha belong to I_n. The proof gives only a_n \le \alpha \le b_n, with nonstrict inequalities, and \alpha may well equal an endpoint. An open interval would exclude it. Now back to the bisection. Its intervals have length 1/2^{n-1}, and 2^{n-1} \ge n for every n \ge 1 (by @fd1:ax-induction), so 1/2^{n-1} \le 1/n. Given \varepsilon > 0, @cor-archimedean-epsilon gives n with 1/n < \varepsilon, and then the n-th interval is shorter than \varepsilon. The rule keeps a_n^2 < 2 < b_n^2 at every step, so a_n < \sqrt{2} < b_n by @thm-ordered-field-rules (g), and every interval contains \sqrt{2}. By @thm-nested-intervals the intersection is exactly \{ \sqrt{2} \}. The bisection traps \sqrt{2} and nothing else. What each hypothesis does @thm-nested-intervals has four hypotheses: the intervals are closed, they are bounded, they are nested, and they live in 
R. The uniqueness clause adds a fifth, that the lengths shrink below every \varepsilon. Each one is needed, and each has a witness. ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Hypothesis dropped Family Intersection ---------------------------------- ------------------------------------------ ----------------------- closed (0, 1/n) \emptyset bounded [n, \infty) \emptyset nested [n, n + 1] \emptyset the field is 
R the rational bisection intervals, in 
Q \emptyset lengths shrink (uniqueness only) [-1/n, 1 + 1/n] [0, 1] ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- We check each row. - Closed. The intervals (0, 1/n) are nested and bounded. A real x \le 0 is not in (0, 1). For x > 0, @cor-archimedean-epsilon gives n with 1/n < x, so x 
otin (0, 1/n). Hence no real number is in every interval. Here the supremum of the left endpoints is \alpha = 0, and it lies in none of the intervals: exactly the step that closedness secured. - Bounded. The intervals [n, \infty) are closed and nested. For any x \in 
R, @thm-naturals-unbounded gives n > x, and then x 
otin [n, \infty). The proof breaks earlier here: the left endpoints form 
Z_{>0}, which has no upper bound, so \alpha does not exist. - Nested. The intervals [n, n + 1] are closed and bounded, but [1, 2] \cap [3, 4] = \emptyset already. - The field is 
R. In 
Q, a closed interval means \{ q \in 
Q : a \le q \le b \}. Take the bisection intervals [a_n, b_n] from the start of this section. They are defined by rational arithmetic alone, because each midpoint c is rational, and c^2 
e 2 by @fd1:thm-sqrt2-irrational, so the rule “keep the half whose endpoints’ squares straddle 2” always applies. We showed that the real intervals [a_n, b_n] have intersection \{ \sqrt{2} \}. So their rational parts have intersection 
Q \cap \{ \sqrt{2} \} = \emptyset. - Shrinking. The intervals [-1/n, 1 + 1/n] are closed, bounded, and nested, and their intersection is [0, 1]: every point of [0, 1] lies in all of them, and a point outside [0, 1] is excluded from some interval by @cor-archimedean-epsilon (@exr-nested-intervals-b2 writes this out). The intersection is nonempty, but it is not a single point. Their lengths 1 + 2/n never drop below 1. Dropping a hypothesis removes the guarantee. It does not force the conclusion to fail. The open intervals (-1/n, 1/n) are nested, and their intersection is \{ 0 \}, which is not empty. A witness that a hypothesis is needed must be a family where the conclusion actually fails, like (0, 1/n). The table’s witness for “closed” uses the open intervals (0, 1/n). Do the half-open intervals (0, 1/n] witness it too? And the half-open intervals [0, 1/n)? Give a reason for each. The half-open intervals (0, 1/n] are nested and bounded, but no real number lies in all of them: x \le 0 is not in (0, 1], and for x > 0 some n has 1/n < x (@cor-archimedean-epsilon). The supremum of the left endpoints is 0, which is excluded from every interval. So (0, 1/n] is a witness too. The intervals [0, 1/n) are not: 0 lies in all of them, so their intersection \{ 0 \} is not empty. Closing the left end puts the supremum 0 of the left endpoints back in. The real numbers cannot be listed Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 3 calls a set countable if its elements can be listed as x_0, x_1, x_2, \dots, repetitions allowed; for a nonempty set this means that it is the image of some function from 
N. That chapter shows that 
N, 
Z, and 
Q are countable. It also shows that 
R is not, by Cantor’s diagonal argument with decimal expansions. Decimal expansions were taken there as a fact from school: every real number has one, and two different expansions such as 0.4999\ldots and 0.5000\ldots can name the same number. Neither fact has been proved from our axioms. Here is a proof with no decimals, using only @thm-nested-intervals. [Uncountability of the Reals] Let x_1, x_2, x_3, \dots be any list of real numbers, that is, any function n \mapsto x_n from 
Z_{>0} to 
R. Then there is c \in 
R with c 
e x_n for every n \ge 1. Consequently 
R is not countable. Build nested closed intervals I_1 \supseteq I_2 \supseteq \cdots, where I_n is chosen to avoid x_n. A point c common to all of them, which @thm-nested-intervals provides, avoids every x_n: it lies in I_n, and x_n does not. To pass from I_n to I_{n+1}, cut I_n into thirds and look at the two outer thirds. They are disjoint closed intervals, so x_{n+1} misses at least one of them; take that one. Before reading on: why thirds, and not halves? We define closed intervals I_n = [a_n, b_n] with a_n < b_n by recursion on n. Let I_1 \coloneqq [x_1 + 1, x_1 + 2]. Then x_1 
otin I_1. Suppose I_n = [a_n, b_n] with a_n < b_n has been defined. Let d \coloneqq b_n - a_n > 0, and let L \coloneqq  igl[ a_n, \ a_n + 	frac{d}{3}  igr], \qquad R \coloneqq  igl[ b_n - 	frac{d}{3}, \ b_n  igr]. Both are closed intervals of length d/3 > 0 contained in I_n. They are disjoint, because a_n + d/3 < b_n - d/3, which is 2d/3 < d. Define I_{n+1} \coloneqq  egin{cases} L & 	ext{if } x_{n+1}

It is irrational by @fd1:thm-sqrt2-irrational. By (a), t is irrational. The direct statement (a) would be awkward to prove as it stands, since “irrational” is a negative property; its contrapositive is one line. That is the reason to reach for the contrapositive (@fd1:prp-contrapositive, Logic and Proof, Chapter 2). [R3] Prove that the real number \sqrt2 + \sqrt3 is irrational. Here \sqrt3 and \sqrt6 are the positive square roots given by @thm-nth-root. First, \sqrt2 \sqrt3 = \sqrt6: the left side is positive and its square is 2 \cdot 3 = 6, so it is the unique positive square root of 6. Suppose, for a contradiction, that r \coloneqq \sqrt2 + \sqrt3 is rational [	ext{assumption for } ulename{
eg I}]. Then r^2 = 2 + 2\sqrt2 \sqrt3 + 3 = 5 + 2\sqrt6 , so \sqrt6 = (r^2 - 5)/2 is rational, because the rationals are closed under the field operations (@exm-ordered-fields-q-r). But no rational number has square 6 (@fd1:exr-negation-and-contradiction-c1). Hence r is irrational [ulename{
eg I}]. Logic and Proof, Chapter 2 could prove only the negative half: no rational squares to 6 (@fd1:exr-negation-and-contradiction-c1). With @thm-nth-root the number \sqrt6 exists in 
R, and the negative statement becomes the positive one, “\sqrt6 is irrational”, which is what the argument uses. [R4] Prove that \abs{x - 1} + \abs{x + 1} \ge 2 for every real x, and find all x for which equality holds. The tool is the triangle inequality (@thm-triangle-inequality), applied to a sum chosen so that x cancels: 2 = \abs{(1 - x) + (x + 1)} \le \abs{1 - x} + \abs{x + 1} = \abs{x - 1} + \abs{x + 1}, using \abs{1 - x} = \abs{x - 1} (@prp-absolute-value-rules (b)). By @exr-ordered-fields-b2 (b), equality holds exactly when (1 - x)(x + 1) \ge 0, that is, when 1 - x^2 \ge 0, that is, when -1 \le x \le 1 (by @thm-ordered-field-rules (g) and @prp-absolute-value-rules (d), x^2 \le 1 means \abs{x} \le 1). So equality holds exactly on [-1, 1]. The look-alike tools work less well. Proof by cases, as in @fd1:exm-triangle-inequality-cases, succeeds but needs three cases (x < -1, -1 \le x \le 1, x > 1) and a formula in each. Squaring both sides leaves the cross term 2\abs{x^2 - 1}, which still has an absolute value in it, so it only postpones the case split.

title: Definition 1.1.2 (Absolute Value)
page: 1.1 Ordered Fields and the Gap in the Rationals
content: Let \(F\) be an ordered field. The absolute value of \(x \in F\) is \[ \abs{x} \coloneqq \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0, \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0. \end{cases} \]

title: Definition 1.1.1 (Ordered Field)
page: 1.1 Ordered Fields and the Gap in the Rationals
content: An ordered field consists of a set \(F\) , two operations, addition \((a, b) \mapsto a + b\) and multiplication \((a, b) \mapsto ab\) , and a relation \(<\) on \(F\) , such that the following hold. The field axioms : for all \(a, b, c \in F\) , \(a + b = b + a\) ; \((a + b) + c = a + (b + c)\) ; there is an element \(0 \in F\) with \(a + 0 = a\) for every \(a \in F\) ; for every \(a \in F\) there is an element \(-a \in F\) with \(a + (-a) = 0\) ; \((ab)c = a(bc)\) ; \(ab = ba\) ; there is an element \(1 \in F\) with \(1 \ne 0\) and \(a \cdot 1 = a\) for every \(a \in F\) ; for every nonzero \(a \in F\) there is an element \(a^{-1} \in F\) with \(a a^{-1} = 1\) ; \(a(b + c) = ab + ac\) . The order axioms : for all \(a, b, c \in F\) , (trichotomy) exactly one of \(a < b\) , \(a = b\) , \(b < a\) holds; (transitivity) if \(a < b\) and \(b < c\) , then \(a < c\) ; (addition) if \(a < b\) , then \(a + c < b + c\) ; (multiplication) if \(0 < a\) and \(0 < b\) , then \(0 < ab\) .

title: Example (A minimal change: the integers)
page: 1.1 Ordered Fields and the Gap in the Rationals
content: The integers \(\nZ\) , with the usual operations and order, satisfy (O1)–(O4) and every field axiom except one. Which one fails, and does the failure matter for inequalities?

title: Example (The rationals and the reals)
page: 1.1 Ordered Fields and the Gap in the Rationals
content: Explain why \(\nQ\) is an ordered field, and what we are assuming when we say \(\nR\) is one.

title: Example (Reading an absolute-value inequality as an interval)
page: 1.1 Ordered Fields and the Gap in the Rationals
content: Find all real \(x\) with \(\abs{4 - 3x} < 2\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 1.1 Ordered Fields and the Gap in the Rationals
content: Here is a derivation, in an ordered field, of “if \(a > 0\) and \(b > 0\) then \(a + b > 0\) ”: from \(b > 0\) we get \(a + b > a + 0\) ; and \(a + 0 = a\) ; and \(a > 0\) ; hence \(a + b > 0\) . Name the axiom that justifies each of the four steps. True or false, with a reason: in an ordered field, if \(a < b\) then \(a^2 < b^2\) . True or false, with a reason: \(\abs{x} = \max \{ x, -x \}\) for every \(x\) in an ordered field. (Here \(\max\{ a, b \}\) is the larger of \(a\) and \(b\) : it is \(a\) if \(a \ge b\) , and \(b\) otherwise.) The integers satisfy all four order axioms. Why is \(\nZ\) not an ordered field?

title: Exercise (B1: Three more rules)
page: 1.1 Ordered Fields and the Gap in the Rationals
content: Let \(F\) be an ordered field and \(a, b, c, d \in F\) . Prove the following from the axioms and @thm-ordered-field-rules . If \(a > 0\) and \(b < 0\) , then \(ab < 0\) . If \(0 \le a < b\) and \(0 \le c < d\) , then \(ac < bd\) . If \(a > 0\) and \(ab > 0\) , then \(b > 0\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Inserting a third point)
page: 1.1 Ordered Fields and the Gap in the Rationals
content: Let \(F\) be an ordered field and \(x, y, z \in F\) . Prove that \(\abs{x - z} \le \abs{x - y} + \abs{y - z}\) . Prove that \(\abs{x + y} = \abs{x} + \abs{y}\) if and only if \(xy \ge 0\) .

page: 1.1 Ordered Fields and the Gap in the Rationals
content: Find all real \(x\) satisfying each inequality. Hence write each solution set as an interval. \(\abs{2x - 3} < 5\) . \(\abs{x - 1} < \abs{x + 1}\) .

page: 1.1 Ordered Fields and the Gap in the Rationals
content:
The field \(\{ 0, 1, 2 \}\) with arithmetic modulo \(3\) has \(1 + 1 + 1 = 0\) . Show that it admits no order satisfying (O1)–(O4). In an ordered field \(F\) , define \(n \cdot 1\) for \(n \in 
N\) by \(0 \cdot 1 \coloneqq 0\) and \((n + 1) \cdot 1 \coloneqq n \cdot 1 + 1\) . Prove that \(n \cdot 1 > 0\) for every \(n \in 
N\) with \(n \ge 1\) , and that \(m \cdot 1 < n \cdot 1\) whenever \(m < n\) . Deduce that the elements \(0, 1, 1 + 1, 1 + 1 + 1, \dots\) of an ordered field are all different, so every ordered field contains a copy of \(

title: Exercise (C2: Max and min without cases)
page: 1.1 Ordered Fields and the Gap in the Rationals
content: Let \(F\) be an ordered field and \(a, b \in F\) . Write \(\max\{ a, b \}\) for the larger of \(a\) and \(b\) and \(\min\{ a, b \}\) for the smaller (as in @exr-ordered-fields-a1 ). Prove that \[ \max \{ a, b \} = \frac{a + b + \abs{a - b}}{2}, \qquad \min \{ a, b \} = \frac{a + b - \abs{a - b}}{2}. \] Hence show that \(\abs{\max\{a, b\} - \max\{c, d\}} \le \max\{ \abs{a - c}, \abs{b - d} \}\) for all \(a, b, c, d \in F\) . Hint: for the last part, bound \(\max\{a, b\}\) above by \(\max\{c, d\} + \max\{ \abs{a - c}, \abs{b - d} \}\) .

title: Lemma 1.1.1 (Field Algebra)
page: 1.1 Ordered Fields and the Gap in the Rationals
content: Let \(F\) be an ordered field (only (F1)–(F9) are used) and let \(a, b \in F\) . The elements \(0\) and \(1\) are unique, and so are \(-a\) and, for \(a \ne 0\) , \(a^{-1}\) . In particular \(-(-a) = a\) . \(a \cdot 0 = 0\) . \((-a)b = -(ab)\) and \((-a)(-b) = ab\) . If \(ab = 0\) , then \(a = 0\) or \(b = 0\) . \((a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2\) , where \(x^2 \coloneqq xx\) and \(2 \coloneqq 1 + 1\) .

title: Proposition 1.1.3 (Rules for Absolute Value)
page: 1.1 Ordered Fields and the Gap in the Rationals
content: Let \(F\) be an ordered field and let \(x, y, r \in F\) . \(\abs{x} \ge 0\) , and \(\abs{x} = 0\) if and only if \(x = 0\) . \(\abs{-x} = \abs{x}\) , \(\abs{xy} = \abs{x} \abs{y}\) , and \(\abs{x}^2 = x^2\) . \(-\abs{x} \le x \le \abs{x}\) . \(\abs{x} \le r\) if and only if \(-r \le x \le r\) ; and \(\abs{x} < r\) if and only if \(-r < x < r\) .

title: Theorem 1.1.2 (Rules for Inequalities)
page: 1.1 Ordered Fields and the Gap in the Rationals
content: Let \(F\) be an ordered field and let \(a, b, c, d \in F\) . \(a < b\) exactly when \(b - a > 0\) , and exactly when \(-b < -a\) ; in particular \(a > 0\) if and only if \(-a < 0\) . If \(a \le b\) and \(c \le d\) , then \(a + c \le b + d\) , and the conclusion is strict if at least one hypothesis is strict. If \(a < b\) and \(c > 0\) , then \(ac < bc\) . If \(a < b\) and \(c < 0\) , then \(ac > bc\) . If \(a \ne 0\) , then \(a^2 > 0\) . Hence \(a^2 \ge 0\) for every \(a\) , and \(1 > 0\) . If \(a > 0\) , then \(1/a > 0\) . If \(0 < a < b\) , then \(0 < 1/b < 1/a\) . If \(a \ge 0\) and \(b \ge 0\) , then \(a < b\) if and only if \(a^2 < b^2\) . \(2 \coloneqq 1 + 1\) is positive, and if \(a < b\) , then \(a < \frac{a + b}{2} < b\) .

title: Theorem 1.1.4 (Triangle Inequality)
page: 1.1 Ordered Fields and the Gap in the Rationals
content: Let \(F\) be an ordered field. For all \(x, y \in F\) , \(\abs{x + y} \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}\) ; \(\bigl| \abs{x} - \abs{y} \bigr| \le \abs{x - y}\) (the reverse triangle inequality ).

title: Definition 1.2.2 (Bounded Sets)
content: Let \(F\) be an ordered field and \(A \subseteq F\) . The set \(A\) is bounded above if it has at least one upper bound, bounded below if it has at least one lower bound, and bounded if it is both bounded above and bounded below.

title: Definition 1.2.5 (Infimum)
content: Let \(F\) be an ordered field and \(A \subseteq F\) . An element \(t \in F\) is an infimum (or greatest lower bound ) of \(A\) in \(F\) if \(t\) is a lower bound of \(A\) , and \(M \le t\) for every lower bound \(M\) of \(A\) .

title: Definition 1.2.3 (Maximum and Minimum)
content: Let \(F\) be an ordered field and \(A \subseteq F\) . An element \(m\) is a maximum (or greatest element) of \(A\) if \(m \in A\) and \(m\) is an upper bound of \(A\) . It is a minimum (or least element) of \(A\) if \(m \in A\) and \(m\) is a lower bound of \(A\) .

title: Definition 1.2.4 (Supremum)
content: Let \(F\) be an ordered field and \(A \subseteq F\) . An element \(s \in F\) is a supremum (or least upper bound ) of \(A\) in \(F\) if \(s\) is an upper bound of \(A\) , and \(s \le M\) for every upper bound \(M\) of \(A\) .

title: Definition 1.2.1 (Upper and Lower Bounds)
content: Let \(F\) be an ordered field and \(A \subseteq F\) . An element \(M \in F\) is an upper bound of \(A\) if \(a \le M\) for every \(a \in A\) . An element \(m \in F\) is a lower bound of \(A\) if \(m \le a\) for every \(a \in A\) .

content: Let \(F\) be an ordered field and \(A \subseteq F\) . If \(s\) and \(s'\) are both suprema of \(A\) in \(F\) , then \(s = s'\) .

title: Theorem 1.3.3 (Greatest Lower Bound Property)
content: Every nonempty subset \(A\) of \(\nR\) that is bounded below has an infimum in \(\nR\) , and \[ \inf A = -\sup(-A) . \]

title: Theorem 1.3.2 (Infimum by Reflection)
content: Let \(F\) be an ordered field, \(A \subseteq F\) , and \(m, t \in F\) . \(m\) is a lower bound of \(A\) if and only if \(-m\) is an upper bound of \(-A\) . \(t\) is an infimum of \(A\) if and only if \(-t\) is a supremum of \(-A\) . In particular, if \(-A\) has a supremum, then \(A\) has an infimum, and \(\inf A = -\sup(-A)\) .

title: Corollary 1.4.2 (Sup Approximation)
content: Let \(A \subseteq \nR\) be nonempty and bounded above. For every \(n \in \nZ_{>0}\) there is \(a_n \in A\) with \[ \sup A - \frac1n < a_n \le \sup A . \]

content: Let \(A, B \subseteq \nR\) be nonempty and bounded above. Prove that \(A \cup B\) is bounded above and \(\sup(A \cup B) = \max\{ \sup A, \sup B \}\) .

content: Let \(A \subseteq \nR\) be nonempty and bounded above, and \(B \subseteq \nR\) nonempty and bounded below. Prove that \[ \sup \{ a - b : a \in A, \ b \in B \} = \sup A - \inf B . \] Give an example showing that the right side cannot be replaced by \(\sup A - \sup B\) .

content: For \(A, B \subseteq \nR\) let \(AB \coloneqq \{ ab : a \in A, \ b \in B \}\) . Show that \(\sup(AB) = \sup A \cdot \sup B\) can fail for nonempty bounded sets \(A, B\) . Prove that it holds when \(A\) and \(B\) are nonempty, bounded above, and contained in \((0, \infty)\) .

content: Let \(A, B \subseteq \nR\) be nonempty. Assume \(A\) and \(B\) are bounded above. Without looking back, prove \(\sup(A + B) = \sup A + \sup B\) . This time, instead of proving \(\ge\) separately, show that \(\sup A + \sup B\) satisfies both hypotheses of @thm-sup-epsilon for the set \(A + B\) . Assume \(A\) and \(B\) are bounded below. State and prove the corresponding formula for \(\inf(A + B)\) . Show that if \(B\) is not bounded above, then neither is \(A + B\) .

title: Exercise (C3: Find the wrong line)
content: Each “proof” below contains a line that is false in general. Find it, give a set for which it fails, and decide whether the claim itself is true. Claim. If \(A \subseteq \nR\) is nonempty and bounded above and \(a < 1\) for every \(a \in A\) , then \(\sup A < 1\) . “Proof.” (1) Let \(s = \sup A\) . (2) Since \(s \in A\) , the hypothesis gives \(s < 1\) . (3) Hence \(\sup A < 1\) . Claim. If \(A, B \subseteq \nR\) are nonempty and bounded above, then \(\sup(A + B) \ge \sup A + \sup B\) . “Proof.” (1) Let \(a = \sup A\) and \(b = \sup B\) . (2) Then \(a \in A\) and \(b \in B\) , so \(a + b \in A + B\) . (3) By (S1), \(a + b \le \sup(A + B)\) , which is the claim.

title: Theorem 1.4.1 (Epsilon Characterization of the Supremum)
content: Let \(A \subseteq \nR\) and let \(s \in \nR\) be an upper bound of \(A\) . Then \(s = \sup A\) if and only if for every \(\varepsilon > 0\) there exists \(a \in A\) with \(a > s - \varepsilon\) .

title: Theorem 1.4.3 (Monotonicity of the Supremum)
content: Let \(A \subseteq B \subseteq \nR\) , where \(A\) is nonempty and \(B\) is bounded above. Then \(\sup A\) and \(\sup B\) exist, and \(\sup A \le \sup B\) .

title: Theorem 1.4.4 (Scaling the Supremum)
content: Let \(A \subseteq \nR\) be nonempty and bounded above, and let \(c \in \nR\) . If \(c > 0\) , then \(cA\) is nonempty and bounded above, and \(\sup(cA) = c \sup A\) . If \(c < 0\) , then \(cA\) is nonempty and bounded below, and \(\inf(cA) = c \sup A\) .

title: Theorem 1.4.5 (Supremum of a Sum)
content: Let \(A, B \subseteq \nR\) be nonempty and bounded above. Then \(A + B\) is nonempty and bounded above, and \[ \sup(A + B) = \sup A + \sup B . \]

content: Prove that \(\inf \{ 1/n : n \in \nZ_{>0} \} = 0\) , and that the set has no minimum.

title: Exercise (B2: Scaled Archimedes)
content: Let \(a > 0\) and \(y \in \nR\) . Prove that there is \(n \in \nN\) with \(n a > y\) . What does this say when \(a\) is the length of a measuring stick?

title: Exercise (B3: Smaller than every 1/n)
content:
Let \(x \in 
R\) with \(0 \le x < 1/n\) for every \(n \in 
Z_{>0}\) . Prove that \(x = 0\) . Then deduce: if \(a, b \in

title: Exercise (B4: Putting a proof in order)
content:
Here are nine lines. Seven of them, in a suitable order, prove that \(\sup A = 1\) for \(A \coloneqq \{  rac{n}{n + 1} : n \in 
N \}\) . Give an admissible order. Then say why each of the other two lines cannot be used. Let \(\varepsilon > 0\) . Hence \(a \coloneqq  rac{n}{n + 1}\) is an element of \(A\) with \(a > 1 - \varepsilon\) . For every \(n \in 
N\) , \(n < n + 1\) and \(n + 1 > 0\) , so \( rac{n}{n + 1} < 1\) . Hence \(1\) is an upper bound of \(A\) . By @cor-archimedean-epsilon there is \(n \in 
Z_{>0}\) , depending on \(\varepsilon\) , with \( rac1n < \varepsilon\) . Choose \(n \in 
Z_{>0}\) such that \( rac1n < \varepsilon\) for every \(\varepsilon > 0\) . Since \(\varepsilon > 0\) was arbitrary, every band \((1 - \varepsilon, 1]\) contains an element of \(A\) . Then \( rac{n}{n + 1} = 1 -  rac1{n + 1}\) , and \( rac1{n + 1} <  rac1n < \varepsilon\) . By @thm-sup-epsilon , \(\sup A = 1\) . Fix \(n \in 
Z_{>0}\) and let \(\varepsilon \coloneqq  rac1n\) ; then \( rac{n}{n + 1} = 1 -  rac1{n + 1} > 1 - \varepsilon\) .

title: Exercise (C1: Exit check: the Archimedean property, and a circular proof)
content:
Without looking back, prove the Archimedean property from the least upper bound axiom. Mark the line that uses the axiom, and explain why that line fails in \(
R(x)\) . A student offers the following proof. “Let \(x \in

title: Exercise (C2: The order on the rational functions)
content: Let \(P \subseteq \nR(x)\) be the set of positive elements defined in this section, and let \(f < g\) mean \(g - f \in P\) . Show that every nonzero \(f \in \nR(x)\) can be written as \(p/q\) with the leading coefficient of \(q\) positive, and that then \(f \in P\) if and only if the leading coefficient of \(p\) is positive. Show that for every nonzero \(f\) , exactly one of \(f \in P\) and \(-f \in P\) holds. Show that if \(f, g \in P\) , then \(f g \in P\) and \(f + g \in P\) . Deduce the order axioms of @def-ordered-field for \(<\) : trichotomy, transitivity, \(f < g \Rightarrow f + h < g + h\) , and \(f, g > 0 \Rightarrow f g > 0\) .

title: Exercise (C3: Archimedean without the axiom)
content: Prove, without using @ax-least-upper-bound , that for every \(r \in \nQ\) there is \(n \in \nN\) with \(n > r\) . Deduce that the Archimedean property does not imply the least upper bound axiom in an ordered field.

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 1.6 Density of the Rationals and the Existence of Roots
content: True or false? Give a reason or a counterexample for each. There is a least positive irrational number. Between any two distinct rational numbers there is an irrational number. Between any two distinct irrational numbers there is a rational number. Every nonempty set of rationals that is bounded above has a supremum in \(\nR\) , and that supremum is rational. In the proof of @thm-nth-root , the constant \(C\) depends on \(h\) . Run Case 1 of the proof of @thm-sqrt2-exists with the value \(\frac75\) in place of \(s\) (so \(s^2 = \frac{49}{25} < 2\) ): compute \(h\) , and check that \((s + h)^2 < 2\) . Which property of a supremum does this show \(\frac75\) lacks?

title: Exercise (B1: Every real number is a supremum of rationals)
page: 1.6 Density of the Rationals and the Existence of Roots
content: Let \(x \in \nR\) . Prove that \(x = \sup \{ q \in \nQ : q < x \}\) .

title: Exercise (B2: The square root of three, finished)
page: 1.6 Density of the Rationals and the Existence of Roots
content: Here is the start of a proof that there is exactly one real \(s > 0\) with \(s^2 = 3\) . Let \(S \coloneqq \{ x \in \nR : x > 0, \ x^2 < 3 \}\) . Then \(1 \in S\) , and if \(x \ge 2\) , then \(x^2 \ge 4 > 3\) ; so \(S\) is nonempty and bounded above by \(2\) . By @ax-least-upper-bound , \(s \coloneqq \sup S\) exists, and \(s \ge 1\) . Case \(s^2 < 3\) . Let \(h \coloneqq (3 - s^2)/(4s + 2)\) . Then \(h > 0\) . Since \(3 - s^2 \le 2\) and \(4s + 2 \ge 6\) , we have \(h \le \frac13\) , so \(h^2 \le h\) , and \((s + h)^2 \le s^2 + (2s + 1)h = \frac{3 + s^2}{2} < 3\) . Hence \(s + h \in S\) , and \(s + h > s\) contradicts (S1). Case \(s^2 > 3\) . \(\ldots\) Name the move, then complete it. Give an explicit \(h\) for the second case and check that it works; then finish the proof, including uniqueness.

title: Exercise (B3: The cube root of five)
page: 1.6 Density of the Rationals and the Existence of Roots
content: Prove that there is exactly one real \(s > 0\) with \(s^3 = 5\) . Hence show that \(1.70 < s < 1.71\) .

page: 1.6 Density of the Rationals and the Existence of Roots
content: A dyadic rational is a number of the form \(m/2^k\) with \(m \in \nZ\) and \(k \in \nN\) . Prove that between any two real numbers \(x < y\) there is a dyadic rational. Hint: compare \(2^k\) with \(k\) .

title: Exercise (C3: Find the faulty line)
page: 1.6 Density of the Rationals and the Existence of Roots
content:
A student proves @thm-rationals-dense as follows. Let \(x < y\) . Let \(R \coloneqq \{ r \in 
Q : r > x \}\) . By @thm-naturals-unbounded some natural number exceeds \(x\) , so \(R\) is nonempty. By well-ordering, \(R\) has a least element \(q\) . By @cor-archimedean-epsilon , choose \(n \in 
Z_{>0}\) with \(1/n < y - x\) . Since \(q - 1/n\) is rational and smaller than the least element \(q\) of \(R\) , it is not in \(R\) . So \(q - 1/n \le x\) , and hence \(q \le x + 1/n < y\) . Therefore \(q \in 
Q\) and \(x < q < y\) . Is the statement the student is proving true? Does the argument prove it? Find the line that fails and say why. Show that for \(x = 0\) the set \(R\) has no least element. Then repair the proof by changing \(R\) so that the faulty line becomes correct.

title: Lemma 1.6.3 (Integer Part)
page: 1.6 Density of the Rationals and the Existence of Roots
content: For every \(y \in \nR\) there is exactly one integer \(m\) with \(m \le y < m + 1\) .

title: Theorem 1.6.2 (Existence of Roots)
page: 1.6 Density of the Rationals and the Existence of Roots
content: Let \(a > 0\) and \(n \in \nZ_{>0}\) . There is exactly one real number \(s > 0\) with \(s^n = a\) .

title: Theorem 1.6.4 (Density of the Rationals)
page: 1.6 Density of the Rationals and the Existence of Roots
content: Let \(x, y \in \nR\) with \(x < y\) . There is \(q \in \nQ\) with \(x < q < y\) .

title: Theorem 1.6.1 (The Square Root of Two Exists)
page: 1.6 Density of the Rationals and the Existence of Roots
content: There is exactly one real number \(s > 0\) with \(s^2 = 2\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 1.7 Nested Intervals and the Uncountability of the Reals
content: For each family \((I_n)_{n \ge 1}\) , say which hypothesis of @thm-nested-intervals fails, and find \(\bigcap_n I_n\) . \(I_n = [0, 1/n)\) . \(I_n = [n, n + 1/n]\) . \(I_n = (-1/n, 1/n)\) . \(I_n = [-n, n]\) . Run the construction in the proof of @thm-reals-uncountable on a list that begins \(x_1 = 0\) , \(x_2 = 1\) , \(x_3 = 2\) : find \(I_1\) , \(I_2\) , and \(I_3\) . Where does the proof of @thm-reals-uncountable use that the intervals \(L\) and \(R\) are closed , and what could go wrong with open thirds?

title: Exercise (B1: Shrinking by a fixed factor)
page: 1.7 Nested Intervals and the Uncountability of the Reals
content: Let \(I_n = [a_n, b_n]\) be nested closed intervals with \(b_n - a_n = 2^{-n}\) for every \(n\) . Prove that \(\bigcap_n I_n\) consists of exactly one point. For \(n \ge 1\) , let \(m_n \coloneqq \floor{10^n \sqrt{2}}\) ( @lem-integer-part ), and let \(a_n \coloneqq m_n / 10^n\) and \(b_n \coloneqq a_n + 10^{-n}\) , so that \(a_n\) is the \(n\) -digit decimal truncation of \(\sqrt{2}\) . Prove that the intervals \([a_n, b_n]\) are nested, and that their intersection is \(\{ \sqrt{2} \}\) . Compute \(a_1\) and \(a_2\) .

title: Exercise (B2: An intersection that is not a point)
page: 1.7 Nested Intervals and the Uncountability of the Reals
content: Prove that \(\bigcap_{n \ge 1} [-1/n, 1 + 1/n] = [0, 1]\) . Which hypothesis of the uniqueness clause of @thm-nested-intervals fails?

title: Exercise (C1: Exit check: nested intervals and the axiom)
page: 1.7 Nested Intervals and the Uncountability of the Reals
content: Without looking back, prove the existence part of @thm-nested-intervals from the least upper bound axiom. Now work in an ordered field \(F\) in which the Archimedean property holds (for every \(t \in F\) some \(n \in \nN\) has \(n > t\) ) and every nested family of closed bounded intervals has a common point. Let \(A \subseteq F\) be nonempty and bounded above by \(M\) , and pick \(a \in A\) . Define intervals \([a_n, b_n]\) by \(a_1 \coloneqq a\) , \(b_1 \coloneqq M\) , and, with \(c \coloneqq (a_n + b_n)/2\) , let \([a_{n+1}, b_{n+1}] \coloneqq [a_n, c]\) if \(c\) is an upper bound of \(A\) , and \([c, b_n]\) otherwise. Prove that for every \(n\) : \(b_n\) is an upper bound of \(A\) ; some element of \(A\) is \(\ge a_n\) ; and \(b_n - a_n = (M - a)/2^{n-1}\) . Let \(s\) be a common point of all the \([a_n, b_n]\) . Prove that \(s = \sup A\) . Deduce that in an ordered field, the nested interval property together with the Archimedean property implies the least upper bound axiom.

title: Exercise (C2: Uncountable pieces)
page: 1.7 Nested Intervals and the Uncountability of the Reals
content: Let \(x < y\) . Prove that the interval \((x, y)\) is not countable. Deduce that \((x, y)\) contains an irrational number, without using \(\sqrt{2}\) or any other named irrational. You may use the facts from Sets, Relations, and Cardinality , Chapter 3 that \(\nQ\) is countable, and that a subset of a countable set is countable. Let \(C \subseteq \nR\) be countable. Show that the real numbers not in \(C\) are dense: every interval \((x, y)\) with \(x < y\) contains a real number that is not in \(C\) .

title: Exercise (C3: Nested intervals in the rational functions)
page: 1.7 Nested Intervals and the Uncountability of the Reals
content:
Work in the ordered field \(
R(x)\) of @exm-nonarchimedean-field . For \(n \in 
Z_{>0}\) , let \(I_n \coloneqq \{ f \in 
R(x) : n \le f \le x/n \}\) . Show that \(n < x/n\) , so \(I_n\) is a closed bounded interval of positive length, and that \(I_{n+1} \subseteq I_n\) . Let \(f = p/q\) with the leading coefficient of \(q\) positive, and suppose \(f \in I_n\) for every \(n\) . Show that \(\deg p > \deg q\) . Show that \(\deg p \ge \deg q + 2\) and \(\deg p = \deg q + 1\) both lead to a contradiction, and conclude that \( igcap_n I_n = \emptyset\) . Which line of the proof of @thm-nested-intervals fails in \(

title: Exercise (C4: A root of a cubic, from half a proof)
page: 1.7 Nested Intervals and the Uncountability of the Reals
content: Let \(g(x) \coloneqq x^3 + x\) . Then \(g(0) = 0\) and \(g(1) = 2\) , so \(g\) passes the value \(1\) somewhere in \([0, 1]\) . Here is the first half of a proof that it takes the value \(1\) . Let \(S \coloneqq \{ x \in \nR : x \ge 0, \ g(x) < 1 \}\) . Then \(0 \in S\) . If \(x \ge 1\) , then \(x^3 \ge 1\) and \(g(x) \ge 2 > 1\) , so every element of \(S\) is less than \(1\) . By @ax-least-upper-bound , \(s \coloneqq \sup S\) exists, and \(0 \le s \le 1\) . Name the move, then complete it. Prove that \(g(s) = 1\) . Then show that \(0.68 < s < 0.69\) , and that \(s\) is the only real number \(t\) with \(g(t) = 1\) .

page: 1.7 Nested Intervals and the Uncountability of the Reals
content: Let \(A \subseteq \nR\) be nonempty, and let \(s\) be an upper bound of \(A\) . Prove that the following are equivalent. \(s = \sup A\) . For every \(n \in \nZ_{>0}\) there is \(a \in A\) with \(a > s - \frac1n\) . No real number smaller than \(s\) is an upper bound of \(A\) .

title: Theorem 1.7.1 (Nested Interval Theorem)
page: 1.7 Nested Intervals and the Uncountability of the Reals
content: For each \(n \ge 1\) , let \(I_n = [a_n, b_n]\) be a closed bounded interval with \(a_n \le b_n\) , and suppose the family is nested: \(I_{n+1} \subseteq I_n\) for every \(n \ge 1\) . Then \(\bigcap_{n \ge 1} I_n \ne \emptyset\) . More precisely, \(\alpha \coloneqq \sup \{ a_n : n \ge 1 \}\) exists and lies in every \(I_n\) . If moreover for every \(\varepsilon > 0\) there is \(n \ge 1\) with \(b_n - a_n < \varepsilon\) , then \(\bigcap_{n \ge 1} I_n = \{ \alpha \}\) .
